farraa:213-213.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَا ٱخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ مِن بَعْدِ مَا جَآءَتْهُمُ ٱلْبَيِّنَاتُ بَغْياً بَيْنَهُمْ فَهَدَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ لِمَا ٱخْتَلَفُواْ فِيهِ مِنَ ٱلْحَقِّ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ — it carries two meanings. One is that you take their disagreement to be some of them disbelieving in the Book of others; ﴿فَهَدَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾ to belief in all that was sent down, and it is the truth. The other interpretation is that you take their disagreement to refer to alteration, as the Torah was altered. Then He said ﴿فَهَدَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾ by it to the truth in that over which they disagreed. And it is permissible for the lām to belong to the disagreement and the min to the truth [Translator's note: i.e. the prepositions are construed with the words in an inverted order: "guided them to the truth of that over which they disagreed"], just as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ومثل الذِين كفروا كمثلِ الذِى ينعِق﴾, and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is "like the likeness of that which is shouted at," because He described them, saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿صُمّ بكم عمى﴾, like the beasts. And the poet said:
كانت فريضةَ ما تقول كما * كان الزِناءُ فريضةَ الرجمِ
(What you say was an obligation, just as fornication was the obligation of stoning.)
whereas in fact stoning is the obligation of fornication. And he said:
إن سِراجا لكريم مفخره * تَحْلَى بِه العَيْنُ إذا ما تَجْهَرُهْ
(Sirāj is noble in his glory; the eye delights in him when it beholds him.)
yet it is not the eye that is delighted; rather Sirāj is delighted in by it, because you say: ḥalīta bi-ʿaynī ("you were pleasing to my eye"), and you do not say: ḥaliyat ʿaynī bika ("my eye was pleased with you") except in poetry.

farraa:91-91.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيَكْفُرونَ بِمَا وَرَآءَهُ﴾ means "what is other than it". This is common in Arabic: a man speaks fine words and the listener says, "There is nothing behind (warāʾ) these words", i.e. he has nothing besides them.
His saying: ﴿فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ أَنْبِيَآءَ ٱللَّهِ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ — someone may say: "تقتلون" is for the future, so how can He say "مِن قَبْلُ" (before)? We do not allow in speech "I will strike you yesterday". It is permissible, however, when by "tafʿalūn" (the imperfect) you mean the past. Do you not see that you rebuke a man for what he has already done, saying: "Woe to you, why do you lie! Why do you make yourself hateful to people!" Similar is the saying of Allah: ﴿وَاتَّبَعْوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾, and He did not say "ما تَلَت الشياطين" (what the devils recited). This is genuine Arabic, common in speech. One of the Arabs recited to me:
إذا ما انتَسَبْنا لم تَلِدْنى لئِيمةٌ * ولم تَجِدِى مِن أَنْ تُقِرِّى بها بُدَّا
(When we trace our lineage, no base woman gave birth to me, and you will find no escape from acknowledging it.)
The conditional (jazāʾ) is for the future, yet the birth has entirely passed; that is because the meaning is known. Similar in speech is: "If you look into the conduct of ʿUmar, may Allah have mercy on him, he does not do wrong (lam yusiʾ)", meaning: you will not find that he did wrong. Since there is no doubt that ʿUmar's affair has passed, it does not occur to the mind that it is future; for that reason "مِنْ قَبْلُ" is sound together with His saying ﴿فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ أَنْبِيَآءَ ٱللَّهِ مِن قَبْلُ﴾. Those addressed about the killing were not themselves the killers; rather, their forebears who had passed away killed the prophets, and they took them as allies in that and were pleased with it, so the killing was attributed to them.

farraa:93-93.t:
His saying: ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾ means: we heard your word and disobeyed your command.
His saying: ﴿وَأُشْرِبُواْ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلْعِجْلَ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ — He meant "the love of the calf". Omissions like this are frequent among the Arabs. Allah said: ﴿واسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الّتِى كُنَّا فِيهَا والْعِيرَ الّتى أَقْبَلْنَا فِيهَا﴾, and the meaning is: ask the people of the town and the people of the caravan. Al-Mufaḍḍal recited to me:
حَسِبْتَ بُغَامَ راحِلَتى عَنَاقاً * وما هِىَ وَيْبَ غَيْرِك بالَعَنَاقِ
(You took the soft cry of my riding camel for a young she-goat — and she is not, woe to someone other than you, a young she-goat.)
Its meaning is: "the cry of a young she-goat". Similar from the Book of Allah: ﴿ولكِنّ البِرَّ مَنْ آمنَ باللَّه﴾, whose meaning — and Allah knows best — is: but righteousness is the righteousness of one who does these deeds which Allah described. The Arabs may say: "If it pleases you to look at generosity, look at Harim or at Ḥātim."
One of them recited to me:
يَقُولون جاهِدْ يا جَمِيلُ بغَزْوَةٍ * وإنّ جِهاداً طَىِّءٌ وقِتالُها
(They say: "Strive, O Jamīl, in a raid" — but striving is [against] Ṭayyiʾ and fighting them.)
Mentioning the name suffices for its deed when [the person] is known for generosity or courage and the like.

farraa:94-94.t: His saying: ﴿قُلْ إِن كَانَتْ لَكُمُ ٱلدَّارُ ٱلآخِرَةُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَالِصَةً مِّن دُونِ ٱلنَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلْمَوْتَ﴾ — He is saying: if the matter is as you say, that none enters Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian, ﴿فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلْمَوْتَ إِن كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ﴾; and they refused. That is because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one says it but that he will choke on his saliva." Then He described them, saying: ﴿وَلَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ عَلَى حَيَاةٍ وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾, whose meaning — and Allah knows best — is: and more eager for life than those who associate partners. Similar is your saying: "This is the most generous of people, and than Harim", because the interpretation of the first is "more generous than people and than Harim". Then He described the Magians, saying: ﴿يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمْ لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ﴾; that is because their greeting among themselves is (زِهْ هَزَارْ سَالْ), whose interpretation is: "Live a thousand years."

farraa:97-97.t: As for His saying: ﴿قُلْ مَن كَانَ عَدُوّاً لِّجِبْرِيلَ فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ [meaning the Qurʾān] ﴿عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾ — [this is a command] which Allah commanded Muḥammad ﷺ with, saying: Say to them, when they said "Jibrīl is our enemy" and Allah informed him of that; so He said: ﴿قُلْ مَن كَانَ عَدُوّاً لِّجِبْرِيلَ فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ﴾, meaning the heart of Muḥammad ﷺ. Had it been "على قلبى" (upon my heart) in this place, meaning Muḥammad ﷺ, it would have been correct. Similar in speech: "Do not say to the people that the good is with me" — and "with you": as for "with you", it is permissible because it is like an address; as for "with me", it is the speaker's own words. This comes from the interpretation of His saying "سَتُغْلَبُونَ" and "سَيُغْلَبُونَ", with tāʾ and with yāʾ.

farraa:102-102.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّبَعُواْ مَا تَتْلُواْ ٱلشَّيَاطِينُ عَلَىٰ مُلْكِ سُلَيْمَانَ وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ﴾ (as you would say "في ملك سليمان", in the reign of Sulaymān). "في" and "على" are both sound in a place like this; you say "I came to him in the time of Sulaymān" and "upon his time" alike.
His saying: ﴿وَمَآ أُنْزِلَ عَلَى ٱلْمَلَكَيْنِ﴾ — al-Farrāʾ read "الملَكَين", from the angels [Translator's note: the text reads "الفرّاء يقرءون" ("al-Farrāʾ read" with a plural verb); it is most likely a corruption of "القرّاء يقرءون", "the Readers read"]. Ibn ʿAbbās used to say "الملِكين", from the kings.
His saying: ﴿فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ مِنْهُمَا مَا يُفَرِّقُونَ بِهِ﴾ — as for sorcery, it is of the work of the devils; and they learn from the two angels words which, when said, a man is bound by them [made impotent] from his wife. Then He said: and of the saying of the two angels when that is learned from them is: "Do not disbelieve."
﴿إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلاَ تَكْفُرْ، فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ﴾ — [فيتعلمون] is not an answer to His saying ﴿وَمَا يُعَلِّمَانِ﴾; it is rather referred back to His saying ﴿يُعَلِّمُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ ٱلسِّحْرَ﴾ ... so they learn what harms them and does not benefit them; this is one view. And "فَيَتعلَّمُونَ" may be connected to His saying ﴿إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ﴾: so they refuse, and learn what harms them; and this seems the better of the two views in Arabic. And Allah knows best.
His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمُواْ لَمَنِ ٱشْتَرَاهُ﴾ — ﴿مَنْ﴾ is in the position of the nominative (rafʿ), and it is conditional (jazāʾ). For when the Arabs introduce this lām onto the conditional, they put its verb in the form faʿala (the past), and they hardly ever put it in the form yafʿalu (the imperfect), disliking that something should come upon the conditional while it is jussive. Do you not see that they say "Ask about whatever you wished (shiʾta)", and you say "I will not come to you as long as you lived (ʿishta)", and they do not say "mā taʿish"? For "ما" has the sense of a conditional and what precedes it has acted upon it, so they turned the verb to faʿala, because the jussive (jazm) does not show on faʿala. Thus they made the occurrence of the lām — even though it does not govern anything — like what does govern. Then they made the answer of the conditional the same as that with which an oath is met — he means: with which it is taken up — either with lām, or with "لا", or with "إنّ", or with "ما". So you say with "ما": "لئن أتيتنى ما ذلك لك بضائع" (If you come to me, that will not be lost to you); with "إنّ": "لئن أتيتنى إنّ ذلك لمشكور لك" (If you come to me, that will surely be appreciated of you) — al-Farrāʾ said: "لئن" is written only with yāʾ, to distinguish it from "لأن" — with "لا": "لَئِنْ أُخْرِجُوا لاَ يَخْرُجُونَ مَعَهُمْ"; and with the lām: ﴿وَلَئِنْ نَصَرُوهُمْ لَيُوَلُّنَّ الأَدْبَارَ﴾. They made the answer of the conditional like the answer of an oath only because the lām which entered His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمُواْ لَمَنِ ٱشْتَرَاهُ﴾, His saying ﴿لَمَا آتَيْتُكُمْ مِنْ كِتَابٍ وَحِكْمَةٍ﴾ and His saying ﴿لَئِنْ أُخْرِجُوا﴾ is the lām of the oath. Its place was at the end of the sentence; when it came to be at its beginning, it became like the oath, so it was met with what an oath is met with. If you put the verb after it overtly in the form yafʿalu, that is permissible and you make it jussive, saying: "لئن تقم لا يقم إليك" (If you stand, he will not stand up to you). The poet said:
لَئِنْ تَكُ قد ضاقتْ عليكم بُيوتُكُمْ * لَيَعْلَمُ ربِّى أنّ بَيْتِى واسِعُ
(If your houses have become too narrow for you, my Lord surely knows that my house is wide.)
One of Banū ʿUqayl recited to me:
لئِن كان ما حُدِّثْتَهُ اليومَ صادِقاً * أَصُمْ فى نهارِ الْقَيْظِ لِلشَّمسِ بادِيَا
وأَرْكَبْ حِماراً بين سَرْجٍ وفَرْوَةٍ * وأُعْرِ مِن الخاتامِ صُغْرَى شِمالِيَا
(If what you were told today is true, I will fast on a summer's day exposed to the sun, ride a donkey between a saddle and a fur, and strip the ring from the little finger of my left hand.)
So he dropped the oath-answer [form] from the verb, whereas the proper way in speech would be to say "لئن كان كذا لآتينك" (If such is the case, I will surely come to you); he imagined the lām to be cancelled, as the other said:
فَلاَ يَدْعُنِى قَوْمِى صَرِيحاً لُحِرَّةٍ * لئنْ كُنتُ مقتولاً ويَسْلَمُ عامِرُ
(Then let my people not call me the pure-born son of a free woman, if I am to be killed while ʿĀmir stays safe.)
The lām in "لئن" is cancelled (mulghāh), but it became so frequent in speech that it took the status of "إِنْ". Do you not see that the poet said:
فَلئِنْ قومٌ أصابُوا غِرَّةً * وأَصَبْنا من زمانٍ رَقَقَا
لَلَقدْ كانوا لَدَى أزمانِنَا * لِصَنِيعين لِبَأْسٍ وتُقَى
(If a people have caught [us] off guard, and we have met with thinness [hardship] from the times, they were indeed, in our days, made for two things: valour and piety.)
So he put another lām on "لَقَد", because the Arabs so constantly attach the lām to "لَقَد" that it became as if part of it. One of Banū Asad recited to me:
لَدَدْتُهُمُ النَّصِيحةَ كلَّ لَدٍّ * فَمَجُّوا النُّصْح ثم ثَنَوْا فقَاءُوا
فَلاَ واللّهِ لا يُلْفَى لِمَا بِى * ولا لِلِمَا بِهِم أبداً دَواءُ
(I poured good counsel into them in every way, but they spat the counsel out, then did it again and vomited. No, by Allah, no cure will ever be found for what is in me, nor for what is in them.)
Similar is the poet's saying:
كَمَا ما امرؤٌ فى مَعْشَرٍ غيرِ رَهْطِهِ * ضَعيفُ الكلامِ شَخْصُهُ مُتضائِلُ
(Just as a man among a company not his own kin is weak of speech, his person shrunken.)
He said "كما" and then added another "ما" to it, because "كما" is so frequent in speech that it became as if part of it. Al-Aʿshā said:
لَئِنْ مُنِيتَ بِنا عن غِبِّ مَعْرَكةٍ * لا تُلْفِنَا مِن دِماءِ القومِ نَنْتَفِلُ
(If you are put to the test by us after a battle, you will not find us disowning the blood of the people.)
He made "لا تلفِنا" jussive, whereas the proper form is the nominative, as Allah said: ﴿لَئِنْ أُخْرِجُوا لاَ يَخْرُجُونَ مَعَهُمْ﴾; but since it came after a particle by which the jussive is intended, it was made jussive as an answer to the jussive, while it has the sense of the nominative. Al-Qāsim ibn Maʿn recited to me (from the Arabs):
حَلَفْتُ له إِنْ تُدْلِجِ اللَّيْلَ لا يَزَلْ * أَمَامكَ بيتٌ مِنْ بُيوتِى سائِرُ
(I swore to him: if you travel by night, a house of my houses will not cease to move ahead of you.)
The meaning is: I swore to him that a house would not cease to be ahead of you; but since it came after the jussive, it was made an answer to the jussive. Similar in Arabic: "I will come to you so that (kay) — (if you tell me a story, I will hear it from you; since it came after the jussive, it was made jussive)."

farraa:214-214.t:
His saying: ﴿أَمْ حَسِبْتُمْ﴾ — He asks a question with am at the beginning, with no alif [Translator's note: the interrogative hamza] before it to which am would be a counterpart. This is among the things I told you are permissible when there is speech before it to which it connects. But if it were a beginning with no speech before it — as when you say to a man: "Do you have something good (aʿindaka khayr)?" — it would not be permissible here to say: "Am ʿindaka khayr?"
But if you said: "You are a man who does not act fairly — or do you have some authority you presume upon (am laka sulṭān tudillu bihi)?", that would be permissible, since speech preceded it and it connected to it.
His saying: ﴿أَن تَدْخُلُواْ ٱلْجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَأْتِكُم مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ خَلَوْاْ مِن قَبْلِكُم﴾ [its meaning: Did you think that you would enter Paradise without there befalling you the like of what befell those before you] so that you are tried? Similar to it is: ﴿أم حسِبتم أن تدخلوا الجنة ولَمّا يعلمِ الله الذِين جاهدوا مِنكم ويَعْلَمَ الصابِرين﴾, and likewise in al-Tawba: ﴿أَمْ حسِبتم أن تُتْرَكُوا ولَمّا يَعْلَمِ الله الذِين جاهدوا منكم﴾.
His saying: ﴿ وَزُلْزِلُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَقُولَ ٱلرَّسُولُ﴾ — the Readers read it in the accusative (naṣb), except Mujāhid and some of the people of Medina, for they read it in the nominative (rafʿ).
It has two possibilities in Arabic: accusative and nominative. As for the accusative, it is because the verb before it is of the kind that is drawn out, like repetition. When the verb has that meaning, what follows ḥattā is put in the accusative, even though it is past in meaning. When the verb before ḥattā is not drawn out and is past, the verb after ḥattā is put in the nominative if it is past.
As for the verb that is drawn out and is past, it is like your saying: "So-and-so kept gazing until he recognized you (ḥattā yaʿrifaka)"; do you not see that continued gazing lasts long? So when what precedes ḥattā is lengthy, what follows it is taken to the accusative, if it is past, because of its being drawn out. He said: al-Mufaḍḍal [one of the Arabs] recited to me:
مَطَوتُ بهم حتَّى تَكِلّ غُزَاتهم * وحتّى الجِيادُ ما يُقَدْنَ بأَرسان
(I pressed on with them by night until their raiders grew weary, and until the steeds no longer needed to be led by halters.)
So he put (تكِلّ) in the accusative while the verb that led to it before ḥattā is past, because travelling hard with camels is drawn out until they grow weary of it. What shows you that it is past is that you can say: "I pressed on with them until their raiders grew weary (kallat)."
So by whether faʿala (the past form) sits well in place of yafʿalu you distinguish the past from the future. Faʿala does not sit well in place of the future; do you not see that you do not say: "I will beat Zayd until he confessed (aqarra)," because you mean: until that comes from him?
Mujāhid read it in the nominative only because faʿala sits well in speech like it, as when you say: "They were shaken until the Messenger said (qāla)." Al-Kisāʾī read it in the nominative for a long time, then went back to the accusative. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is: "وزلزِلوا ثم زلزِلوا ويقول الرسول" ("they were shaken, then shaken again, and the Messenger says"), and that is evidence for the meaning of the accusative.
Ḥattā has three meanings with yafʿalu and three meanings with nouns.
If you see a past verb faʿala before it and yafʿalu after it with a past meaning, and what precedes (ḥattā yafʿalu) is not lengthy, then put the yafʿalu after it in the nominative, as when you say: "I came until I am (akūnu) near you." Most grammarians used to put the verb after ḥattā in the accusative, even if it was past, when it belonged to someone other than the first [subject]; they say: "I travelled until Zayd enters it (ḥattā yadkhulahā Zaydun)." But al-Kisāʾī claimed that he heard the Arabs say: "We travelled until the sun rises (taṭluʿu) for us at Zubāla," in the nominative, while the verb belongs to the sun; and he heard: "We were sitting, and we did not notice until a stone falls (yasquṭu) among us," in the nominative. He said: al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
وقد خُضْن الهَجِير وعُمْن حتى * يفرّج ذاك عنهنّ المَسَاءُ
(They waded through the midday heat and swam through it until the evening relieves them of that.)
And he recited (the saying of another):
ونُنكِر يوم الروع ألوانَ خيلِنا * من الطعن حتى نحسب الجَوْن أشقرا
(On the day of terror we fail to recognize the colours of our horses, from the spearing, until we reckon the black one to be sorrel.)
Here he used the accusative because not recognizing is drawn out. This is the second type in the chapter on ḥattā.
That is, when what precedes ḥattā and what follows it are both past, and both are of the kind that is drawn out, so that yafʿalu in it, while past in meaning, is better than faʿala; so he used the accusative although it is past, because yafʿalu sits well in it. Al-Kisāʾī said: I heard the Arabs say: "The camel grows so old that it comes to (ḥattā yajʿala), when it drinks water, spit it out." That is something that has passed, yet (يجعل) is better in it than (جعل). It is better only because it is a description applying to the individual in the sense of the collective; its meaning is: this happens often among camels.
Similar to it: "The man grows so haughty that he passes by (ḥattā yamurra) and does not greet people." You put (يمرّ) in the accusative because yafʿalu sits well in it although it is past. And Abū Tharwān recited to me:
أحِبّ لِحبّها السودان حتى * أحِبَّ لحبّها سُودَ الكلابِ
(For love of her I love black people, so much that for love of her I love black dogs.)
Had he put it in the nominative because of its past meaning, it would have been correct; indeed some of Banū Asad recited it to me in the nominative. When you insert lā into it, the nominative and the accusative become equal in it, as when you say: "The man befriends you until he does not hide (ḥattā lā yaktumuka) a secret from you" — you use the nominative because of the insertion of lā when the meaning is past, and the accusative with the insertion of lā is permissible.
Similar to it is what is read in the nominative and the accusative when lā is inserted, in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿وحسِبوا ألاّ تكون فِتنة﴾, in the nominative and the accusative. And similar to it: "أَفَلاَ يَرَوْنَ أَلاَّ يَرْجِعَ إليهِم قولا ولا يَمْلِك لهم ضُرّا ولا نفعا" — both are put in the accusative and the nominative; but if you drop lā from it they do not say it except in the accusative. That is because laysa is suitable in place of lā for those who use the nominative with ḥattā and for those who use the nominative with an; do you not see that you say: "He befriends you so that he no longer (ḥattā laysa) hides anything from you," and you say with an: "I thought that you are not (an lasta) going, so I stayed behind." Every place where laysa sits well in place of lā, treat it this way: the nominative at one time and the accusative at another. And if the verb after an were put in the nominative without lā, it would be correct, as when you say: "I thought that you say (an taqūlu) that," because the hāʾ [Translator's note: the pronoun of the matter] sits well with an, so you say: "I thought that he says (annahu yaqūlu) that." And al-Qāsim ibn Maʿn recited to me:
إنى زَعيم يا نُوَيْـ * قَةُ إن نَجوتِ مِن الزَوَاحِ
وسلِمتِ مِن عَرضِ الحُتُو * فِ مِن الغُدوّ إِلِى الرواحِ
أن تهبِطين بِلاد قو * م يَرتَعُون مِن الطِلاحِ
(I guarantee, O little she-camel, if you escape from departing and are safe from the deaths that present themselves from morning till evening, that you will descend to the land of a people who graze on the ṭalḥ trees.)
So he used the nominative in (أن تهبِطين) and did not say: an tahbiṭī.
When lā is such that laysa is not suitable in its place, neither with ḥattā nor with an, there is only the accusative, as in your saying: "I will not cease until I do not leave (ḥattā lā uḥkima) your affair unsettled." [Translator's note: the text reads lā aḥkumu/uḥkimu amraka; translated as written.] And similar to it with an: "I wanted you not to say (an lā taqūla) that." The nominative is not permissible here.
The third type of yafʿalu with ḥattā is that what follows ḥattā is future — and do not mind what the thing before it was like — so you use the accusative, as in the saying of Allah, Majestic and Mighty: ﴿لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عليهِ عاكِفين حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلينا مُوسى﴾ and ﴿فَلَنْ أَبْرَحَ الأَرْضَ حَتَّى يَأْذَنَ لِى أبِى﴾, and this is frequent in the Qurʾān.
As for the three types with nouns: you see after ḥattā a noun, and there is nothing before it matching it onto which what follows ḥattā could be conjoined; or you see after it a noun with nothing before it.
The word after ḥattā is in the genitive (makhfūḍ) in both cases. Of this is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿تَمَتَّعُوا حتى حِينٍ﴾ and ﴿سَلاَمٌ هِىَ حَتَّى مَطْلعِ الفجر﴾ — they can only be genitive, because there is no noun before them onto which what follows ḥattā could be conjoined, so ḥattā is taken in the sense of ilā ("up to"). The Arabs say: "I guarantee it until Wednesday or Thursday (ḥattā al-arbiʿāʾi aw al-khamīsi)," in the genitive and nothing else, and "I guarantee the people until Wednesday." The meaning is: that I guarantee the people on Wednesday, because Wednesday is one of the days and does not match "the people" so as to be conjoined onto them.
The second type is that what precedes ḥattā among nouns is a large number, and then after that comes the single noun or a few nouns. If it is so, look at what follows ḥattā: if the nouns after it have been affected by the same genitive, nominative or accusative that affected what precedes ḥattā, then two possibilities are in it: the genitive, and following (itbāʿ) what precedes ḥattā. Of that: "The people were beaten, even their elder (ḥattā kabīruhum)," and "ḥattā kabīrihim"; and he is the one acted upon — in both cases the beating struck him.
That is because ilā can sit well both with what the action has reached and with what it has not reached. Of that is your saying: "Free your slaves up to (ḥattā) the most honoured of them to you," meaning: and free the most honoured of them to you. This is among the cases where ilā sits well and the action has reached it. And you say, regarding a case where it does not sit well that the action reaches what follows ḥattā: "The days are all fasted up to (ḥattā) the day of the Fiṭr and the days of Tashrīq," meaning that one abstains from [fasting] these days, so they are not fasted; and ilā sits well in it.
The third type is that what follows ḥattā is not affected by anything of what affected what precedes ḥattā; that is genitive, and nothing else is permissible, as when you say: "He fasts the day until the night (ḥattā al-layli)" — al-layl can only be genitive — and "I ate the fish up to its head (ḥattā raʾsihā)": if the head was not eaten, it can only be genitive.
As for the poet's saying:
فيا عجبا حتى كُلَيْب تَسُبُّنِى * كأَنّ أباها نَهْشَل أو مُجاشِع
(How amazing! Even Kulayb insults me, as if its father were Nahshal or Mujāshiʿ.)
the nominative in it is good even though there is no noun before it, because the nouns that are fit to come alone after ḥattā come only from times, as when you say: "Stay until the night (ḥattā al-layli)." You do not say: "Beat until Zayd (ḥattā Zaydin)," because he is not a time; therefore isolating Zayd and the like does not sit well, so it is put in the nominative by its verb, as if he had said: "How amazing! Do the base insult me, until even a Kulaybī insults me?" It is as though he conjoined it onto implied nouns before it. Those who used the genitive imagined in Kulayb what they imagine in times, and made the verb as if resumed after Kulayb, as though he had said: "The matter has brought me as far as Kulayb," then paused, and then said: "insults me."

farraa:104-104.t:
His saying: ﴿يَاأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ لاَ تَقُولُواْ رَاعِنَا وَقُولُواْ ٱنْظُرْنَا﴾ — it is from al-irʿāʾ and al-murāʿāh (heeding, giving attention). (In) the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "لاَ تَقُولُوا راعُونَا". That is because it was a word of abuse in the language of the Jews. When the Jews heard the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ saying "O Prophet of Allah, rāʿinā", they seized the opportunity and said: "We used to revile him in ourselves; now it has become possible for us to show him the abuse openly." So they began saying to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "rāʿinā", laughing to one another. A man of the Anṣār perceived it and said to them: "By Allah, no man speaks it but that I will strike off his neck." So Allah revealed ﴿لاَ تَقُولُواْ رَاعِنَا﴾, forbidding the Muslims from it, since it was abuse among the Jews. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read it "لاَ تَقُولُوا رَاعِناً" with tanwīn (nunation), meaning: do not say folly (ḥumq); and he puts it in the accusative by "saying", as you say "they said good" and "they said evil".
His saying: ﴿وَقُولُواْ ٱنْظُرْنَا﴾ means: wait for us. And (أَنْظِرنا) means: grant us respite. (Allah said): ﴿[قَالَ] أَنْظِرْنِى إِلَى يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾, meaning: grant me respite. And in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd: ﴿[يَوْمَ يَقُولُ المُنَافِقُونَ وَالْمنافِقَاتُ] لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا انْظُرُونَا نَقْتَبِسْ مِنْ نُورِكُمْ﴾, with a light (connective) alif, in the sense of waiting. Ḥamza al-Zayyāt read it "لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْظِرُونَا", in the sense of granting respite.

farraa:105-105.t: His saying: ﴿مَّا يَوَدُّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مِنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَابِ وَلاَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ — its meaning is: "and of the polytheists". Had it been "المشركون" in the nominative, referred back to "الّذِينَ كَفَروا", it would have been correct [you would mean: neither those who disbelieve nor the polytheists wish]. Similar to it in al-Māʾida: ﴿[يَأَيُّهَا الّذِينَ آمَنُوا لاَ تَتَّخِذُوا الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا دِينَكُمْ هُزُواً وَلَعِباً] مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتَابَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ وَالْكُفَّارَ أَوْلِيَاءَ﴾; it was read both ways: [والكفارِ and والكفارَ], and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "ومِن الكفّارِ أولِياء". Likewise His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is in the position of the genitive (khafḍ), [conjoined] onto His saying ﴿مِن أَهلِ الكِتابِ﴾: "and of the polytheists"; had it been nominative it would have been correct, referred back to "الذين كفروا".

farraa:106-106.t: His saying: ﴿مَا نَنسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنسِهَا﴾ (أَوْ نُنْسِئْهَا — أَوْ نُنْسِهَا): most of the Readers take it from forgetting (nisyān). In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "مَانُنْسِكَ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نَنْسَخْها نَجِئْ بِمِثْلها أَوْ خَيْرٍ مِنها", and in the reading of Sālim, the client of Abū Ḥudhayfa: "مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنْسِكَهَا"; this strengthens [the sense of] forgetting. Abrogation (naskh) is that a verse is acted upon, then another is revealed and acted upon, and the first is left. Nisyān here has two senses. One is leaving: We leave it and do not abrogate it, as Allah, exalted be His mention, said: ﴿نسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ﴾, meaning they left Him so He left them. The other sense is from the forgetting by which one forgets, as Allah said: ﴿وَاذْكُرْ رَبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ﴾. Some used to read "أَوْ نَنْسَأْهَا" with a hamza, meaning "We postpone it", from al-nasīʾa (deferment); and all are good. Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Qays narrated to me from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, with a chain raising it to the Prophet ﷺ, that he heard a man reciting and said: "May Allah have mercy on this one; he has reminded me of verses I had been made to forget."

farraa:108-108.t:
His saying: ﴿أَمْ تُرِيدُونَ أَن تَسْأَلُواْ رَسُولَكُمْ﴾ — (أَمْ) (in meaning) is a return upon a question in two ways. One of them is that it separates [alternatives] with the sense of "أىّ" (which?); the other is that a question is asked by it. [The first] is by way of conjunction (nasaq); and [in the second] what is intended by it is a fresh start (ibtidāʾ), except that it is a fresh start connected to speech. If you began speech with nothing before it and then asked a question, it could only be with the alif or with "هل". Of this is the saying of Allah: ﴿الم تَنْزِيلُ الْكِتَابِ لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ مِنْ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ. أَمْ يَقُولُونَ افْتَرَاهُ﴾: "أَمْ" came with no question before it, and this is proof that it is a question begun upon speech which preceded it. As for His saying ﴿أَمْ تُرِيدُونَ أَن تَسْأَلُواْ رَسُولَكُمْ﴾, if you wish you may take it like this, and if you wish you may say: there is a question before it and it is returned onto it, namely the saying of Allah: ﴿أَلَمْ تَعْلَمْ أَنَّ اللّهَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدِيرَ﴾. Likewise His saying: ﴿مَالَنَا لاَنَرَى رِجَالاً كُنّا نَعُدُّهُم مِّنَ الأَشْرَارِ. اتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ سِخْرِيًّا أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ الأَبْصَارُ﴾: if you wish you may make it a question begun, preceded by speech, and if you wish you may make it referred back to His saying ﴿مَالَنَا لاَ نَرَى رِجَالاً﴾. Some of the Readers read "أَتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ سخْرِيّاً", asking a question in "أَتَّخَذْناهُمْ سِخْرِيّاً" with a disjunctive alif (hamzat al-qaṭʿ), so that "أَمْ" may be conjoined to it, because it mostly comes with the alif; and all is correct. Similar to it: ﴿أَلَيْسَ لِى مُلْكُ مِصْرَ وَهَذِهِ الأَنْهَارُ تَجْرِى مِنْ تَحْتِى﴾, then He said: ﴿أَمْ أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِنْ هَذَا﴾; the explanation of both is one. Sometimes the Arabs, when "أَمْ" is preceded by a question in which "أىّ" is not suitable, make it in the sense of "بل" (rather); they say: "Do you have a right against us, or (am) are you a man known for injustice?", meaning: rather, you are a man known for injustice. The poet said:
فَوَاللّهِ ما أدْرِى أَسَلْمَى تَغَوّلَتْ * أَمِ النَّوْمُ أَمْ كُلٌّ إِلَىّ حَبِيبٌ
(By Allah, I do not know: did Salmā take on changing shapes, or was it sleep — or rather, each is dear to me.)
Its meaning is: [rather, each is dear to me].
The Arabs do the same with "أَوْ": they make it a conjunction separating, with the meaning of that in which "أحد" (one) and "إحدى" are suitable, as when you say "Strike one of the two, Zayd or ʿAmr". When it occurs in speech in which "one of" is not meant, even if suitable, they make it in the sense of "بل", as you say in speech: "Go to so-and-so — or (aw) leave that and do not budge today." This shows you that the man has gone back on his first command, and he made "أو" in the sense of "بل". Of this is the saying of Allah: ﴿وَأَرْسَلْنَاهُ إِلَى مِائَةِ أَلْفٍ أَوْ يَزِيدُونَ﴾. One of the Arabs recited to me:
بَدَتْ مِثْلَ قَرْنِ الشّمسِ فى رَوْنَقِ الضُّحى * وصُورَتـِها أَوْ أَنْتِ فى الْعَيْنِ أَمْلَحُ
(She appeared like the rim of the sun in the brightness of forenoon and in its form — or rather, you are lovelier to the eye.)
He means: rather, you are.
His saying: ﴿فَقَدْ ضَلَّ سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ﴾ — "سواء" in this place is the straight course (qaṣd). "سواء" may also go in the direction of "غير" (other than), as when you say to a man: "I came to someone other than you (sawāʾaka)."

farraa:109-109.t:
His saying: ﴿كُفَّاراً﴾ — here the sentence ends. Then He said (حَسَداً) as an explanation; it is not put in the accusative as a naʿt (adjective) of "كفار". It is only like your saying to a man: "He wants evil for you out of envy and transgression."
His saying: ﴿مِّنْ عِنْدِ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ — on their own part; they were not commanded to it in their scriptures.

farraa:111-111.t: His saying: ﴿وَقَالُواْ لَن يَدْخُلَ ٱلْجَنَّةَ إِلاَّ مَن كَانَ هُوداً أَوْ نَصَارَىٰ﴾ — He means "Jewish" (yahūdiyyan); He dropped the extra yāʾ and returned to the verb from al-yahūdiyya. In the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh it is: "إِلاّ مَنْ كان يهودِيا أو نصرانِيّا". It may also be that you take "يهود" (hūd) as a plural whose singular is hāʾid (with a long vowel; it is like ḥāʾil, with a long vowel — of she-camels — and [its plural] ḥūl), and ʿāʾiṭ with [plurals] ʿūṭ, ʿīṭ and ʿūṭaṭ.

farraa:114-114.t:
His saying: ﴿أُوْلَـٰئِكَ مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلاَّ خَآئِفِينَ﴾ — these are the Byzantines (al-Rūm); they had raided Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), killed, burned and ruined the mosque. Allah gave the Muslims victory over them only in the time of ʿUmar, may Allah have mercy on him, and they rebuilt it; (and) the Byzantines did not enter it except in hiding — had they been known about, they would have been killed.
His saying: ﴿لَّهُمْ فِي ٱلدُّنْيَا خِزْيٌ﴾ — it is said that Allah gave the Muslims victory over their first city, so they killed their fighting men and took captive the children and women; that is the disgrace.
His saying: ﴿وَلَهُمْ فِي ٱلآخِرَةِ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ — He says [this] regarding what Allah promised the Muslims of the conquest of the Byzantines, which had not yet happened.

farraa:116-116.t: His saying: ﴿كُلٌّ لَّهُ قَانِتُونَ﴾ — He means "obedient"; and this is particular to the people of obedience, not general.

farraa:117-117.t:
His saying [Translator's note: the text reads "وقوبه", a slip for "وقوله"]: ﴿فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ﴾ — nominative (rafʿ); it cannot be accusative (naṣb). It is referred back to "يقول" [so He only says, and it is].
Likewise His saying ﴿وَيَوْمَ يَقُولُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ قَوْلُهُ الْحَقُّ﴾ is nominative and nothing else. As for the one in al-Naḥl: ﴿إِنَّمَا قَوْلُنَا لِشَىْءٍ إِذَا أَرَدْنَاهُ أَن نَّقُولَ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونَ﴾, it is accusative, and likewise the one in "Yā Sīn" is accusative, because it is referred back to a verb made accusative by "أن"; yet most of the Readers read both in the nominative. The nominative is correct; that is, you take the sentence as self-sufficient at His saying ﴿إِذَا أَرَدْنَاهُ أَن نَّقُولَ لَهُ كُنْ﴾ — the sentence is complete — then He said: so what Allah willed will be.
It is the dearer of the two views to me, even though al-Kisāʾī does not permit the nominative in them and goes for conjunction (nasaq).

farraa:118-118.t:
His saying: ﴿تَشَابَهَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ — He says: their hearts resembled one another in their agreement upon disbelief; so He made it a mutual resemblance. "تشّابهت" with doubling (tathqīl) is not permissible, because the entry of two extra tāʾs is not sound in tafāʿaltu or its like.
Assimilation (idghām) is permissible only when you say in the imperfect "تتشابه" (with the sense of [it will happen] shortly), so you assimilate the second tāʾ into the shīn.

farraa:119-119.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُسْأَلُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ ٱلْجَحِيمِ﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbās [and Abū Jaʿfar] Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn read it in the jussive (jazm), and some of the people of Medina read it in the jussive, and the exegesis came with that [except that the exegesis is] with the tāʾ vowelled with fatḥa, as a prohibition.
The Readers [since then] read it in the nominative as a statement: "and you are not asked". In the reading of Ubayy: "وما تُسألُ", and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "ولن تُسألَ"; both are witnesses for the nominative.

farraa:123-123.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يُقْبَلُ مِنْهَا عَدْلٌ﴾ — it is said: a ransom.

farraa:215-215.t:
His saying: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ — you make mā in the position of the accusative and have yunfiqūna act on it; you do not put it in the accusative by (يَسْألونك), because the meaning is: they ask you what thing they should spend. If you wish, you can make it nominative in two ways. One of them is that you make dhā a noun that puts mā in the nominative, as if you had said: "What is it that they spend (mā alladhī yunfiqūn)?"
The Arabs sometimes take hādhā and dhā in the sense of alladhī ("the one who"); they say: "And who is it that (man dhā) says that?" in the sense of: "Who is the one who (man alladhī) says that?" And they recited:
عَدَسْ ما لِعبّادٍ عليكِ إِمارة * أَمِنْتِ وهذا تحمِلين طَلِيق
(Hush, [mule]! ʿAbbād has no authority over you; you are safe, and this one you carry is free.)
as if he had said: "and the one whom you carry is free." The other nominative is that you make every interrogative on which you have a verb after it act be in the nominative, because the verb cannot be put before the interrogative; so they treated it like alladhī, since the verb coming after it does not govern it. Do you not see that you say: "The one whom you hit is your brother (alladhī ḍarabta akhūka)," so that alladhī is in the position of the nominative by al-akh, and the verb that follows it does not act on it?
If you intend that, you put His saying in the nominative: ﴿قلِ العفو كذلك﴾ [Translator's note: the text is quoted as written; the reading meant is «qul al-ʿafwu» in the nominative, as with ﴿قُلِ ٱلْعَفْوَ﴾ of 2:219], just as the poet said:
ألا تسأَلانِ المرء ماذا يُحاوِل * أَنَحْبٌ فَيُقْضَى أم ضَلالٌ وباطِل
(Will you two not ask a man what he is striving for: is it a vow to be fulfilled, or error and falsehood?)
He put naḥb in the nominative because he intended to make mā in the position of the nominative. Had he said: "a-naḥban fa-yuqḍā am ḍalālan wa-bāṭilā," it would have been clearer in the speech of the Arabs. Most of the Arabs say: "And which of them (ayyuhum) did I not hit," and "Which of them have I not hit (ayyuhum illā qad ḍarabtu)," in the nominative, for the reason of resumption (istiʾnāf) belonging to the interrogative particles, and that nothing precedes them.
Among what resembles the interrogative — what is put in the nominative when the verb that acts on it comes after it — is their saying: "All the people I hit (kullu al-nāsi ḍarabtu)." That is because in (كلّ) there is something like the meaning of "Is there anyone [but] I have hit?" and like the meaning of "Which man did I not hit?" and "Which town did I not enter?" Do you not see that when you say: "All the people I hit," it carries the meaning: "There is no one of them but I have hit him," and the meaning: "Which of them did I not hit?" And Abū Tharwān recited to me:
وقالوا تعرَّفْها المنازلَ ممن مِنىً * وما كُلُّ من يغشى مِنىً أنا عارف
(They said: Seek to know her [abode] among the halting-places of Minā; but I do not know everyone who comes to Minā.)
in the nominative, and I have not heard anyone put kull in the accusative. He said: and they recited to us:
وما كُلُّ مَنْ يَظَّنُّنِى أنا مُعتِب * وما كُلُّ ما يُرْوَى علىَّ أقول
(I do not appease everyone who suspects me, and I did not say all that is reported of me.)
Do not imagine that they put it in the nominative by the verb that preceded it [Translator's note: i.e. as the ism of mā or by an earlier verb], for they recited to us:
قد عَلِقَت أُمّ الخيار تدَّعى * علىَّ ذنبا كُلُّه لم أصنع
(Umm al-Khiyār has taken to claiming against me a sin, none of which I committed.)
in the nominative. And Abū al-Jarrāḥ recited to me:
أرَجَزا تريد أم قريضا * أم هكذا بينهما تعريضا * كلاهما أجِدُ مستريضا
(Is it rajaz you want, or qarīḍ verse, or something like this between the two as an allusion? Both of them I find ample.)
He put kilā in the nominative while after it comes (أجد), because the meaning is: there is neither one of them but I find it easy and ample.
What shows you that there is an implied negation in it is the poet's saying:
فكلهمُ جاشاك إلا وجدته * كعين الكذوب جهدها واحتفالها
(Every one of them — [Translator's note: the text reads جاشاك, apparently corrupt, perhaps حاشاك "save you"] — I found him only like the eye of a liar: all its effort and its show.)

farraa:217-217.t:
His saying: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلشَّهْرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍ فِيهِ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "عن قتال فيه" ("about fighting in it"), so he put it in the genitive on the intention of an implied (عن).
﴿قُلْ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ وَصَدٌّ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — in al-ṣadd ("barring") there are two possibilities. If you wish, you make it referred back to kabīr, meaning: Say: fighting in it is grave, and a barring from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him.
And if you wish, you make the barring [itself] grave, meaning: Say: fighting in it is grave; and grave is the barring from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him.
﴿وَٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾ is in the genitive by His saying: they ask you about fighting and about the Mosque.
Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وإِخراج أَهلِه﴾ — the people of the Mosque — ﴿مِنْهُ أَكْبَرُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ than fighting in the sacred month. Then He explained, Blessed and Exalted, and said: ﴿وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ﴾ — meaning idolatry (shirk) — is worse than fighting in it.

farraa:219-219.t: His saying: ﴿قُلِ ٱلْعَفْوَ﴾ — the proper way of the speech in it is the accusative, meaning: Say: they spend al-ʿafw. It is the surplus of wealth; the zakat [has] abrogated it. [You say: qad ʿafā.]

farraa:220-220.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلْيَتَامَىٰ﴾ — it is said of a boy: yatima yaytamu yutman and yatman ("to be orphaned"). He said: and yatama yaytimu was reported to me.
﴿وَإِنْ تُخَالِطُوهُمْ فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ﴾ — you put al-ikhwān in the nominative on the implied pronoun (fa-hum), as if you had said (fa-hum ikhwānukum, "then they are your brothers"). Had you put it in the accusative, it would be correct, meaning: then it is your brothers that you mix with. Similar to it: ﴿فإن لم تعلموا آباءهم فإخوانُكم فى الدِينِ وموالِيكم﴾, and [it would be possible] if you put it in the accusative here on an implied verb ("call them your brothers and your clients"). In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "إِن تغذِّبْهُمْ فعِبادُكَ" [Translator's note: so written, for تعذبهم], and in our reading: "فإنَّهم عبادك". Of this, only what is a noun with which huwa sits well along with the nominative is put in the nominative. If huwa does not sit well in it, you run it on what precedes it, saying: "If you buy food, then good (fa-jayyidan)," i.e. then buy the good; and "If you wear clothes, then white (fa-l-bayāḍa)" — you use the accusative because huwa does not sit well here. The meaning in these two here differs from the first; do you not see that you find the people to be brothers even if they are denied, but you do not find everything that is worn to be white, nor everything that is bought to be good? But if you intend that whatever he takes charge of buying is good, you use the nominative, when the man is known for good buying and for wearing white.
Likewise the saying of Allah: ﴿فإن خفتم فرِجالا﴾ is accusative, because it is something not permanent, and huwa is not suitable in it. Do you not see that the meaning is: if you fear to pray standing, then pray on foot (rijālan) or riding [rijālan meaning: rajjāla, on foot]? So the two are in the accusative because they are ḥāls (circumstantials) of the verb and are not fit to be a predicate.
﴿وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ ٱلْمُفْسِدَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِ﴾ — the meaning in similar speech is: Allah knows which of them corrupts and which of them sets right. Had you put ayy or man in place of the first, you would put it in the nominative, saying: "I know which of them stood (ayyuhum qāma) from the one sitting." [Al-Farrāʾ] said: I heard the Arabs say: "He does not know which from which (ayyun min ayyin)." That is because (أىّ) and (مَن) are interrogatives, and al-mufsid is a predicate. Similar to it: "I do not care whether you stand or sit (qiyāmaka aw quʿūdaka)"; if you put an interrogative in the speech, the verb's action on it is cancelled, so you say: "I do not care whether you are standing or sitting (a-qāʾimun anta am qāʿid)." And if you drop the interrogative, the verb connects to what precedes it, so it becomes accusative.
Every interrogative is cut off from what precedes it, because of its inherent nature of being begun with.
His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لأَعْنَتَكُمْ﴾ — it is said: the man ʿanita ʿanatan ("fell into hardship"), and Allah aʿnatahu iʿnātan ("brought him into hardship").

farraa:221-221.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَنْكِحُواْ ٱلْمُشْرِكَاتِ﴾ — He means: do not marry. The Readers are agreed on this. Had it been: wa-lā tunkiḥū al-mushrikāti, i.e. do not give them in marriage to the Muslims, it would have been correct. It is said: nakaḥahā nakḥan and nikāḥan.
His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أَعْجَبَتْكُمْ﴾ is like His saying: "even if (in) they please you." Law and in are close in meaning; for that reason it is permissible for law to be answered with the apodosis of in, and in with the apodosis of law, as in His saying: ﴿ولئن أَرْسَلْنا رِيحاً فَرأَوْه مُصْفَراً لظَلُّوا من بعدِه يَكْفُرون﴾. His saying "فرأَوه" — by the hāʾ He means the crops.

farraa:222-222.t:
His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَطْهُرْنَ﴾ with the yāʾ. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, if Allah wills, it is "يتطهرن" with the tāʾ. The Readers since then read "ḥattā yaṭhurna" and "yaṭṭahharna". [Yaṭhurna]: the blood stops for them; and yataṭahharna: they wash with water. The more preferred of the two to us is: yaṭṭahharna.
﴿فَأْتُوهُنَّ مِنْ حَيْثُ أَمَرَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ — He did not say: "fī ḥaythu" ("in where"), which is the private part. He said "مِنْ حَيْثُ" ("from where") only as you say to a man: "Come to Zayd from his approach," i.e. from the direction from which he is approached.
Had the private part been mentioned overtly and not alluded to, you would say in speech: "Come to the woman in her private part." ﴿فَأْتُوهُنَّ مِنْ حَيْثُ أَمَرَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ — it is said: come to the private part from wherever you wish.

farraa:223-223.t: His saying: ﴿فَأْتُواْ حَرْثَكُمْ أَنَّىٰ شِئْتُمْ﴾ [i.e.] however you wish. Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: a shaykh narrated to me from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbās: The Jews claim that if a man comes to his wife from behind her in her front passage, the child comes out cross-eyed. He said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: The Jews lied. ﴿نِسَآؤُكُمْ حَرْثٌ لَّكُمْ فَأْتُواْ حَرْثَكُمْ أَنَّىٰ شِئْتُمْ﴾ — He says: come to the private part from wherever you wish.

farraa:224-224.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَجْعَلُواْ ٱللَّهَ عُرْضَةً لأَيْمَانِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّواْ﴾ — He says: do not make swearing by Allah an obstructing barrier ﴿أَن تَبَرُّواْ وَتَتَّقُواْ وَتُصْلِحُواْ بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ﴾. He says: let none of you refrain from doing good because of an oath if he has sworn it; rather let him expiate his oath and do that which is better.

farraa:225-225.t: His saying: ﴿لاَّ يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِٱلَّلغْوِ فِيۤ أَيْمَانِكُمْ﴾ — there are two views on it. It is said: it is what runs in speech, such as their saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes indeed, by Allah." The other view: oaths are four. Two oaths carry expiation and seeking forgiveness: your saying "By Allah, I will not do it," and then you do it; and "By Allah, I will surely do it," and then you do not. In these two there is expiation and seeking forgiveness [because the act in them is future]. The two in which there is seeking forgiveness and no expiation are your saying: "By Allah, I did not do it," when you did; and your saying: "By Allah, I did do it," when you did not. These two are said to be laghw ("idle"), since there is no expiation in them. The first view — and it is the view of ʿĀʾisha: that laghw is what runs in speech without intent — is closer to the speech of the Arabs.

farraa:226-226.t:
His saying: ﴿تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾ — the waiting is attached to (in construct with) the four. The Readers are agreed on that. Had it been said in similar speech: "tarabbuṣun arbaʿata ashhurin" ("a waiting of four months," with the accusative), it would be correct, just as they read: "أو إِطعامٌ فى يومٍ ذِى مَسْغَبَةٍ يتيما ذا مقربة", and as He said: ﴿أَلَم نجعلِ الأَرْض كِفَاتاً أحياء وأمواتا﴾, the meaning being: it gathers them in, living and dead.
Had it been said in similar speech: "kifāta aḥyāʾin wa-amwātin" (in construct), it would be correct. And [it would be correct] had it been said: "tarabbuṣun: arbaʿatu ashhurin" (both nominative), as is said in speech: "Between me and you is a long journey: a month or two months" — you make the journey be the month, and the waiting be the four. Similar to it: ﴿فشهادةُ أَحدِهِم أَرْبَعُ شهادات﴾ and arbaʿa shahādāt (accusative). And similar to it: ﴿فجزاء مِثل ما قتل من النعم﴾ — whoever puts (مثل) in the nominative means: then his recompense is the like of what he killed. He said: and so I saw it in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh: "فجزاؤه" with the hāʾ. And whoever puts (مثل) in the accusative means: then it is upon him to recompense the like of what he killed of livestock.
﴿فإن فاءوا﴾ — it is said: fāʾū yafīʾūna fayʾan and fuyūʾan. Al-fayʾ is that he returns to his wife and has intercourse.

farraa:228-228.t: His saying: ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "بردتهن".

farraa:1-2.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿الۤمۤ ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ﴾. The spelled-out letters (al-hijāʾ) are pausal throughout the Qurʾān. This is not a jazm (jussive) that can properly be called jazm; it is only speech made quiescent by the intention of pausing on each of its letters. So treat all the spelled-out letters this way, whether few or many. The readers read "آلمَ اللهُ" in "Āl ʿImrān", giving the mīm a fatḥa, only because the mīm was quiescent through the intention of pausing on it; and when a letter is intended to be paused on, what follows it is intended as a fresh start, so the reading was "ا ل مَ اللهُ": the Arabs dropped the hamza of the alif of "الله", and its fatḥa passed to the mīm because the mīm was quiescent. Had the mīm been quiescent in a way that truly required quiescence, it would have been given a kasra, as in "قِيل ادخلِ الجنة". One of the grammarians — Abū Jaʿfar al-Ruʾāsī, who was a righteous man — read it ﴿الۤمۤ أَلله﴾, cutting off the alif [Translator's note: i.e. pronouncing the hamza], whereas the [Translator's note: accepted] reading drops the hamza. Al-Farrāʾ said: It has reached me that ʿĀṣim read it with the hamza cut off.

When the spelled-out letters come at the beginning of a surah and consist of a single letter, as in His words "ص", "ن" and "ق", there are two ways in Arabic. If you intend them as spelled-out letters, you leave them quiescent and write them as a single letter. If you make them a name for the surah, or treat them as an oath, you write them as they are spelled out — "نون", "صاد" and "قاف" — and give kasra to the dāl of صاد and the fāʾ of قاف, and fatḥa to the final nūn of "نون", saying: "نونَ والقلم", "صادِ والقرآن" and "قافِ", because it has become like a particle (adāt), just as they said رجلانِ, giving kasra to the nūn of رجلانِ because an alif precedes it, and fatḥa to the nūn in "المسلمونَ" and "المسلمينَ" because a yāʾ and a wāw precede it.

Do the same with "ياسينَْ والقرآن": you may give the nūn of "ياسين" a fatḥa or leave it quiescent.

Likewise "حم" and "طس". But this is not permissible in anything longer than these letters, such as "طا سين ميم", because they do not resemble nouns, while "طس" resembles قابيل (Qābīl). Nor is this permissible in anything of the Qurʾān such as "الم", "المر" and the like.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ﴾. (ذَلِكَ) is appropriate here in two respects, and "هذا" would be appropriate in one respect. One of the two respects of "ذلك" is the meaning: These letters, O Aḥmad, are that Book which I promised you I would reveal to you. The other is that "ذلك" has a meaning in which "هذا" would also be appropriate, because "هذا" and "ذلك" are both appropriate in any speech where something is mentioned and you then follow it with one of them to report about it. Do you not see that you say: "So-and-so has arrived", and the listener says: "That has reached us" or "That news has reached us"? "هذا" is appropriate there because the thing is close to his answer, so it is like something present to which you point; and "ذلك" is appropriate because it has ended, and what has ended is like something absent. But if it were something standing there and visible, "هذا" would not be permissible in place of "ذلك", nor "ذلك" in place of "هذا". Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ﴾ up to His words ﴿وَكُلُّ مِنَ الأَخْيَارِ﴾, then He said: ﴿هَذَا ذِكْرٌ﴾.

And He, Majestic and Mighty is He, said in another place: ﴿وَعِنْدَهُمْ قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ أَتْرَابٌ﴾, then He said: ﴿هَذَا مَا تُوعَدُونَ لِيوْمِ الْحِسَابِ﴾. And He, Majestic is His mention, said: ﴿وَجَاءَتْ سَكْرَةُ الْمَوْتِ بِالْحَقِّ﴾, then He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ مَا كُنْتَ مِنْهُ تَحِيد﴾. Had "هذا" been said in such speech in place of "ذلك", or "ذلك" in place of "هذا", it would have been correct.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd it is "هَذَا فَذُوقُوهُ", and in our reading "ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ".

As for where "هذا" is not permissible in place of "ذلك", nor "ذلك" in place of "هذا": if you saw two men, one of whom you did not know, you would say to the one you know: مَن هذا الذى معك؟ (who is this with you?); and here مَن ذلك؟ (who is that?) is not permissible, because you see him with your own eyes.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿هُدىً لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾, it is nominative in two ways and accusative in two ways. If you intend «الكتاب» to be a naʿt (adjective) of "ذلك", then «الهدى» is in the position of the nominative because it is the khabar (predicate) of "ذلك", as though you had said: ذلك هُدًى لا شكّ فيه (that is guidance in which there is no doubt). And if you make ﴿لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ its khabar, you also put ﴿هُدىً﴾ in the nominative, making it follow the position of "لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ", as Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَهَذَا كِتَابٌ أَنْزَلْنَاهُ مُبَارَكٌ﴾, as though He said: This is a Book, and this is blessed, and this is of such-and-such a description. There is a third way of the nominative: if you wish, you put it in the nominative as a fresh start (istiʾnāf), since what precedes it is complete, just as the readers read "الم. تِلْكَ آيَاتُ الْكِتَابِ الْحَكيم. هُدًى وَرَحْمَةٌ لِلْمُحْسِنينَ" in the nominative and the accusative; and like His words in the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿أَأَلِدُ وأَنَا عَجُوزٌ وَهَذَا بَعْلِى شَيْخٌ﴾, which in our reading is "شَيْخاً".

As for the accusative, one of its two ways is that you make «الكتاب» the khabar of "ذلك" and put "هُدًى" in the accusative by qaṭʿ (detachment) [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's Kufan term, corresponding to ḥāl (circumstantial)], because "هُدًى" is an indefinite joined to a definite whose khabar is already complete, so you put it in the accusative, since an indefinite cannot serve as a descriptor of a definite. And if you wish, you put "هُدىً" in the accusative by qaṭʿ from the hāʾ in "فيه", as though you had said: لا شك فيه هاديا (there is no doubt in it, as guidance).

Know that when "هذا" is followed by a noun bearing alif and lām, it runs on three meanings. The first: you see the noun after "هذا" just as you see "هذا" [Translator's note: i.e. it is present before you], and then its predicate (fiʿl) [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ uses «فعل» here for the predicate/complement] is nominative, as in your saying: هذا الحمار فارهٌ (this donkey is sprightly): you made «الحمار» an adjective of «هذا» since both are present, and the accusative is not permissible here. The second: what follows "هذا" is a single item standing for its whole genus, and then the predicate is accusative, as in your saying: ماكان من السباع غير مخوف فهذا الأسد مخوفا (whatever beasts of prey are not feared, this — the lion — is feared): do you not see that you are reporting fearsomeness of all lions? The third meaning: what follows "هذا" is a single thing that has no peer, and then too the predicate is accusative. You put the predicate in the accusative only because "هذا" is not an adjective qualifying «الأسد»; it is introduced only as taqrīb [Translator's note: a Kufan term for this use of the demonstrative, which functions like kāna], and the statement would be better without "هذا": do you not see that if you said: ما لا يضرّ من السباع فالأسد ضارّ (whatever beasts of prey do no harm, the lion does harm), it would be clearer? As for the meaning of taqrīb: "this is the first thing I tell you about"; they could not avoid putting «هذا» in the nominative by means of "الأسد" [Translator's note: in the Kufan view of mutual government (al-murāfaʿa), subject and predicate raise each other], while its khabar is still awaited; and when «الأسد» was occupied with the mutual government with "هذا", its predicate, which it used to govern in the nominative, was put in the accusative because it was left free. The like is "والله غفور رحيم": if you introduce "كان" into it, [Translator's note: the subject] becomes nominative through it, and the khabar that completes the speech is still awaited, so you put it in the accusative because it is left free. As for their putting in the accusative the predicate of a single thing that has no peer, as when you say: هذه الشمس ضياءً للعباد (this — the sun — is a light for the servants) and هذا القمر نوراً (this — the moon — is a radiance): the moon is a single thing that has no peer, so it too has no need of your saying "هذا"; do you not see that when you say: طلع القمر (the moon has risen), the mind does not go to some absent thing so that you need to say "هذا" to show that it is present? So it was put in the nominative by «هذا» and was not an adjective, and you put its khabar in the accusative because of the need for it.

farraa:7-7.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ وَعَلَىٰ أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾. The meaning of the sealing ends at His words ﴿وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ﴾. "الغشاوة" was put in the nominative by "على"; had you put it in the accusative by implying "وجعل" (and He placed), it would have been correct. Al-Mufaḍḍal claimed that ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd used to read it in the accusative, after the pattern of His words in al-Jāthiya: ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتَ مَنِ اتَّخذَ إِلهَهُ هَوَاهُ وأَضَلَّهُ اللَّهُ عَلَى عِلْمٍ وَخَتَمَ عَلَى سَمْعِهِ وقلْبِهِ وجَعَلَ عَلَى بَصَرِهِ غِشَاوةً﴾; and the meaning of the two is one — and Allah knows best. Implication (iḍmār) is good only in speech whose parts belong together and whose beginning points to its end, as in your saying: قد أصاب فلان المال، فبنى الدورَ والعبيدَ والإماءَ واللباسَ الحسن (so-and-so came into wealth, and built houses, and slaves, and slave-girls, and fine clothing): you see that building does not apply to slaves and slave-girls, nor to riding animals, nor to clothes; but they are all among the marks of affluence, so the implication was good since it was understood. Similar to it in Sūrat al-Wāqiʿa: ﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدَانٌ مُخَلَّدُنَ. بِأَكْوَابٍ وَأَبَارِيقَ وَكَأْسٍ مِنْ مَعِينٍ﴾, then He said: ﴿وَفَاكِهَةٍ مِمَّا يَتَخَيَّرونَ. ولَحْمِ طَيْرٍ مِمّا يَشْتَهُونَ. وحُورٍ عِينٍ﴾: some readers read الحور العين in the genitive and some in the nominative.

Those who read it in the nominative said: The ḥūr ʿīn are not carried around; so they read it in the nominative with the meaning: "and with them are ḥūr ʿīn", or "and along with that, ḥūr ʿīn". Then it was said [Translator's note: in reply]: Fruit and meat are not carried around either; only wine is carried around — and Allah knows best — yet the end of the speech was made to follow its beginning. This is frequent in the speech of the Arabs and their poetry. Someone of the Banū Asad recited to me, describing his mare:
عَلَفْتُهَا تِبْناً وماءً بارداً * حتى شَتَتْ هَمَّالةً عَيْنَاهَا
(I fed her straw and cool water, until she wintered with her eyes streaming.) [Translator's note: water is not "fed"; the verb for "giving to drink" is implied — the point of the citation.]
And the Book is more eloquent Arabic and stronger as proof than poetry. As for where the implied element is not good because the parts rarely belong together, it is your saying: قد أعتقت مبارَكا أمس وآخرَ اليوم ياهذا (I freed Mubārak yesterday, and another one today, you there), when you mean: "and I bought another one today"; because these are different and it is not known that you meant "I bought". Nor may you say: ضربت فلانا وفلانا (I struck so-and-so and so-and-so), meaning by the second "and I killed so-and-so", because there is no indication here.

In these two ways there is that by which you can recognise whatever comes before you, if Allah wills.

farraa:16-16.t: His words: ﴿فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِّجَارَتُهُمْ﴾. Someone might say: How can trade profit, when it is only the man, the trader, who profits? That is part of the speech of the Arabs: ربح بَيْعُك وخسر بيعُك (your sale has profited, your sale has lost); saying so is good because profit and loss occur only in trade, so its meaning is known. Similar to it in the speech of the Arabs: هذا ليل نائم (this is a sleeping night). And similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿فَإذَا عَزَمَ اْلأَمْرُ﴾, though resolve belongs only to men. Such implication is permissible only in the like of this. If someone said: قد خسر عبدك (your slave has lost), it would not be permissible, (if you) mean to make the slave a piece of merchandise on which profit or loss is made; because the slave may himself be a trader who profits or loses, so the meaning when he himself profits cannot be told apart from the meaning when he is the thing traded in. But if someone said: قد ربحتْ دراهمُك ودنانيرُك، وخسر بَزُّك ورقيقك (your dirhams and dinars have profited, and your cloth and your slaves have lost), it would be permissible, because each part points to the other.

farraa:17-17.t:
His words: ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي ٱسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾. The parable was struck — and Allah knows best — for the action, not for the persons of the men; it is only a parable of hypocrisy. So He said: "their likeness is as the likeness of the one who kindled a fire", and did not say: "those who kindled". It is as Allah said: ﴿تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهْم كالَّذِى يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْْتِ﴾, and His words: ﴿مَاخَلْقُكُمْ وَلاَ بَعْثُكُمْ إِلاَّ كَنَفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ﴾, whose meaning — and Allah knows best — is: except like the raising of a single soul. Had the comparison been to the men themselves, it would have been plural, as He said: ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ خُشُبٌ مُسَنَّدَةٌ﴾, meaning their statures and bodies; and He said: ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍ﴾: it was plural when He meant to compare the persons of the men. So run the speech on this basis. If you come across, in poetry, a comparison of a plural of men made singular, allow it; and if you come across, in poetry, a comparison of a single person made plural, the action is likewise intended, so allow it — as when you say: ما فِعْلك إلا كفعل الحَمِير (your doing is nothing but like the doing of donkeys) and ما أفعالكم إلا كفعل الذِّئب (your doings are nothing but like the doing of the wolf). Build on this; then you drop «فعل» and say: ما فعلك إلأا كالحَمِير وكالذِّئب (your doing is nothing but like donkeys, like the wolf).

Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said ﴿ذَهَبَ ٱللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْْ﴾ only because the meaning turned to the hypocrites, so He used the plural for that reason. Had it been singular, it would have been correct, like His words: ﴿إنّ شَجَرَةَ الزَّقُّومِ. طَعامُ الأَثِيمِ. كالْمُهْلِ تغْلِى فى الْبُطُونِ﴾ and "يَغْلِى": whoever uses the feminine refers to the tree, and whoever uses the masculine refers to «المهل» (the molten metal). Similar to it are His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أَمَنَةً نُعَاساً تَغْشَى طَائِفَةً منْكُمْ﴾ — [Translator's note: with tāʾ] referring to «الأمنة» (security), and "ويَغْشَى" [Translator's note: with yāʾ] referring to «النعاس» (slumber).

farraa:18-18.t:
His words: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لاَ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾. They are nominative although the nouns they refer to at the beginning of the speech are accusative, because the speech was complete and a verse ended with it; then ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ was begun afresh in another verse, which made the fresh start (istiʾnāf) stronger. Had the speech been complete without being the end of a verse, the fresh start would also have been permissible. Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿جَزَاءً مِنْ رَبِّكَ عَطَاءً حِسَاباً. رَبُّ السَّمَوات وَالأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا الرَّحْمَنُِ﴾: "الرحمن" is read nominative and genitive in its i'rab, and what precedes it is not the end of a verse. As for fresh starts at the heads of verses, they are many; among them the word of Allah: ﴿إنَّ اللهَ اشْتَرَى مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ﴾ up to His words ﴿وَذَلِكَ هُوَ الْفَوْزُ الْعَظِيمُ﴾; then He, Majestic is His countenance, said: ﴿التَّائِبُونَ الْعَابِدُونَ الْحامِدُونَ﴾, in the nominative in our reading, while in the version (ḥarf) of Ibn Masʿūd it is "التائِبِين العابِدِين الحامِدِين". And He said: ﴿أَتَدْعُونَ بَعْلاً وَتَذَرُونَ أَحْسَنَ الْخَالِقِينَ.اللهُ رَبُّكُمْ﴾, which is read in the nominative and the accusative, as I have explained to you. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "صُمّاً بُكْماً عُمْياً", in the accusative.

Its accusative can be explained in two ways: if you wish, with the meaning "He left them deaf, dumb and blind"; and if you wish, you let «الترك» (leaving) fall on them [Translator's note: only] "in darkness", and then begin "صُمّاً" afresh as a censure of them.

The Arabs put words in the accusative for censure and for praise, because with such nouns there is something like the meaning of their sayings: وَيْلاً له (woe to him), وثَوَاباً له (reward to him), and بُعْداً (away!), سَقْياً (watering!), رَعْياً (care!).

farraa:19-19.t:
His words: ﴿أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾ refer back to His words: ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾. ﴿أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ﴾ means: or like the likeness of a downpour. The mention of ﴿الَّذِى اسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾ made it unnecessary, so the nouns that ought to have accompanied «الصيّب» were dropped, and the meaning points to them, because the parable was struck for hypocrisy. So He said: ﴿فِيهِ ظُلُمَاتٌ وَرَعْدٌ وَبَرْقٌٌ﴾: He likened the darkness to their unbelief, the lightning — when it lights up for them and they walk in it — to their faith, and the thunder to the threats that come in the Qurʾān. Another view has been given about it: it was said that the thunder was mentioned only as a parable for their fear of fighting when they are called to it. Do you not see that He said in another place: ﴿يَحْسَبونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, i.e. they think they will always be defeated?

Then He said: ﴿يَجْعَلُونَ أَصَابِعَهُمْ فِيۤ آذَانِهِم مِّنَ ٱلصَّوَاعِقِ حَذَرَ ٱلْمَوْتِ﴾. He put "حَذَرَ" in the accusative without the verb falling on it [Translator's note: as its object]: He does not mean "they make them [Translator's note: their fingers] a caution"; it is only like your saying: أعطيتك خَوْفاً وفَرَقاً (I gave to you out of fear and dread): you do not give him fear; you give to him because of fear. So it is put in the accusative as tafsīr [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term here for what is later called mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose)], not by the verb, as in His words, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿يَدْعُونَنَا رَغَباً وَرَهَباً﴾, and His words: ﴿ادْعُوا رَبَّكُمْ تَضَرُّعاً وَخُفْيَةً﴾. Both definite and indefinite nouns serve as tafsīr in this position, and its accusative is not due to the dropping of "مِن". This is something from which the beginner can draw guidance for learning.

farraa:124-124.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذِ ٱبْتَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِمَاتٍ﴾ — it is said: He commanded him with ten practices of the Sunna, five in the head and five in the body. Those in the head are: parting the hair, trimming the moustache, rinsing the nose, rinsing the mouth and the tooth-stick (siwāk).
Those in the body are: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, clipping the nails, and plucking the rufghayn, meaning the armpits. Al-Farrāʾ said: * and the singular is called rufgh * — and cleansing after relieving oneself (istinjāʾ).
﴿فَأَتَمَّهُنَّ﴾: he acted upon them. So Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿إِنِّي جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَاماً﴾: your guidance will be followed and your practice taken as a model. So he said: "My Lord, ﴿وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِي﴾", by way of request.
His saying: ﴿لاَ يَنَالُ عَهْدِي ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾ — He says: the Muslims will not have a polytheist leader. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمُونَ". This is explained by the fact that whatever reaches you, you have reached it, as you say: "I attained your good" and "your good reached me".

farraa:125-125.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ جَعَلْنَا ٱلْبَيْتَ مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ﴾ — they return (yathūbūn) to it — from al-mathāba and al-mathāb; He meant: from every place. Al-mathāba in the speech of the Arabs is like the singular [form without tāʾ], like al-maqām and al-maqāma.
His saying: ﴿وَأَمْناً﴾ — it is said that whoever commits a crime or incurs a ḥadd (prescribed punishment) and then takes refuge in the Sanctuary, his ḥadd is not carried out on him until he leaves the Sanctuary; and it is ordered that he not be mixed with or traded with, and that he be pressed (until he leaves) so that the ḥadd may be carried out on him; that is his security. Whoever of the people of the Sanctuary commits a crime or incurs a ḥadd, it is carried out on him in the Sanctuary.
His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّخِذُواْ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ مُصَلًّى﴾ — the Readers have read it in the sense of the jussive [i.e. as an imperative] [and the exegesis is with those who read the jussive]. Whoever reads "واتَّخَذوا" with fatḥa on the khāʾ makes it a statement; He says: We made it a place of return for them, and they took it as a place of prayer. All is correct, if Allah wills.
His saying: ﴿أَن طَهِّرَا بَيْتِيَ﴾ — He means: from the idols, that they not be hung in it.
His saying: ﴿لِلطَّائِفِينَ وَٱلْعَاكِفِينَ﴾ means its people, ﴿والرُّكَّعِ السُّجُودِ﴾ means the people of Islam.

farraa:126-126.t: His saying: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ is from the speech of Allah, blessed and exalted; ﴿فَأُمَتِّعُهُ﴾ is a statement. In the reading of Ubayy: "وَمنْ كَفَرَ فَنُمَتِّعُه قَلِيلاً ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُ إلى عذابِ النارِ" (this is one view). Ibn ʿAbbās used to make it connected to the request of Ibrāhīm, Allah bless him, in the sense: "My Lord, and whoever disbelieves, give him enjoyment (fa-amtiʿhu) a little, then compel him (iḍṭarrahu)" (accusative [i.e. with fatḥa], connected). He means "then iḍṭarir-hu"; when you drop the unfolding of the doubled letter you give it fatḥa; and in this approach the kasra on the rāʾ is permissible in the dialect of those who say "muddihi". Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read: "فَإِمْتِعُه قلِيلا ثم إضطَرُّة" with kasra on the alif, as you say "أَنا إعلَم ذلك" (I know that).

farraa:127-127.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ﴾ — it is said they are the foundations of the House. Its singular is qāʿida; and of women who have ceased menstruating, [one says] qāʿid, without the hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa]. A man's wife is called his qaʿīda.
His saying: ﴿رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ﴾ — He means: the two of them say, "Our Lord". In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "ويقولانِ ربنا".

farraa:128-128.t: His saying: ﴿وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "وأَرِهِم مناسِكهم", referring to the offspring. In "وأرِنا" he joined them to himself, so they became like those speaking for themselves. What shows you this is His saying ﴿وابعث فيهم رسولا﴾: He returned to the offspring specifically.

farraa:130-130.t: His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ — the Arabs make "سفِه" act upon (نَفْسه) although it is definite. Likewise His saying ﴿بِطرت معِيشتها﴾; it is a definite noun functioning like an indefinite, because it is an explanatory element (mufassir, i.e. tamyīz), and the explanatory element in most speech is indefinite, as in your saying "ḍiqtu bihi dharʿan" (I was at a loss with it, lit. narrow in reach), and His saying ﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَنْ شَىءٍ مِّنْهُ نَفْساً﴾. The verb belongs to "dharʿ", because you say "ḍāqa dharʿī bihi"; when you made the narrowness attributed to yourself and said "ḍiqtu", "dharʿ" came as an explanation, because the narrowness is in it — as you say "He is the most spacious of you in house (dāran)": "house" came in to show that the spaciousness is in it, not in the man. Likewise their saying "wajiʿta baṭnaka" (your belly ached), and "wathiqta raʾyaka" — or "wafiqta" [Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: I most likely think it is "wathiqta" with thāʾ] — the verb really belongs to the thing; when the verb was attributed to the man, the accusative became sound in what refers back to him, by way of explanation (tafsīr). For that reason it may not be put first: one does not say "raʾyahu safiha Zaydun", just as "dāran anta awsaʿuhum" is not permissible; because even though it is definite it has the sense of an indefinite, and receives the accusative in the position of the accusative of the indefinite and does not go beyond it.

farraa:132-133.t:
His saying: ﴿وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ﴾ — in the codices of the people of Medina: "وأَوصى"; both are correct and common in speech.
His saying: ﴿وَيَعْقُوبُ﴾ — i.e. and Yaʿqūb also enjoined this. In one of the two readings, the reading of ʿAbd Allāh or the reading of Ubayy: "أَنْ يَا بنَىَّ إن الله اصطفى لكم الدين" — he makes "وصّى" act upon "أن", meaning: he enjoined them "that…". There is no "أن" in our reading, and all is correct. Whoever drops it says: enjoining (waṣiyya) is a saying, and any speech that goes back to saying permits the entry of "أَنْ" and permits dropping "أنْ", as Allah, mighty and majestic, said in al-Nisāʾ: ﴿يوصِيكم اللّهُ فى أولادِكم لِلذكرِ مثل حظِّ الأنثيين﴾, because enjoining is like saying. Al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
إنى سأُبدى لك فيما أُبدى * لى شَجَنان شَجن بنجد * وشجَن لى ببلاد السِنْد
(I shall disclose to you, in what I disclose: I have two longings — a longing in Najd, and a longing of mine in the land of Sind.)
— because disclosing is, in meaning, with his tongue. Similar is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿وَعَدَ اللّهُ الَّذينَ آمنُوا وعَمِلوا الصالِحاتِ مِنْهم مغفِرةً﴾, because a promise is a saying. Upon this is built whatever comes of its kind.
The saying of the grammarians, "he only meant 'أن' and it was dropped", is nothing; because if that were so, it would be permissible to drop it both with what has the sense of saying and with other than it.
When the place contains something whose meaning is the meaning of saying, and then "أن" appears in it overtly, it has fatḥa on the alif. And when that word does not go back to the meaning of saying, "أن" falls out of the speech.
As for what comes with the meaning of saying and "أن" appears in it with fatḥa: the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿إنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحاً إلى قَوْمِه أَنْ أَنذِر قومك﴾ — "أن" came with fatḥa because a message is a saying.
Likewise His saying ﴿فانْطَلَقُوا وهم يَتَخَافَتُونَ. أَنْ لاَ يَدْخُلنا﴾ — and whispering is a saying. Likewise everything in the Qurʾān, and it is much; of it is the saying of Allah ﴿وآخِرُ دَعْوَاهُمْ أَنِ الحمدُ لِلّه﴾.
Similar is: ﴿فَأَذَّنَ مُؤَذِّنٌ بَيْنَهُمْ أَنْ لَعْنَةُ اللّهِ [عَلَى الظَّالِمين]﴾ — calling out is a saying, and a claim (daʿwā) is originally a saying.
As for what has no sense of saying and so "أن" did not enter it: the saying of Allah ﴿ولو تَرَى إِذ المجرِمون ناكِسُوا رُءُوسِهِم عِندَ رَبّهِم رَبَّنَا أَبْصِرنَا﴾. Since in "أبصرنا" there is no word indicating saying, you imply "saying" and drop "أن", because what follows saying is a quotation (ḥikāya) with which "أن" does not occur. Of it is the saying of Allah ﴿والملائِكةُ باسِطوا أَيدِيهم أَخرِجوا أَنفسكم﴾, meaning: saying, "Bring out…". And of it is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبراهِيمُ القَواعِدَ مِن البيتِ وإِسمعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنّا﴾, meaning: the two of them say "رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ منَّا"; and this is much. So measure by this whatever comes to you.
[And His saying: … قَالُواْ نَعْبُدُ إِلَـٰهَكَ وَإِلَـٰهَ آبَائِكَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ إِلَـٰهاً وَاحِداً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ 133].
The Readers read "نعبد إِلهك وإِله آبائِك", and some of them read "وإِله أَبِيك" in the singular. It is as if the one who said "أبيك" (thought that an uncle is not permissible among the fathers), so he said "وإِله أبِيك إِبراهِيم" and then, after the father, enumerated the uncle. The Arabs treat paternal uncles like fathers, and the mother's kin like maternal uncles; that is frequent in their speech.

farraa:135-135.t: His saying: ﴿قُلْ بَلْ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفاً﴾ — Allah commanded Muḥammad ﷺ. If you put it in the accusative by "نكون" it is correct; and if you put it in the accusative by an implied verb it is correct, as if you said: "rather, we follow «مِلّة إِبراهِيم»". Allah only commanded the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, saying: "قل بل مِلّة إِبراهِيم".

farraa:136-136.t: His saying: ﴿لاَ نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِّنْهُمْ﴾ — He says: we do not believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and the Christians did.

farraa:138-138.t: His saying: ﴿صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ is accusative, referred back to "the religion" (al-milla). It was only said "صبغة اللهِ" (the dye of Allah) because some of the Christians, when a child was born, would put him in a water of theirs, making that a purification for him like circumcision. So it is too in one of the two readings. Say: "صِبغة اللّهِ", and it is circumcision; Ibrāhīm ﷺ was circumcised, so He said "صِبغة اللّهِ", commanding Muḥammad ﷺ with it. So "dye" was applied to circumcision because they dyed the boys in water. Had you put "الصبغة" and "الملّة" in the nominative it would have been correct, as the Arabs say "jadduka lā kadduka" and "jaddaka lā kaddaka" (your fortune, not your toil). Whoever uses the nominative means: it is the religion of Ibrāhīm, it is the dye of Allah, it is your fortune. Whoever uses the accusative implies a verb such as I told you.

farraa:143-143.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنَاكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطاً﴾ means just (ʿadl). ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ﴾ — it is said that every prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection and say "I conveyed", and his nation will say "No", thus belying the prophets. (Then the nation of Muḥammad ﷺ will be brought, and they will confirm the prophets and their Prophet.) Then the Prophet ﷺ will come and confirm his nation. That is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكُمْ شَهِيداً﴾. And of it is the saying of Allah: ﴿فكيف إذا جِئنا مِن كل أمَّةٍ بِشهيدٍ [وجئنا بك على هؤلاء شهيدا]﴾.
His saying: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَانَكُمْ﴾ — He attributed the faith to the living among the believers, while the meaning concerns those Muslims who died before the qibla was changed. They said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What of the prayer of our brothers who died upon the first qibla?"
