So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَانَكُمْ﴾, meaning their faith, because they are included with them in the religion. It is like your saying to a people, "We killed you and routed you", meaning "we killed some of you": you confront them with the killing while they are alive.

farraa:144-144.t: His saying: ﴿فَوَلُّواْ وُجُوِهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾ — He means: towards it and facing it. Similar in speech: "Turn your face shaṭrahu (towards it), tilqāʾahu and tujāhahu."

farraa:145-145.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلْكِتَابَ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ مَّا تَبِعُواْ قِبْلَتَكَ﴾ — (لئن) was answered with what "لو" is answered with. "لو" is past in meaning and "لئن" is future, but the verb appeared in both in the form faʿala, so they were answered with one answer and each was likened to the other. The answer of (لئن) in speech is with the future, as in your saying: "la-in qumta la-aqūmanna" (if you stand, I will surely stand), "la-in aḥsanta la-tukramanna" (if you do good, you will surely be honoured), and "la-in asaʾta lā yuḥsan ilayka" (if you do wrong, no good will be done to you). And you answer "لو" with the past, saying "law qumta la-qumtu" (had you stood, I would have stood); you do not say "law qumta la-aqūmanna". This is what is practised. When "لو" is answered with the answer of "لئن", [the reason is] what I told you about the form of both their verbs being past. Do you not see that you say "law qumta" and "la-in qumta", and you hardly see (yafʿalu coming) after them, though it is permissible? For that reason He said ﴿ولئن أرسلنا رِيحا فرأَوْه مُصْفَرّاً لَظَلُّوا﴾, answering (لئن) with the answer of (لو); and He answered (لو) with the answer of (لئن), saying ﴿ولو أنهم آمنوا واتقَوْا لمثوبة مِن عِندِ الله خير﴾ — the verse.

farraa:146-147.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّ فَرِيقاً مِّنْهُمْ لَيَكْتُمُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾ — the meaning is that they do not believe that the qibla to which Muḥammad ﷺ was turned is the qibla of Ibrāhīm, Allah bless him and all the prophets. Then He began afresh with (الحقُّ), saying: O Muḥammad, it is ﴿ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾ — it is the qibla of Ibrāhīm — ﴿فَلاَ تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْمُمْتَرِينَ﴾: so do not doubt that at all. Al-mumtarī is the doubter.

farraa:229-230.t:
His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ أَن يَخَافَآ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "إلا أَنْ تخافوا" ("unless you fear"), and Ḥamza read it in line with this meaning: "ألا أَنْ يُخافا" ("unless the two are feared for") [Translator's note: so written; read إلا أن يُخافا], and that does not please me. Some of the people of Medina read it as Ḥamza read it. In the reading of Ubayy it is "إِلا أَنْ يَظنَّا أَلاَّ يُقيِمَا حُدُودَ الله" ("unless they think that they will not keep the limits of Allah"); fear and thinking are close to each other in the speech of the Arabs.
Of that: a man says: "Your slave has gone out without your permission," and you say: "I thought so (ẓanantu dhāka)," and "I feared so (khiftu dhāka)," and the meaning is one. The poet said:
أتانى كلامَ عن نُصَيب بقوله * وما خفتُ يا سلاَّم أنك عائبى
(Words reached me from Nuṣayb in what he said — and I did not think, O Sallām, that you would find fault with me.)
And the other said:
إذا مت فادفنّى إلى جَنْب كَرْمة * تُرَوِّى عظامى بعد موتى عروقها
[ولا تدفنَنِّى فى الفلاة فإننى * أخاف إذا ما متُّ أن لا أذوقُها]
(When I die, bury me beside a vine whose roots will water my bones after my death; [and do not bury me in the desert, for I fear that once I die I shall not taste it.])
Fear in this place is like thinking. He put "أذوقُها" in the nominative just as they put in the nominative ﴿وحَسِبُوا ألا تكون فِتنة﴾. And it is narrated from him ﷺ: "I was commanded to use the tooth-stick until I feared that I would surely lose my teeth (la-adradanna)," just as you say: "He thought he would surely go (la-yadhhabanna)."
As for what Ḥamza said: if he intended to follow the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, he did not get it right — and Allah knows best — because the fear falls only on (أن) alone, since he [ʿAbd Allāh] said: "unless you fear that … not," while Ḥamza made the fear fall on the man and the woman and on an; do you not see that their [dual] noun in the fearing is nominative as the deputy agent of a verb whose agent is not named? Had he meant: "unless they are feared for in this (ʿalā hādhā)," or "feared for by this," or "because of this," so that it is not based on following ʿAbd Allāh's reading, it [would have been] permissible, as you say to a man: "You are feared because you are wicked," and "for that you are…," and "on account of your being…."
His saying: ﴿فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا﴾ — it is asked: how did He say "there is no sin upon the two of them," when the sin — according to what people take it to be — is only upon the husband, because he took back what he gave? There are two ways regarding that. One: that the husband is meant and not the woman, even though both have been mentioned. In Sūrat al-Raḥmān: ﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْهُمَا اللُّؤْلُؤُ وَالْمَرْجَانُ﴾, whereas pearls and coral come out only from the salt water, not from the fresh. And of it: "نَسِيَا حُوتَهُما" ("the two forgot their fish"), whereas the one who forgot was Moses' companion alone. Similar to it in speech is that you say: "I have two mounts that I ride and draw water with," whereas one of them is ridden and water is drawn with the other; and it is possible that both are ridden and both used to draw water. This is from the breadth of Arabic, whose breadth is cited as proof. Similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿وَمِنْ رَحْمَتِهِ جعل لكم الليل والنهار لِتسكنوا فِيهِ ولتبتغوا مِن فضله﴾. It is sound in speech to say: "Allah has made for us night and day in which we earn our living and in which we sleep," and if you wish you assign the sleeping to the night and the earning of a living to the day.
The other way is that both share in there being no sin upon them, since she gives that in which sin has been negated from the husband; she was made to share in it because when she gives that in which the sin is removed, she herself needs the same. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فمن تعجَّلَ فى يومين فلا إِثم عليهِ ومن تأخَّر فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾, whereas the place for removing sin is in the one who hastens; so He granted to the one who delays — and he is the one who did not fall short — the like of what He granted to the one who falls short. Similar to it in speech is your saying: "If you give charity in secret, it is good, [and if you give charity openly, it is good]."
In His saying ﴿ومن تأخّر فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾ there is another way: that He means: let not the one who hastens say to the one who delays, "You fall short," nor the one who delays say the like to the one who hastens; so His saying ﴿فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾ means: let neither of them accuse the other of sin.
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَآ أَن يَتَرَاجَعَآ﴾ — He means: there is no sin upon them in returning to each other. (أَن) is in the position of the accusative when the preposition (al-ṣifa) is removed, as if you said: there is no sin upon them that he take her back. He said: al-Kisāʾī used to say: its position is genitive. Al-Farrāʾ said: I do not recognize that.
His saying: ﴿إِن ظَنَّآ أَن يُقِيمَا﴾ — (أن) is in the position of the accusative because the thinking falls on it.

farraa:231-231.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَاراً لِّتَعْتَدُواْ﴾ — when a man among them divorced his wife, he had the greater right to take her back so long as she had not washed from the second menstruation. When he wanted to harm her, he would leave her until she menstruated the third menstruation and then take her back, and he would do that in the second divorce as well. So his prolonging her return is the harming of her.

farraa:232-232.t:
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾ — He says: do not constrain them from returning to their husbands with a new dower when one of them has been separated from her husband. This was the sister of Maʿqil: she wanted to marry her first husband after her waiting period had ended, and Maʿqil said to her: "My face is forbidden to your face if you go back to him." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ أَن يَنكِحْنَ أَزْوَاجَهُنَّ﴾.
His saying ﴿ذٰلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾ — He did not say: dhālikum, and both are correct. It is permissible to address a people with "dhālika" only because it is a word that has become so frequent in speech that the kāf is imagined to be (part of the word) and not an address. Whoever says "dhālika" makes the kāf with fatḥa even when addressing a woman, two women or women. Whoever says "dhālikum" drops that imagining, and so he says when addressing one [woman]: "What did that man (dhāliki al-rajul) do?" and "those two men (dhālikumā)," and "those men (ulāʾikum)." [And] what occurs is measured on this. In the rest of the nouns, when you address, it is not permissible to say it except by bringing out the addressee in the dual, the plural and the feminine, as when you say to a woman: "Your boy (ghulāmuki) did that"; it is not permissible to give the kāf a fatḥa, nor to make it singular, in ghulām, because the kāf here is not imagined to be part of ghulām.
And it is permissible to say: "Your boy (ghulāmuki) did dhāki" and "dhāka," according to what I explained to you: taking the kāf to be part of the noun.

farraa:233-233.t:
His saying: ﴿ٱلرَّضَاعَةَ﴾ — the Readers read it with fatḥa on the rāʾ. Al-Kisāʾī claimed that some of the Arabs say: al-riḍāʿa with kasra. If so, it is like al-wikāla and al-wakāla, al-dilāla and al-dalāla, and "mahartu al-shayʾa mihāratan and mahāratan"; and al-raḍāʿ and al-riḍāʿ are similarly so, except that fatḥa on the rāʾ is more common. Similar to it: al-ḥiṣād and al-ḥaṣād.
His saying ﴿لاَ تُضَآرَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا﴾ — He means: lā tuḍārar, and it is in the position of the jussive (jazm). Kasra in it is permissible: "lā tuḍārri wālidatun." It is not permissible to give the rāʾ ḍamma with the intention of the jussive, but we would read it with ḍamma as a statement (khabar). As for His saying ﴿وإِن تَصْبِرُوا وتَتَّقُوا لا يضرُّكم كَيْدُهُمْم شَيْئا﴾, it may be ḍamma with the intention of the jussive, because the first rāʾ originally has ḍamma, so it is permissible for the second to have ḍamma following it. (لا تضارُّ) with ḍamma is not permissible, because if the rāʾ is tufāʿal it has fatḥa, and if it is tufāʿil it has kasra; so ḍamma does not come to it unless it is in the sense of the nominative. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb read: "ولا يضارَرْ كاتِب ولا شهيد".
The meaning of ﴿لاَ تُضَآرَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا﴾: He says: let her child not be taken from her while she is healthy and has milk, and handed over to someone else. ﴿ وَلاَ مَوْلُودٌ لَّهُ بِوَلَدِهِ﴾ means the husband. He says: when she has nursed her infant and it has grown attached to her and knows her, let her not harm the husband regarding handing his child over to him.

farraa:234-235.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجاً يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾ — it is asked: how did the predicate (khabar) come to be about the women, with no predicate for the husbands, when the predicate ought to have been about (الذين)? That is permissible: when nouns are mentioned and then nouns attached to them are mentioned that carry the meaning of the predicate, you leave the first and the predicate is about what is attached to it. This is of that kind, because the meaning — and Allah knows best — is only: whoever's husband dies, she waits. So the first was left without a predicate and the second was aimed at, because the predicate and the meaning are in it. He said: and someone recited to me:
بنى أسَد إنّ ابن قيس وقتلَه * بغير دم دارُ المذَلَّة حُلَّت
(O Banū Asad, Ibn Qays — and his being killed for no blood — is the abode of humiliation that has been entered.)
So he dropped (ابن قيس) and gave a predicate about his killing, that it is humiliation. Similar to it:
لعلِّىَ إن مالت بِىَ الرِّيح مَيْلة * على ابن أبى ذِبَّان أن يتندَّما
(Perhaps, if the wind swings me once against Ibn Abī Dhibbān, he may come to regret.)
He said "laʿallī" and then said "an yatanaddamā," because the meaning is: perhaps Ibn Abī Dhibbān will regret if the wind swings me. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿والذِين يتوفَّوْن مِنكم ويذرون أَزواجا وصِيَّةً لأزواجِهِم﴾, except that the hāʾ in His saying ﴿وصِيَّة لأزواجِهِم﴾ refers back to (الذين), so the i'rab in it is clearer, because the returning reference can be a predicate, as when you say: "ʿAbd Allāh, I hit him."
He said: ﴿وَعَشْراً﴾ and did not say "ʿasharatan." That is because when the Arabs leave a number of nights and days unspecified, they give the nights precedence over it, so much so that they say: "We have fasted ten (ʿashran) of the month of Ramaḍān," because of how often they give nights precedence over days. When they state the specification alongside the number, the feminines take it without the hāʾ and the masculines with the hāʾ, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿سَخَّرها عليهِم سبع ليالٍ وثمانية أَيامٍ حُسُوما﴾ — He put the hāʾ on [the number of] the days when they were stated, and it was not put on [the number of] the nights when they were stated.
If you make the number not connected to the days as the governing genitive is connected to what follows it, you again give the nights precedence over the days. If they are mixed, being nights and days, you give the feminine precedence, saying: "Seven (sabʿ) have passed for him," and then after it you say: "days in which there was severe cold." As for the mixed case, it is the poet's saying:
أقامت ثلاثا بين يوم وليلة * وكان النكير أن تضِيف وتَجْارا
(She stayed three [nights and days], between day and night, and her only protest was to shy away and cry out.)
He said thalāthan and among them are days. And you say: "I have three (thalātha) between a slave boy and a slave girl," and thalāth is not permissible here, because [only] nights, with regard to days, take precedence over days. Similar to that in speech is that you say: "I have ten (ʿashr) camels," even if you mean male camels, and "ten of sheep and cattle." And every collective whose singular has the hāʾ and whose plural drops the hāʾ — such as al-baqar, whose singular is baqara — you say: "I have ten (ʿashr) of the cattle," even if you intend males. When they are mixed and the specifying item of one of the two kinds comes before its companion, you run the number on it, saying: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) she-camels and he-camels," making it feminine because you began with the she-camel and gave it precedence.
If you begin with the he-camel you say: "I have fifteen (khamsata ʿashara) he-camels and she-camels." If you say "between she-camel and he-camel," so that it is not a specification, you give the feminine precedence and do not mind whether you began with the he-camel or the she-camel; you say: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) between he-camel and she-camel." It is not permissible to say: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) slave women and slave men," nor "between slave woman and slave man," except with the masculine, because the males of anything other than what I mentioned to you are not covered by the females, and because the male of them is marked with a mark other than the female's mark; whereas with sheep and cattle, shāt and baqara apply to the male and the female, so it is permissible to make the masculine feminine because of this hāʾ which has attached to both the masculine and the feminine.
His saying ﴿مِنْ خِطْبَةِ ٱلنِّسَآءِِ﴾ — al-khiṭba is a maṣdar (verbal noun) like al-khiṭb, and it is like your saying: "He has a fine way of sitting (al-qiʿda wa-l-jilsa)," meaning sitting (al-quʿūd wa-l-julūs). Al-khuṭba is like a letter that has a beginning and an end. He said: I heard one of the Arabs [say]: "O Allah, lift from us this ḍughṭa (distress)," as if he took it to have a beginning and an end; had he meant one time he would have said: al-ḍaghṭa, and had he meant the manner of the act he would have said al-ḍighṭa, as one says al-mishya. And I heard another say: "[So-and-so] overpowered me over a quṭʿa of my land," meaning a plot set apart like a piece, not divided; if you mean that it is a piece of something [cut from it], you say: qiṭʿa.
His saying: ﴿ أَوْ أَكْنَنتُمْ﴾ — the Arabs have two dialects for aknantu al-shayʾa when you have concealed it: kanantuhu and aknantuhu. He said: and they recited to me the poet's saying:
ثلاثٌ من ثلاثِ قُدَامياتٍ * من اللاتى تَكُنّ من الصَقِيع
(Three [feathers] from three foremost ones, of those that shelter from the frost.)
and some of them [narrate it] tukinnu, from aknantu. As for His saying: "لؤلؤ مكنون" and "بَيْض مكنون", it is as though it is a way of speaking of a thing that is guarded, and each of the two is close to the other.
His saying: ﴿وَلَـٰكِن لاَّ تُوَاعِدُوهُنَّ سِرّاً ﴾ — He says: let none of you describe himself to her during her waiting period as desiring marriage and doing much of it. Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Ḥibbān narrated to me from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: al-sirr in this place is marriage [Translator's note: i.e. intercourse]. And he recited on his authority the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays:
ألا زعمت بَسْباسة اليوم أننى * كبِرتُ وأَلاَّ يشهدَ السِرَّ أَمثالى
(Bisbāsa claimed today that I have grown old, and that the likes of me do not attend to al-sirr.)
Al-Farrāʾ said: and he holds that it is among the things Allah alluded to by metonymy, [as] He said: "أو جاء احد منكم من الغائط".

farraa:236-236.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ عَلَى ٱلْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُ وَعَلَى ٱلْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُ﴾ in the nominative. Had it been put in the accusative it would be correct, on the repetition of the verb in intention, i.e. let the well-off give according to his means, and the one in straitened circumstances according to his means. It is like the saying of the Arabs: "I took their alms: for every forty sheep, a sheep (shātun)"; had you put the last shāt in the accusative it would be correct.
His saying ﴿مَتَاعاً بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is accusative, coming out of al-qadar [Translator's note: i.e. as a ḥāl from it], because it is indefinite and al-qadar is definite.
And if you wish, it comes out of His saying "وَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ" — matāʿan and mutʿatan [i.e. as its maṣdar].
As for ﴿حَقّاً﴾, it is accusative from the intention of the statement, not as an adjective of al-matāʿ. It is like your saying in speech: "ʿAbd Allāh is in the house, truly (ḥaqqan)." Al-ḥaqq is put in the accusative only from the intention of the informant's speech, as if he said: "I inform you of a true report," and "of that, truly"; and it is ugly to make it follow definites or indefinites, because truth and falsehood are not in the nouns themselves; they come only with statements. Of that: you say: "You owe me the money, truly (ḥaqqan)," and it is ugly to say: "You owe me the true money (al-māl al-ḥaqq)," or "You owe me true money (māl ḥaqq)," unless you take it to mean that it is a right of mine against you, so that you treat it as [describing] the money and not in the manner of the statement.
Everything in the Qurʾān in which there is an indefinite or definite form of al-ḥaqq, or what is in the meaning of al-ḥaqq, the proper way of speech in it is the accusative, such as His saying "وَعْدَ الحقِ" and "وعد الصدق", and like His saying ﴿إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُم جَمِيعا وَعْدَ اللّهِ حقاً﴾; this is according to the first explanation.
As for His saying ﴿هنالِك الوَلاية لِلّه الحقِّ﴾, the accusative in al-ḥaqq is permissible, meaning ḥaqqan, i.e. I inform you that that is true. If you wish, you put al-ḥaqq in the genitive, making it an attribute of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And if you wish, you put it in the nominative, making it an attribute of al-walāya. Likewise His saying ﴿ورُدُّوا إلى اللّهِ مَوْلاَهُم الحقّ﴾: you make it an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Had you put it in the accusative it would be correct, and had it been put in the nominative on the intention of a fresh start (istiʾnāf) it would be correct, as He said: ﴿الْحَقُّ مِن ربَّك فَلاَ تَكُونَنَّ مِن المُمْتَرِين﴾. And you would say, when you hear a man relating something: [ḥaqqan, i.e.] you have spoken truly, and al-ḥaqqu, i.e. that is the truth. As for His saying in Ṣād ﴿قَالَ فالْحقُّ والحقَّ أقول﴾, al-Farrāʾ [Translator's note: so in the text; the sense requires "the Readers" (al-qurrāʾ)] have read the first in the nominative and in the accusative. It is narrated from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās that they read the first in the nominative and said its explanation is: the truth is from Me, and I speak the truth; so they put the second in the accusative by "aqūlu". Many of them put both in the accusative, taking the first in the sense of: by the truth "لأملأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ", and putting the second in the accusative because the saying falls on it. His saying ﴿ذلِكَ عِيسَى بنُ مَرْيَمَ قَوْلَ الحقّ﴾ — Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read it in the nominative, and they took al-Ḥaqq to be Allah, Blessed and Exalted, because in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "ذَلِكَ عِيسَى بْنُ مَرْيَمَ قالَ اللّهِ", like your saying: "the Word of Allah"; so they make (qāl) equivalent to qawl, as they said al-ʿāb and al-ʿayb.
Some read it in the accusative, meaning: that is Jesus son of Mary — a true saying.

farraa:237-237.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِن طَلَّقْتُمُوهُنَّ مِن قَبْلِ أَن تَمَسُّوهُنَّ﴾ — tumāssūhunna and tamassūhunna are one, and it is intercourse: al-mumāssa and al-mass.
He said ﴿إَلاَّ أَن يَعْفُونَ﴾ with the nūn only because it is the verb of the women, and the verb of women has the nūn in every case. One says: hunna yaḍribna, lam yaḍribna, lan yaḍribna, because if you dropped the nūn from them for the accusative or the jussive, their femininity would not be evident. The Arabs said "lan yaʿfū" for a group [of men] and "lan yaʿfuwā" for two men only because they added for the dual an alif and a nūn to the verb; so when they drop the nūn of the dual for the jussive or the accusative, the alif indicates the dual. Likewise the wāw of yafʿalūna indicates the plural when the nūn is dropped in the jussive or the accusative.
﴿أَوْ يَعْفُوَاْ ٱلَّذِي بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ ٱلنِّكَاحِ﴾ — and he is the husband.

farraa:238-238.t: His saying: ﴿حَافِظُواْ عَلَى ٱلصَّلَوَاتِ وٱلصَّلاَةِ ٱلْوُسْطَىٰ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "وعلى الصلاة الوسطى" ("and over the middle prayer"); for that reason the Readers preferred the genitive. Had it been put in the accusative, as urging it with an implied verb, it would have been a good way. It is like your saying in speech: "Hold to your kin — and the mother!", singling her out for kindness.

farraa:240-240.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجاً وَصِيَّةً﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is: "كتب عليهم الوصية لأزواجِهم" ("the bequest to their wives is prescribed for them"), and in the reading of Ubayy: "يتوفون منكم ويذرون أزواجا فمتاع لأزواجهم" ("…then a provision for their wives"). This is evidence for the nominative of al-waṣiyya. Some put it in the accusative, among them Ḥamza, on an implied verb as though it were a command, i.e. let them bequeath a bequest to their wives.
It cannot be accusative by having "wa-yadharūna" act on it.
﴿غَيْرَ إِخْرَاجٍ﴾ — He says: without your turning them out. Similar to it in speech: "I came to you out of desire for you." Similar to it: ﴿وأَدْخِل يَدَكَ فى جَيْبِك تَخْرُجْ بيْضَاء مِن غيرِ سُوءٍٍ﴾; had you dropped "min" you would say: ghayra sūʾin. Al-sūʾ here is leprosy (al-baraṣ). Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Sharīk narrated to us from Yazīd ibn Ziyād from Miqsam from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: without leprosy. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is as though He said: it will come out white, not leprous.

farraa:245-245.t: His saying: ﴿مَّن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يُقْرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضاً حَسَناً فَيُضَاعِفَهُ لَهُ﴾ — it is read in the nominative and the accusative. Whoever uses the nominative makes the fāʾ conjoined onto the ṣila (relative clause) of (الذى); whoever uses the accusative takes it out of the ṣila and makes it an answer to (من), because it is an interrogative. The one in al-Ḥadīd is like it.

farraa:20-20.t:
His words: ﴿يَكَادُ ٱلْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ﴾. The readers read "يَخَطِّفُ أَبْصاَرَهُمْ", with fatḥa on the yāʾ and the khāʾ and with doubling. Some give fatḥa to the yāʾ, kasra to the khāʾ and double the ṭāʾ, saying: "يَخِطِّفُ". Some give kasra to the yāʾ and the khāʾ and double, saying: "يِخِطِّفُ". And some of the readers of the people of Medina make the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ quiescent, combining two quiescent letters, saying: "يَخْطِّف". As for the one who says "يَخَطِّفُ", he transferred the vowel of the assimilated tāʾ to the khāʾ, since the khāʾ was quiescent. As for the one who gives kasra to the khāʾ, he was seeking the kasra of the alif in اختطف and الاختطاف. Some grammarians have said about it: The khāʾ was given kasra only because it was quiescent and the tāʾ after it was made quiescent, so two quiescent letters met and you gave the first a kasra, as one says: اضربِ الرجل, giving kasra to the bāʾ because it meets the lām.

What they said is worth nothing, because if it were as they said, the Arabs would have said in يَمُدّ: يَمِدّ, since the mīm (was) quiescent and the first of the two dāls was made quiescent; and they would have said in يَعَضّ: يَعِضّ. As for the one who gives kasra to both the yāʾ and the khāʾ, he too was seeking the kasra of the alif, because it had kasra at the beginning of the word. As for the one who combines the two quiescent letters, he is like one who builds on clear separate pronunciation (tibyān), except that it is a hidden assimilation. In His words ﴿أَم مَّنْ لاَ يَهِدِّى إلاَّ أَنْ يُهْدَى﴾ and in His words ﴿تَأخُذُهُمْ وَهُمْ يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾ the same explanation applies — except that Ḥamza al-Zayyāt read "تَأخُذُهُمْ وَهُمْ يَخْصِمُونَ" with a quiescent khāʾ, and that is a different meaning.

His words: ﴿كُلَّمَا أَضَآءَ لَهُمْ مَّشَوْاْ فِيهِ﴾: there are two dialects in it; one says أضاءَ القمرُ and ضاءَ القمرُ (the moon shone). Whoever says ضاء القمرُ says: يضوء ضَُوءا. And الضّوء has two dialects: ḍamma on the ḍād and fatḥa.

﴿وَإِذَآ أَظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْْ﴾: there are two dialects in it: أظلم الليل and ظَلِم (the night grew dark).

His words: ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَذَهَبَْ﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: had Allah willed, He would have taken away (لأذهب) their hearing. It is the way of the Arabs to say أذهبت بصره (I took away his sight), with the alif, when they drop the bāʾ; and when they make the bāʾ overt, they drop the alif from "أذهبت". Some readers read: "يَكَادُ سَنَا بَرْقِهِ يُذْهبُ بِالأَبْصَارِ", with ḍamma on the yāʾ and with the bāʾ in the phrase. And some read: "وَشَجَرَةً تَخْرُجُ مِنْ طُورِ سَينَاءَ تُنْبِتُ بالدُّهْنِ". So you see — and Allah knows best — that those who used ḍamma, with the meaning of the alif, likened the presence and absence of the bāʾ in these two words to their saying: خذْ بالخطام and خُذِ الخطامَ (take hold of the halter), and تعلَّقتُ بزيدٍ and تعلَّقتُ زيدا (I clung to Zayd). This is frequent in speech and poetry, but I do not favour it [Translator's note: i.e. combining the alif and the bāʾ] because it is rare. Of this kind are His words: ﴿آتِنَا غَدَاءَنَا﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: bring us (ايتنا) our morning meal; when the bāʾ was dropped they added an alif to faʿaltu [Translator's note: i.e. made it a fourth-form verb]. Of this kind too are His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَالَ آتُونِى أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْراً﴾, the meaning — according to what has come down — being: bring me molten copper that I may pour over it. And of this kind are His words: ﴿فَأَجَاءَهَا الْمَخَاضُ إِلَى جِذْعِ النَّخْلَةِ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: the pains of childbirth brought her (فجاء بها) to the trunk of the palm tree.

farraa:23-23.t: His words: ﴿فَأْتُواْ بِسُورَةٍ مِّن مِّثْلِهِِ﴾: the hāʾ is a pronoun (kināya) referring to the Qurʾān: so bring a surah like the Qurʾān. ﴿وَٱدْعُواْ شُهَدَآءَكُمْ﴾: He means your gods. He says: call on them for help. It is like your saying to a man: If you meet the enemy when you are alone, call (فادع) the Muslims — meaning: seek the help and support of the Muslims.

farraa:24-24.t:
His words: ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ تَفْعَلُواْ وَلَن تَفْعَلُواْ فَٱتَّقُواْ ٱلنَّارَ ٱلَّتِي وَقُودُهَا ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱلْحِجَارَةُ﴾: people are its fuel and stones are its fuel. They claimed that it [Translator's note: the stone] is like sulphur that is heated, and that it is the hottest of stones when heated. Then He said: ﴿أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ﴾, meaning the Fire.

His words: ﴿وَأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشَابِهاً﴾: it seemed alike to them, according to what has been mentioned, in its colour; but when they tasted it they knew that it was other than what had come before it. [Translator's note: this phrase belongs to verse 25; it stands in this entry in the source.]

farraa:26-26.t:
His words: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لاَ يَسْتَحْى أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلاً مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا﴾. If someone says: Where is the speech to which this is the answer? We do not see it in Sūrat al-Baqara. It has been mentioned to us that when Allah said: ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللهِ أَوْلِيَاءَ كَمَثَلِ الْعَنْكَبُوتِ اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتاً﴾, the Jews, the enemies of Allah, said: "What kind of parable is this?" And they said the like of that when He revealed: ﴿يَأَيُّهَا النَّاسُ ضُرِبَ مَثَلٌ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ منْ دُون اللَّهِ لَنْ يَخْلُقُوا ذُبَاباً﴾ — up to His words — ﴿ضَعُفَ الطَّالِبُ وَالْمَطْلُوبُ﴾, because of the mention of the fly and the spider. So Allah revealed: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لاَ يَسْتَحْى أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلاً مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا﴾. By what is "فَوْقَهَا" (above it) He means what is bigger than it, namely the spider and the fly. Had you used "فما فوقها" in similar speech meaning smaller than it, that would be permissible, but I do not consider it good, because the gnat is, as it were, the extreme of smallness, so I prefer to take "مَا فوقها" as bigger than it. Do you not see that you say: يُعطَى من الزكاة الخمسُون فما دونها (fifty and below is given from the zakāt) and الدرهمُ فما فوقه (a dirham and above)? The expression would be awkward if you said "above it" in both, or "below it" in both. As for where it is good in speech: someone says: إن فلانا لشريف (so-and-so is noble), and the listener says: وفوق ذاك (and above that), meaning praise; or he says: إنه لبخيل (he is miserly), and the other says: وفوق ذاك, meaning by both a greater degree. But if you know the man and say: دونَ ذلك (below that), it is as if you lower him from the extreme of nobility or the extreme of miserliness. Do you not see that when you say: إنه لبخيلٌ وفوق ذاك, you mean above miserliness, and "above that" [Translator's note: in the other case means] above nobility? And when you say: دون ذاك, you are someone who knows him and has brought him down a little from his rank. So never say وفوق ذاك except in praise or censure.

Al-Qurrāʾ [Translator's note: so in the text — "the readers"; probably a slip for al-Farrāʾ] said: As for their putting "بعوضة" in the accusative, it can be in three ways. The first: you let «الضرب» (striking [Translator's note: a parable]) fall on «البعوضة» and make "ما" a ṣila (redundant particle), as in His words: ﴿عَمّا قَلِيلٍ لَيُصْبِحُنَّ نَادِمِينَ﴾ [meaning عن قليل]; the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: Allah is not ashamed to strike a gnat and what is above it as a parable.

The second way: you make "ما" a noun and «البعوضة» its ṣila (complement), and you give it the inflection of "ما". That is permissible with "مَنْ" and "ما" because they are definite in one case and indefinite in another, as Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:
فَكَفَى بِنا فَضْلاً علَى مَنْ غَيْرِنا * حُبُّ النَّبِىءِ مُحَمّدٍ إِيّانا
(It suffices us as a distinction over anyone other than us, that the Prophet Muḥammad loves us.)
[Al-Farrāʾ said: It is also narrated: * ...على مَنْ غَيرُنا *.] The nominative in "بعوضة" here is permissible, because the ṣila is nominative while its noun [Translator's note: i.e. «ما»] is accusative or genitive. As for the third way — and it is the one I like best — you take the meaning to be: Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of whatever lies between a gnat and what is above it. When the Arabs drop "بَيْنَ" from speech at whose end "إِلَى" would be appropriate, they put in the accusative the two words that would have been genitive, one governed by "بَيْنَ" and the other by "إلى". So they say: مُطرْنا ما زُبالَةَ فالثّعْلبيةَ (we had rain from Zubāla to al-Thaʿlabiyya), له عشرون ما ناقةً فجملاً (he has twenty, from she-camel to he-camel), and هى أحسن الناس ما قَرْناً فقدَماً (she is the most beautiful of people from head to foot), meaning: between her head and her foot. You may also make القرن and القدم definite and say: هى حسنةٌ ما قرنَها فقدمَها.

When "إلى" is not appropriate at the end of the speech, dropping "بَيْن" is not permissible. An example is your saying: دارى ما بَيْنَ الكوفة والمدينة (my house is between Kufa and Medina): you may not say: دارى ما الكوفةَ فالمدينةَ, because "إلى" is appropriate only if everything between Medina and Kufa is your house, just as the rain covered everything from Zubāla to al-Thaʿlabiyya. Nor is the fāʾ appropriate in place of the wāw where "إلى" is not appropriate, as in your saying: دار فلان بَيْنَ الحِيرة فالكوفة — that is absurd; and جلست بين عبد الله فزيدٍ (I sat between ʿAbd Allāh then Zayd) — absurd, unless your seat takes up the whole space between them. The fāʾ is excluded where "إلى" is not appropriate only because the action there does not come in a continuous succession, whereas "إلى" requires two nouns between which the action runs [Translator's note: continuously] — even if it is like the blink of an eye, and however short the existing distance between them. So the fāʾ is appropriate where "إلى" is, because you say: the rain took its first part, then such-and-such, up to its end. And since the action is, in meaning, extensive, one thing after another, there is in it an interpretation akin to the conditional (jazāʾ). Similar to this is that they said: إن تأتنى فأنت مُحسنٌ (if you come to me, then you are doing good), while it is absurd to say: إن تأتنى وأنت محسن; they accepted the fāʾ as an apodosis in the conditional, but the wāw was not appropriate.

Al-Kisāʾī said: I heard a Bedouin who had seen the new crescent say: الحمد لله ما إِهلالَك إلى سَرارِك (praise be to Allah, from your appearing to your vanishing), meaning: between your appearing and your vanishing. They placed the accusative that would have been on "بَيْنَ" onto what follows it when it was dropped, so that it would be known that the meaning of "بَيْنَ" is intended. Al-Kisāʾī reported from some Arabs: الشّنَقُ: ما خَمْسا إلى خمس وعشرين (al-shanaq is what is between five and twenty-five), meaning: between five and twenty-five. Al-shanaq is the number of camels on which the obligatory levy is not due; the [Translator's note: corresponding term] for cattle is al-awqāṣ.

His words: ﴿مَاذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَـٰذَا مَثَلاً يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيراً وَيَهْدِي بِهِ كَثِيراً﴾: as though they said — and Allah knows best — What did Allah intend by a parable that not everyone understands, by which this one is led astray and that one is guided? Allah said: ﴿وَمَا يُضِلُّ بِهِ إِلاَّ الْفَاسِقِينَ﴾.

farraa:28-28.t:
His words: ﴿كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً﴾ is by way of wonder and rebuke, not a pure question; [i.e.] woe to you, how can you disbelieve! It is like His words: ﴿فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ﴾. His words: ﴿كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is "while you had been (وقد كنتم)"; were it not for the implied "قد", the like of it would not be permissible in speech. Do you not see that He said in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿إِنْ كَانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ دُبُرٍ فَكَذَبَتْ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: then she has lied (فقد كذبت)? And your saying to a man: أصبحتَ كَثُرَ مالُك (you have come to be with your wealth increased) is permissible only when you mean قد كَثُرَ مالُك, because both have already happened, so the second is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the first, and a ḥāl [Translator's note: that is a past verb] can only be with «قد» implied or overt. Similar to it in the Book of Allah: "أَوْ جَاءُوكُمْ حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ", meaning — and Allah knows best — [they came to you with their breasts already constricted]. One of the readers — al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī — read: "حَصِرَةً صدورهم".

It is as though he did not know the way [Translator's note: the past verb works] in أصبح عبد الله قام (ʿAbd Allāh came to be standing) or أقبل أخذ شاة (he came forward, having taken a sheep), as though he meant: فقد أخَذَ شاة. When the first [Translator's note: verb] has not [Translator's note: really] passed, the second is not permissible either with قد or without it, as in your saying: كاد قام (he almost stood) or أراد قام (he wanted, stood), because wanting is something that may happen while the action does not. For that reason your saying عسى قام (perhaps he stood) is absurd: although عسى has the form faʿala, it refers to the future; so one may not say عسى قد قام, nor عسى قام, nor كاد قد قام, nor كاد قام, because what follows them cannot be past. But if you bring يكون with عسى and كاد it becomes sound, and you say: عسى أن يكون قد ذهب (perhaps he has gone), as Allah said: ﴿قُلْ عَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُمْ بَعْضُ الَّذى تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾.

His words: ﴿وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً فَأَحْيَاكُمْ﴾ means: sperm-drops; and everything that separates from the body, such as hair or a sperm-drop, is dead — and Allah knows best. He says: then He gave you life from the sperm-drops, then He will cause you to die after life, then He will give you life for the Resurrection.

farraa:29-29.t: His words: ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَسَوَّاهُنَّ﴾. Al-istiwāʾ in the speech of the Arabs has two senses. One is that a man reaches full maturity [and] his youth comes to its peak, or that something straightens out from crookedness — these are two senses. A third sense is that you say: He was turned towards so-and-so, then he «استوى» towards me (عليّ) reviling me — and "إليّ" is the same — meaning he turned to me and against me. This is the meaning of His words ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾ — and Allah knows best. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Then He «استوى» to the heaven" means: He ascended. This is like your saying of a man: He was standing and then «استوى» sitting, or he was sitting and then «استوى» standing. All of this is permissible in the speech of the Arabs. As for His words: ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَسَوَّاهُنَّ﴾, «السماء» (the heaven) has a plural meaning, so He said "فَسَوَّاهُنّ" according to the known meaning, namely that they are seven heavens. Likewise the plural is applied to the earth, though it is one; and the singular [Translator's note: i.e. dual] is applied to the two of them though they are plural: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ﴾, then He said: ﴿وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ and did not say «بينهن» (between them [Translator's note: plural]). This is proof of what (I have told you).

farraa:31-31.t: His words: ﴿وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ ٱلأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلْمَلاَئِكَةِ﴾. ﴿عرضهم﴾ (He presented them) [Translator's note: with the masculine plural pronoun] follows the approach of the persons of the beings and the rest of creation. Had the names alone been intended, without the persons, "عرضهنّ" and "عرضها" would have been permissible. In the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh it is "ثم عرضهنّ", and in the version of Ubayy "ثم عرضها". If you say "عرضها", it may refer to the names without the persons, or to the persons without the names.

farraa:33-33.t: His words: ﴿يَآءَادَمُ أَنبِئْهُمْ بِأَسْمَآئِهِمْْ﴾. If you pronounce the hamza, you say ﴿أَنْبِئْهُمْ﴾, and kasra of the hāʾ and the mīm is not permissible, because it is a hamza, not a yāʾ that would make it like "عليهِم". If you drop the hamza, whether you then keep the yāʾ or not, ḍamma or kasra of "هِمُ" is permissible, as I described to you for "عليهِم" and "عليهُم".

farraa:148-148.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ﴾ means a qibla; ﴿هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا﴾: facing it. The verb belongs to "كلّ" (each); He means: turning his face to it.
Turning (tawliya) in this place is facing towards; in ﴿يولُّوكُم الأدبار﴾ and ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيتم مُدْبِرين﴾ it is turning away. It is like your saying in speech "inṣarif ilayya", i.e. come to me, and "inṣarif ilā ahlika", i.e. go to your family. Ibn ʿAbbās and others read "هو مُوَلاَّها", and so did Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, making the verb fall upon him [i.e. passive]. The meaning is one. And Allah knows best.
His saying: ﴿أَيْنَ مَا تَكُونُواْ...(148)﴾ — when you see interrogative particles joined to (ما), such as "أينما", "متى ما", "أىٌّ ما", "حيث ما", "كيف ما" and ﴿أيّاًمَّا تدعوا﴾, they are conditional (jazāʾ) and not interrogative. When they are not joined to (ما), the interrogative predominates in them, and the conditional is permissible in them.
When they are conditional, you put both verbs in the jussive: the verb with "أينما" and its sisters, and its answer, as in His saying ﴿أَيْنَ مَا تَكُونُواْ يَأْتِ بِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾. If you put the fāʾ in the answer, you put the answer in the nominative; you say in the like of it in speech: "aynamā takun fa-ātīka" (wherever you are, I come to you). So too the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿ومن كفر فَأُمتِّعه﴾.
When they are interrogative, you put the verb following "أين" and "كيف" in the nominative, then you put the second verb in the jussive, so that it is an answer to the question in the sense of a conditional; as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿هل أَدُلُّكُمْ على تجارةٍ تُنْجِيِكم مِن عَذابٍ أليم﴾, then He answered the question with the jussive, saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿يغفرْ لَكُمْ ذنوبَكم﴾.
When you put a fāʾ in the answer to a question, you use the accusative, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿لولا أَخَّرْتنِى إلى أَجلٍ قرِيبٍ فأَصَّدّقَ﴾ — so He used the accusative.
When you come to the conjoined verbs (ʿuṭūf) in the conditional, having answered it with the fāʾ, you have three options in the conjoined verb. If you wish, you put the conjoined verb in the nominative, as in your saying "in taʾtinī fa-innī ahlu dhāka, wa-tuʾjaru wa-tuḥmadu" (if you come to me, I am worthy of that, and you will be rewarded and praised); this is the normal way of speech. If you wish, you put it in the jussive, making it as if referred back to the position of the fāʾ; the nominative is on [the pattern of] what follows the fāʾ. The Readers have read "من يضلِلِ الله فلا هادِى له ويَذَرْهُم" in the nominative and the jussive. Likewise ﴿إِنْ تُبْدُوا الصّدقاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِى وإنْ تُخْفُوها وتُؤْتُوها الفقراءَ فَهْوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ ويُكَفِّرْ﴾, jussive and nominative. Had you used the accusative, on the pattern by which the conjoined verbs of a conditional take the accusative when it is complete, you would be right, as the poet said:
فإن يَهْلِكِ النعمانُ تُعْرَ مِطَّيةٌ * وتُخْبَأَ فى جوفِ العِيابِ قُطُوعُها
(If al-Nuʿmān perishes, a mount will be left unsaddled, and its saddle-gear hidden away inside the bags.)
And if you use the jussive for a conjoined verb after having used the accusative, referring it back to the first, it is correct, as he said after this verse:
وتَنْحِطْ حَصَانٌ آخِرَ اللّيلِ نَحْطةً * تَقَصَّمُ مِنها - أَو تَكادُ - ضُلوعها
(And a chaste woman will heave a sigh at the end of the night, from which her ribs break — or nearly.)
This is frequent in poetry and speech. The accusative in conjoined verbs is most common when there is no fāʾ in the answer of the conditional; when there is the fāʾ, it is the nominative and the jussive.
When you answer a question with the fāʾ and use the accusative, put the conjoined verbs in the accusative; if you put them in the jussive, it is correct. Of this is His saying regarding the hypocrites: ﴿لَوْلاَ أَخَّرْتَنِى إلى أَجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ فَأَصَّدَّق وأَكُنْ﴾ — you refer "وأَكُنْ" back to the position of the fāʾ, because it is in the position of the jussive, since the verb, had it occurred in its place without the fāʾ, would be jussive. The accusative is by referring it to what follows it, so you say "وأكونَ"; and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd it is "وأكون" with the wāw, and some of the Readers have read it so. He said: I consider that correct, because the wāw is sometimes omitted in writing while intended, because of how often it is dropped and added in speech. Do you not see that they write "الرحمن" and "سليمن" dropping the alif, while it is pronounced? For this reason it is permissible. The wāw has been dropped from His saying ﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِية﴾ and from His saying ﴿وَيَدْعُ الإِنْسانُ بالشّرِّ﴾ — the verse — while the recitation intends the wāw to be present. And they dropped two alifs from "الأيكة", writing it in one place "ليكة", while in another place it is "الأَيْكة"; and the Readers read it in full. This is a witness for the permissibility of "وأكون من الصَّالِحينَ".
One of the poets said:
فأَبلُونِى بَلِيَّتَكُم لَعَلِّى * أُصلُكُمْ وأَسْتَدْرِجْ نَوَيّا
(So grant me your favour; perhaps I will make peace with you and draw back my intention.) [Translator's note: "أُصلُكُمْ" as printed is unclear; it is commonly cited as "أُصالِحُكُمْ", which the gloss follows.]
He put (وأستدرجْ) in the jussive. If you wish, you refer it to the position of the implied fāʾ in "لعلّى"; and if you wish, you take it as being in the position of the nominative and the jīm was made quiescent because of the many successive vowels. Some of the Readers read "لا يَحْزُنْهُمُ الفَزَعُ الأَكْبَر" with the jussive while intending the nominative, and they read "أَنُلْزِمْكُموها وأَنْتُمْ لها كارِهون"; and the nominative is dearer to me than the jussive.
His saying: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ...(148)﴾ — the Arabs say: "This is a matter that has no wijha, no jiha, no wajh (direction)". I heard them say: "Turn the stone — jihatun mā lahu, wijhatu mā lahu, wajhun mā lahu" (it has some direction). And they say: "Put it other than this waḍʿa, ḍiʿa, ḍaʿa (placing)." Its meaning is: turn the stone, for it has a direction. It is a proverb whose origin is in building: they say, when you see a stone in a building not settling in its place, turn it around, for you will hit upon its right side. Had they used the accusative, on [the sense of] "turn it to its direction", it would have been correct.

farraa:150-151.t:
His saying: ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَيْكُمْ حُجَّةٌ إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾ — someone may say: how did He except "those who did wrong" in this place? Perhaps they imagined that what follows "إلاّ" differs from what precedes it: if what precedes "إلاّ" is an agent [of an affirmed verb], what follows it is excluded from the verb mentioned; and if the verb is negated of what precedes it, it is affirmed for what follows "إلا". As you say "The people went except Zayd" — Zayd is excluded from going; and "The people did not go except Zayd" — Zayd went, and the going is affirmed for Zayd.
So His saying ﴿إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾ [means: except those of them who did wrong] — they have no argument, ﴿فلا تَخْشَوْهُمْ﴾. It is as you say in speech: "All the people praise [you] except the one who wrongs you and transgresses against you", for his enmity is of no account, nor is his abandoning praise because of the enmity.
Likewise the wrongdoer has no argument; and he has been called a wrongdoer.
Some of the grammarians have said: "إلا" in this place has the status of the wāw (and), as if He said ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَيْكُمْ حُجَّةٌ﴾ nor for those who did wrong. This is correct in exegesis but wrong in Arabic. "إلا" has the status of the wāw only when you conjoin it to an exception before it; there it takes the status of the wāw, as in your saying "So-and-so owes me a thousand except ten except a hundred": by the second (إلاّ) you mean to go back to the thousand, as if you had overlooked the hundred and then made it up, saying "oh, except a hundred". So the meaning is: he owes me a thousand and a hundred. And [similarly] you say "The people went except your brother — oh, except your father", excepting the second, meaning: except your father and except your brother; as the poet said:
ما بالمدينةِ دار غيرُ واحدةٍ * دارُ الخليفة إلا دارُ مَروْانا
(There is no house in Medina but one — the house of the Caliph — except the house of Marwān.)
As if he meant: there is no house in Medina except the house of the Caliph and the house of Marwān.
His saying: ﴿وَٱخْشَوْنِي﴾ — the yāʾ is retained in it and not retained elsewhere, and all of that is correct. They only allowed dropping the yāʾ because the kasra of the nūn indicates it; the Arabs are not shy of dropping the yāʾ from the end of a word when what precedes it has kasra. Of that is "رَبِّى أَكْرَمَنِ" and "أَهانَنِ" in Sūrat al-Fajr, and His saying ﴿أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ﴾; and without the nūn, "المُناد" and "الداع"; and it is much. They make do for the yāʾ with the kasra of what precedes it, and for the wāw with the ḍamma of what precedes it, as in His saying ﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانيةَ﴾ and ﴿وَيدْعُ الإنْسانُ﴾ and the like. The Arabs may even drop the wāw when it is the plural wāw, making do with the ḍamma before it: they say for "ḍarabū" "qad ḍarabu", and for "qālū" "qad qālu dhālika"; this is among Hawāzin and Upper Qays. One of them recited to me:
إذا ما شاءُ ضرُّوا من أرادوا * ولا يألو لهم أحد ضرارا
(Whenever they wish, they harm whom they want, and no one spares effort in harming them.)
Al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
متى تقول خَلَتْ من أهلِها الدارُ * كأنهم بجناحى طائر طاروا
(Whenever you say "the abode is empty of its people", it is as if they had flown off on the two wings of a bird.)
And one of them recited to me:
فلو أَن الأطبّا كانُ عِندِى * وكان مع الأَطِباءِ الأسَاة
(Had the physicians been with me, and with the physicians the healers…)
They do that with the feminine yāʾ, as in the saying of ʿAntara:
إن العدوّ لهم إِليك وسِيلة * إِن يأْخذوكِ تكحَّلِى وتَخَضَّبِ
(The enemy has a means of reaching you: if they take you, put on kohl and dye yourself with henna.)
They drop (the feminine yāʾ), though it is the sign of the female, making do with the kasra.
His saying: ﴿كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا فِيكُمْ﴾ is an answer to His saying ﴿فاذْكُرونِى أَذْكُرْكُمْ﴾: "as We sent"; so this is an answer (placed before and after [i.e. with inversion]).
There is another view: you make it part of what precedes it, of His saying ﴿أذكركم﴾. Do you not see that He has given His saying ﴿اذكرونى﴾ a jussive answer? (That is evidence) that the kāf in (كما) belongs to what precedes it; for you say in speech "As I have done good, do good", and you do not need to set a condition for (أحسن), because the kāf is a condition; its meaning is: do as I have done. This is more sound (anfadh) in Arabic than the first view, which is what the exegesis brought. And it is correct, like a conditional that has two answers, as in your saying "If so-and-so comes to you, go to him; you will please him": "فأتِه" and "ترضه" have become two answers.

farraa:152-152.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱشْكُرُواْ لِي﴾ — the Arabs hardly ever say "shakartuka" (I thanked you); they say "shakartu laka" and "naṣaḥtu laka" (I gave you sincere counsel).
They do not say "naṣaḥtuka", though both are sometimes said. One of the poets said:
هُمُ جَمعوا بُؤْسَى ونُعْمَى عَليكُمُ * فهلاّ شكرتَ القومَ إذ لم تقاتِلِ
(They heaped upon you both hardship and favour; so why did you not thank the people, since you did not fight?)
And al-Nābigha said:
نصحتُ بنِى عوفٍ فلم يَتَقبّلوا * رسولى ولم تَنجحْ لديهِم وسائلِى
(I counselled Banū ʿAwf, but they did not receive my messenger, and my means of approach did not succeed with them.)

farraa:154-154.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَقُولُواْ لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ﴾ — nominative, by implying a pronoun standing for their names, as in your saying: Do not say "they are dead"; rather they are alive.
The accusative is not permissible in "أموات", because saying does not act upon nouns when their subjects are implied or made overt; just as "qultu ʿAbd Allāha qāʾiman" is not permissible, so the accusative of "أموات" is not permissible, because you are implying their names. The accusative after "saying" is permissible only when the noun has the sense of a saying. Of that is "qultu khayran" and "qultu sharran" (I said good, I said evil): you see "good" and "evil" in the accusative because they are sayings, as if you said: I said fine or ugly words. You say "qultu laka khayran" and "qultu laka khayrun", and both are permissible: if you make "good" a saying you put it in the accusative, as if you said "I said words to you"; if you put it in the nominative, it is not the saying, but rather it is like your saying "qultu laka mālun" [Translator's note: i.e. "I said to you: [there is] wealth", a quoted sentence].
So build on this whatever comes to you. Of the nominative is His saying ﴿سيقولُون ثَلاثَةٌ رَابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ﴾, and "خمسةٌ" and "سبعةٌ": it cannot be accusative, because it is a report about them containing implied nouns, as in your saying "they are three", "they are five". As for His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ طَاعةٌ﴾, it is nominative on a different basis. That is, it used to be said to the Arabs: "You must go on raids in winter and summer", and they would say "hearing and obedience", meaning: from us is hearing and obedience; so the speech ran in the nominative. Had it been accusative, in the sense of "we hear a hearing and obey an obedience", it would have been correct.
Likewise His saying, blessed and exalted, in Sūrat Muḥammad ﷺ: ﴿فَأَوْلَى لَهُم طَاعةٌ وقَوْلٌ مَعْرُوف﴾. He reproached and threatened them with His saying "فأولى لهم" (woe to them), then mentioned what they say, so He said: they say, when they are commanded, "Obedience!" — "فإذا عزم الأمر" (but when the matter was resolved) they shrank back and lied and did not do it. So Allah, blessed and exalted, said ﴿فلَوْ صَدَقُوا الله لكانَ خَيْراً لهم﴾. Some of them may say: "طاعة" is nominative only by His saying "لهم", [i.e.] "they should have obedience"; and that is nothing.
And Allah knows best. It is also said [that it means]: "وذكِر فيها القِتال" (and fighting was mentioned in it) "and obedience", the wāw being implied; but that is not, in our view, among the ways of the Arabs; yet if it agrees with the exegesis, it is correct.

farraa:155-155.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُمْ بِشَيْءٍ مِّنَ ٱلْخَوْفِ وَٱلْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ ٱلأَمَوَالِ وَٱلأَنفُسِ وَٱلثَّمَرَاتِ﴾ — He did not say (بأشياء) (with things) although they differ. That is because "مِن" indicates that for each kind of them there is an implied "شىء": with something of fear and something of such-and-such. Had it been "بأشياء" it would have been correct.

farraa:156-156.t:
His saying: ﴿قَالُواْ إِنَّا للَّهِ﴾ — the Arabs do not give kasra to (إنا) except in this place, with the lām, specifically in expressing grief. When they do not say (لِلّه), they give it fatḥa and say "innā li-Zaydin muḥibbūn" (we love Zayd) and "innā li-rabbinā ḥāmidūn ʿābidūn" (we praise and worship our Lord).
It was given kasra in ﴿إِنَّا للَّهِ﴾ only because it was so used that it became like a single word, so the nūn was inclined towards kasra (imāla) because of the kasra of the lām in "لِلّه"; as they say "hālik" and "kāfir" — the kāf of "kāfir" is given kasra [i.e. imāla] because of the kasra [after] the alif, since it is a single word. So "إنا لِلّهِ" became like a single word because of their frequent use of it, as they said "al-ḥamdi lillāhi".

farraa:158-158.t:
His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ حَجَّ ٱلْبَيْتَ أَوِ ٱعْتَمَرَ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا﴾ — the Muslims had disliked going between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa because of two idols that were on them; they disliked that it should be a veneration of the two idols. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلصَّفَا وَٱلْمَرْوَةَ مِن شَعَآئِرِ ٱللَّهِ فَمَنْ حَجَّ ٱلْبَيْتَ أَوِ ٱعْتَمَرَ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا﴾. Some read it "أَلاَّ يطَّوف" (that he not go round), and this can be in two ways. One is that you make "لا" with "أنْ" a ṣila (filler) in the sense of cancellation, as He said ﴿ما مَنَعَك أَلاَّ تَسْجُدَ إذْ أَمَرْتُك﴾, meaning: what prevented you from prostrating. The other is that you make going between them something whose omission is permitted. The first is what is acted upon.
His saying: ﴿وَمَن تَطَوَّعَ خَيْراً﴾ — you give it fatḥa (as a past verb). The companions of ʿAbd Allāh, and Ḥamza, [read] "وَمَنْ يَطَّوَّعْ", because in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it is "يتطوع".

farraa:159-159.t:
His saying: ﴿أُولَـٰئِكَ يَلعَنُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَيَلْعَنُهُمُ ٱللاَّعِنُونَ﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbās said: "اللاعِنون" (those who curse) are everything on the face of the earth except the two weighty ones (al-thaqalān, mankind and jinn).
[And] ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: When two men curse each other, and one of them curses his fellow while neither deserves the curse, the curse returns to whoever deserves it; and if neither of them deserves it, it returns to the Jews who concealed what Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed. So he made the curse [come] from people who curse one another, according to what he explained.

farraa:246-246.t:
His saying: ﴿ٱبْعَثْ لَنَا مَلِكاً نُّقَاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — (نُقَاتِلْ) is jussive (majzūm); its nominative is not permissible. If it were read with the yāʾ, "yuqātil," both its nominative and its jussive would be permissible. As for the jussive, it is as the apodosis to the command; as for the nominative, it is that you make (yuqātilu) a ṣila (relative clause) for al-malik, as if you had said: send for us the one who will fight.
So when you see after the command an indefinite noun, after which comes a verb that refers back to it by a pronoun, or in which verb it is suitable to imply the noun, both the nominative and the jussive are permissible in it. You say in speech: "Teach me knowledge that I may benefit from (antafiʿu bihi)," as if you said: "Teach me that from which I benefit"; and if you put (antafiʿ) in the jussive, making it a condition [i.e. apodosis] for the command, as if you had not mentioned the knowledge, that is permissible. If you drop "bihi," it can only be jussive, because the pronoun is not permissible in (antafiʿ); do you not see that you do not say: "Teach me knowledge that I benefit it (antafiʿuhu)"?
If you say: "Why then did you not use the nominative, intending the implied (bihi)?" I say: it is not permissible to imply two words [Translator's note: the preposition and its pronoun]; therefore only the jussive is permissible in His saying (نقاتل).
Similar to it: ﴿اقتُلُوا يُوسُفَ أو اطْرَحُوهُ أرْضاً يَخْلُ لَكُمْ وَجْه أبيكم﴾ — only the jussive is permissible, because "yakhlu" does not refer back with a mention of the land. Had it been "a land that will be free (takhlu) for you," the nominative and the jussive would be permissible, as He said: ﴿رَبَّنَا وابْعَثْ فِيهم رَسُولا مِنهم يَتْلُو عليهم آياتِك ويعلِّمُهُمُ الكتَابَ والحِكمة ويزكِّيهم﴾, and as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿خُذْ مِن أَمْوَالِهِم صدقة تُطَهِّرهم وتُزَكِّيهِم﴾; had it been jussive it would be correct, for in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "أنزِل علينا مائدة من السماءِ تَكُنْ لنا عِيدا", while in our reading it is with the wāw: "takūnu".
Of it is what in which the jussive is better: that is when the verb that may be put in the jussive or nominative is in one verse, and the noun for which the verb would be a ṣila is in the verse before it; then the jussive is better because the noun is cut off from its ṣila. Of that: ﴿فهَبْ لِى مِن لدنك ولِيّاً. يرِثنى﴾ — Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read it in the jussive — and Ḥamza read it in the nominative, "yarithunī" [Translator's note: so in the text; elsewhere Ḥamza is reported with the jussive here], for this reason, and some of the Readers also read it in the nominative — since (وليا) was the end of a verse, His saying (يرثنى) was cut off from it, so the jussive was good. Of that is His saying: ﴿وابْعَثْ فى المدائن حاشِرين. يَأتُوك﴾ in the jussive. Had it been nominative as a ṣila of "al-ḥāshirīn," you would say: yaʾtūnaka.
If the noun after which comes a verb referring back to it is definite — of the kind in whose indefinite two possibilities are allowed — you use the jussive, saying: "Send your brother to me, he will bring (yuṣib) news"; it can only be jussive, because al-akh is definite and a definite cannot take a ṣila [of this kind]. Of it is His saying: ﴿أَرْسِلْهُ مَعَنَا غَداً يَرْتَعْ وَيَلْعَبْ﴾ — the hāʾ is definite, and "ghadan" is definite, so there is only the jussive in it; and like His saying: ﴿قاتِلوهم يُعَذِّبْهُمُ الله﴾ — jussive and nothing else.
Of this there is a type where, when after its definite noun there is a verb belonging to it, the nominative and the jussive are both permissible; like His saying: ﴿فَذَرُوهَا تَأْكُلْ فى أَرْضِ الله﴾ and His saying: ﴿ذَرْهُمْ يأْكُلُوا﴾; had it been nominative it would be correct, as He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ثُمَّ ذَرْهُمْ فى خَوْضِهِم يَلْعَبُون﴾, and did not say: yalʿabū.
As for its nominative, it is that you make "yalʿabūna" in the position of the accusative, as if you said in speech: "Leave them playing (lāʿibīna)." Likewise daʿhum, khallihim and utrukhum. Every verb that can act on a definite noun and on its action has these two possibilities, and the jussive is the proper way of speech in it, because the condition sits well in it and because the command in it is easy; do you not see that you say: "Tell him, and let him stand with you"?
If you see that the second verb admits the test of the command [i.e. can be recast as a command], it has both possibilities in the same manner. In one of the two readings: "ذَرْهُمْ يَأْكُلُونَ ويَتَمَتَّعون ويلهِيهم الأَمل".
There is another way in it that sits well with the first verb. Of that: "Instruct him to come (yaʾti) to Zayd," or "Command him," or "Send to him." This goes the way of speech [qawl], and its jussive is akin to a command intended for him anew. It is put in the jussive only as a condition [apodosis] of its first [part]. Of that is your saying: "Command ʿAbd Allāh, he will go (yadhhab) with us"; do you not see that "say" can be put in the place of (mur)? And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿قُلْ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَغْفِرُوا لِلذين لاَ يَرْجُونَ أيَّامَ الله﴾ — "yaghfirū" is in the position of the jussive, and the interpretation — and Allah knows best — is: Say to those who believe: forgive; as a condition [apodosis] of the command that carries the interpretation of reported speech (ḥikāya). Similar to it: ﴿قل لِعبادِى يَقُولُوا الَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَن﴾ — you put it in the jussive by the condition "qul." Some said: [it is jussive] by the intention of a command in these words: of saying, commanding and instructing. It was said to them: if it is jussive as reported speech, then you ought to say to a man to his face: "I told you you stand (taqum)," and you ought to say: "I commanded you you go (tadhhab) with us." This is evidence that it is a condition of the command. If you say: "But the poet said:
فلا تستطِلْ منّى بقائى ومُدّتِى * ولكن يكن للخير فيك نصيب
(Do not find my survival and my lifespan too long; rather, let goodness have a share in you.)"
I say: this is jussive by the intention of a command, because the beginning of the speech is a prohibition, and his saying (ولكن) is a conjunction and not an apodosis; he meant: but let goodness have a share in you. Similar to it is the other's saying:
من كان لا يزعم أنى شاعرُ * فَيَدْنُ منى تنهَه المزاجِر
(Whoever does not allow that I am a poet, let him draw near me — the rebukes will restrain him.)
He made the fāʾ the answer of the condition and implied in (fa-yadnu) a lām that puts [it] in the jussive. And the other said:
فقلت ادْعِى وأَدْعُ فإنَّ أَنْدَى * لصوتٍ أن ينادِىَ داعيان
(So I said: Call out, and let me call, for the farthest-carrying for a voice is that two callers call.)
He meant: wa-li-adʿu. And in his saying (وأَدْع) there is a trace of the condition, even though it is a command whose first part is conjoined on its last. It is like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿اتَّبِعوا سبِيلنا ولْنحمِل خطاياكم﴾, and Allah knows best. As for His saying: ﴿ذَرُونِى أَقْتُلْ مُوسَى وَلْيَدْعُ رَبَّه﴾, it does not have the interpretation of a condition; it is purely a command, because dropping the wāw and turning it back to the condition (does not sit well, so it is not a condition); do you not see that it does not sit well to say: "Leave me, I will kill him, he will call (yadʿu)," as "Follow our way, we will carry (taḥmil) your sins" sits well? [Translator's note: so in the text: تَحْمل.]
The Arabs do not give an apodosis to a prohibition as they give one to a command. That is because the prohibition comes with negation, and the Arabs do not give an apodosis to any negation; they answer it only with the fāʾ. And they joined the prohibition, when it is with lā, to laysa and mā and their sisters among negations. So if you see a prohibition after whose noun there is a verb, put that verb in the nominative. You say: "Do not let him hit him (yaḍribuhu)," and "Do not leave him hitting you (yaḍribuka)." They made it nominative since its end did not match its beginning, since in its beginning there is negation and in its end there is no negation. If you said: "Do not leave him — let him not harm you (lā yuʾdhika)," the jussive and the nominative would be permissible, since its beginning is like its end; as you say in the command: "Leave him, he sleeps (yanāmu)," and "Leave him, he will sleep (yanam)," since there is no negation in either. If you command and then put (lā) in the verb, you use the nominative, again because of their difference, saying: "Come to us — we will not harm you (lā nusīʾu ilayka)," as in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿وأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بالصَّلاَةِ واصْطَبِرْ عليها لا نسألك رِزقا﴾ — [since] the beginning of the speech was a command and its end a negation with (lā), and they differed, (lā) was made in the sense of laysa, so it was put in the nominative. Of that is His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فَقَاتِلْ فِى سَبِيلِ الله لاَ تُكَلَّفُ إلاّ نَفْسَكَ﴾ and His saying: ﴿يَأَيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا عَلَيْكُم أَنْفُسَكم لا يَضُرُّكُم مَنْ ضَلَّ إذَا اهْتديتم﴾ — nominative. And of it is His saying: ﴿فاجعل بيننا وبينك مَوْعِداً لا نُخلِفُهُ﴾ — you use the nominative, and had you intended the condition it would be permissible by the analogy of grammar. Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and Ḥamza read: "فاضْرِبْ لهم طرِيقا فى البحر يَبَساً لا تخف دركا ولا تخشى" as a pure apodosis.
If you say: "Then how was the yāʾ kept in (تخشى)?" I say: there are three ways regarding that. If you wish, you make "wa-lā takhshā" a fresh start after the jussive. If you wish, you make (takhshā) in the position of the jussive even though the yāʾ is in it, because some of the Arabs do that; one of Banū ʿAbs said:
ألم يأتيك والأنباءُ تَنْمِى * بما لاقت لَبُونُ بنى زياد
(Has it not reached you — and the news spreads — what the milch-camels of Banū Ziyād met with?)
So the yāʾ was kept in (يأتيك) while it is in the position of the jussive, because he saw it as quiescent and left it in its quiescence, as is done with the other letters. And one of Banū Ḥanīfa recited to me:
قال لها مِن تحتها وما استوى * هُزِّى إليِك الجِذْع يَجنِيك الجَنَى
(He said to her from beneath her, before he had grown: Shake the trunk toward you, it will yield you the ripe fruit.)
and he ought to have said: yajniki. And one of them recited to me with the wāw:
هجوتَ زَبّان ثم جئت معتذِرا * من سبّ زَبَّان لم تهجو ولم تدع
(You lampooned Zabbān, then came apologizing for insulting Zabbān — you did not [truly] lampoon, nor did you leave off.)
The third way is that the yāʾ is an extension (ṣila) of the fatḥa of the shīn, as Imruʾ al-Qays said:
* ألا أيُّها الليلُ الطويل ألا انجلى *
(O long night, will you not clear away?)
This yāʾ is not the final radical of the verb; it is an extension of the kasra of the lām, just as rhymes are extended by the vowel of their rhyme-letter, like the saying of al-Aʿshā:
* بانت سُعَادُ وأمسى حبلُها انقطاعا *
(Suʿād has gone away, and her bond has come to be severed.)
and the other's saying:
* أمِن أُمِّ أوفى دِمْنةٌ لم تكلمى *
(Is it of Umm Awfā — a campsite trace that does not speak?)
The second [verb] may be jussive, when it has (lā), on the intention of a prohibition while carrying some meaning of the condition, just as in His saying ﴿وَلْنَحْمِلْ خَطَايَاكُمْ﴾ there is a trace of the condition while it is a command. Of that is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿يأيُّها النَّمل ادْخُلُوا مَساكِنَكُم لا يَحْطِمَنَّكُم سُلَيْمانُ وجُنُوده﴾ — the meaning, and Allah knows best: if you do not enter, you will be crushed; and it is a pure prohibition, because had it been an apodosis neither the heavy nor the light nūn would enter it; do you not see that you do not say: "If you hit me I will surely hit you (aḍribannaka)," except in poetic necessity, as in his saying:
فمهما تشأ منه فَزَارةُ تُعْطِكُم * ومهما تَشَأ منه فَزَارةُ تمنعَا
(Whatever of it Fazāra wishes, it will give you; and whatever of it Fazāra wishes, it will surely withhold.)
His saying: ﴿وَمَا لَنَآ أَلاَّ نُقَاتِلَ﴾ — (أَن) came in one place and was dropped in another. He said in another place: ﴿وَمَا لَكُمْ لا تُؤْمِنونَ بالله والرَّسُولُ يَدْعُوكم﴾, and He said in another place: ﴿وما لنا ألاَّ نتوكّل على الله﴾. Whoever drops (an), the word is in the manner of Arabic in which there is no problem, and the verb is in the position of the accusative [Translator's note: as a ḥāl], like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فما لِلَّذينَ كفروا قِبَلَكَ مُهْطعين﴾ and like His saying: ﴿فما لَكُمْ فى المنافِقِين فِئَتَيْنِ﴾. This is the proper way of speech in your saying: mā laka? mā bāluka? and mā shaʾnuka?: that you put what follows it in the accusative when it is a noun, and in the nominative when it is a verb beginning with yāʾ, tāʾ, nūn or alif, like the poet's saying:
* مالك تَرْغِين ولا تَرْغُو الخَلِفْ *
(What is wrong with you that you groan, while the pregnant she-camel does not groan?)
Al-khalifa: the one with her young in her belly.
As for when He said (أن), it is of what goes toward the meaning that admits the entry of (an); do you not see that your saying to a man: "What is wrong with you that you do not pray in congregation?" means "What prevents you from praying?" So (an) was put into (mā laka) since its meaning agreed with the meaning of preventing. The proof of that is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿مَا مَنَعَكَ أن لا تسجد إذ أمرتك﴾ and in another place: ﴿مالك ألاّ تكون مع الساجدين﴾; the story of Iblīs is one, and He said it in two wordings whose meaning is one even though they differ.
Similar to it — what is carried on a meaning different from its counterpart in wording — is the poet's saying:
يقول إذا اقْلَوْلى عليها وأقْرَدَتْ * ألا هل أخو عيشٍ لذيذ بدائم
(He says, when he mounts high upon her and she grows still: Is the man of a pleasant life ever lasting?)
He put the bāʾ in (hal), which is interrogative, whereas the bāʾ enters only the mā of negation, as when you say: "You are not one to say (mā anta bi-qāʾil)." Since the intention in (hal) was negation, the bāʾ was put in for it. Similar to it is His saying in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "كَيْفَ يكونُ لِلمشْرِكين عَهْدٌ": [meaning] the idolaters have no [covenant]. Likewise the poet's saying:
فاذهب فأىُّ فتىً فى الناس أحرزه * من يومه ظُلَمٌ دُعْج ولا جَبَل
(Go, then: what young man among people have pitch-dark shadows protected from his fated day — nor a mountain?)
(he answered it with lā) as though the meaning of "what young man among people have they protected" is: pitch-dark shadows do not protect the young man from his fated day, nor does a mountain. Al-Kisāʾī said: I heard the Arabs say: "Where were you to escape me (ayna kunta li-tanjuwa minnī)!" because the meaning is: you were not going to escape me; so he put the lām in (ayna) because its meaning is negation: you were not going to escape me. And the poet said:
فهذى سيوف يا صُدَىُّ بن مالك * كثير ولكن أين بالسيف ضارب
(Here are swords, O Ṣudayy ibn Mālik, many — but where is one who strikes with the sword?)
He meant: there is no one striking with the sword; had he not meant (laysa), the expression would not be permissible, because the bāʾ belongs to the ṣila of (ḍārib), and the complement of a noun is not put before it; do you not see that you do not say: "I struck with the slave girl a guarantor," until you say: "I struck a guarantor with the slave girl"? [Translator's note: the example is as written; the point is the word order of the prepositional complement.] And it is permissible to say: "There is no guarantor for the slave girl (laysa bi-l-jāriya kafīl)," because (laysa) is the counterpart of (mā), since it is not proper for it to put the noun in the nominative just as (mā) does not put it in the nominative.
Al-Kisāʾī said of their putting (an) in (mā laka): it is like His saying: "What is wrong with you in not fighting (mā lakum fī allā tuqātilū)." Had it been as he said, it would be permissible in speech to say: "What is wrong with you that you stood (an qumta)," and "What is wrong with you that you are standing (annaka qāʾim)," because you say "in your standing" both past and future; that is not permissible, because preventing comes only with the future: you say: "I prevented you from standing (an taqūma)," and you do not say: "I prevented you that you stood (an qumta)."
Therefore it comes in (mā laka) with the future and does not come with the continuous or the past. That is a witness to the agreement of the meaning of mā laka and mā manaʿaka. Some grammarians have said: it is among the cases where the wāw is implied, deleted from what is like your saying in speech: "What have you to do with going to so-and-so (mā laka wa-li-an tadhhaba)?" — so the wāw was dropped from it because (an) is a word not firmly established among nouns.
It was said [to him]: "Do you permit me to say: mā laka an taqūma, and not permit: mā laka al-qiyāma?" [He said]: "Because al-qiyām is a sound noun and (an) is a noun that is not sound." He argued from the saying of the Arabs: "Beware of speaking (iyyāka an tatakallama)," and claimed that the meaning is: iyyāka wa-an tatakallama. This was refuted against him by the fact that the Arabs say: "Beware of uttering falsehood (iyyāka bi-l-bāṭili an tanṭiqa)"; had the wāw been implied with (an), the verbs after the wāw could not act on what precedes it; do you not see that it is not permissible to say: "I hit you with the slave girl, and you are a guarantor," meaning: and you are a guarantor for the slave girl? And you say: "I saw you, and it is us you want (wa-iyyānā turīdu)," and it is not permissible: "I saw you us, and you want." The poet said:
فبُحْ بالسرائر فى أهلها * وإيّاك فى غيرهم أن تبوحا
(Disclose secrets among those fit for them, and beware of disclosing them among others.)
So the verb after (an) was allowed to act on his saying (فى غيرهم), and that shows that implying the wāw with (an) is not permissible.
As for the poet's saying:
* فإياك المَحَايِن أن تحينا *
(Beware of the places of perdition, lest you perish.)
he warned him, saying "iyyāka," then intended a pause, then began (al-maḥāyin) with another command, as if he said: beware of the places of perdition. Had he meant something like "iyyāka wa-l-bāṭila," dropping the wāw would not be permissible, because it is a noun made to follow a noun in its accusative, so it would be like his saying outside [the case of] the command: "You and your opinion," and "every garment and its price"; just as "You your opinion" or "every garment its price" is not permissible, so "iyyāka al-bāṭila" is not permissible when you mean: iyyāka wa-l-bāṭila.

farraa:249-249.t:
His saying: ﴿فَشَرِبُواْ مِنْهُ إِلاَّ قَلِيلاً مِّنْهُمْ﴾ — in one of the two readings: "إلا قليلٌ منهم" (in the nominative).
The proper way with (illā) is that what follows it is put in the accusative when what precedes it contains no negation. When what precedes illā contains negation, you make what follows it follow what precedes it [in case], whether it is definite or indefinite.
As for the definite, it is your saying: "The people did not go except Zayd (illā Zaydun)." As for the indefinite, it is your saying: "There is no one in it except your slave (illā ghulāmuka)"; this has not come from the Arabs except with what follows illā following what precedes it. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ما فعلوه إلاّ قليل مِنهم﴾, because in (faʿalūhu) there is a definite noun [Translator's note: the pronoun], so the nominative was the proper way in the negation that negates the act of them and affirms it for what follows illā. In the reading of Ubayy it is "ما فعلوه إلا قليلا", as if he negated the act and made what follows illā as though cut off from the beginning of the speech, as when you say: "The people did not stand — except, O Allah, a man (illā rajulan)." So if you intend the cut-off [exception] you use the accusative, and if you intend the connected [exception] you use the nominative. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿فلولا كانت قرية آمنت فنفعها إِيمانها إلا قوم يونس﴾ — this is on this meaning; and similar to it: ﴿فلولا كان مِن القُرُونِ مِن قَبْلِكم أُولُو بقِيّةٍ ينهون عن الفساد فى الأرض﴾, then He said: ﴿إلا قلِيلا ممن أَنجينا منهم﴾. The beginning of the speech — even though it is a question — is a negation, because lawlā is equivalent to hallā; do you not see that when you say to a man: (hallā qumta, "why did you not stand?") its meaning is: you did not stand. Had what follows (illā) in these two verses been nominative with the intention of connection, it would have been correct, like His saying: ﴿لو كان فيهما آلهة إلاَّ اللّهُ لفسدتا﴾ — this is the intention of connection, because it is not permissible to pause on what precedes (illā).
If you do not see a noun before (illā), make what precedes it act on what follows it. You say: (mā qāma illā Zaydun) — you put (Zayd) in the nominative because you make (qāma) act, since you found no noun for (qāma) [before illā]. Likewise: "I hit none but your brother (illā akhāka)," and "I passed by none but your brother (illā bi-akhīka)."
When what precedes (illā) is indefinite with a negation, you make what follows illā follow what precedes it, as when you say: "There is no one with me except your brother (illā akhūka)." If you put illā first, you put in the accusative what you used to put in the nominative, saying: "None came to me except your brother — no one (mā atānī illā akhāka aḥadun)." That is because (illā) was conjoined onto what preceded it, so it followed it; when it was put first, it was prevented from following something that is after it, so they chose the exception [accusative]. Similar to it is the poet's saying:
لَمِيَّة مُوحِشاً طَلَلٌ * يلوح كأنه خِلَل
(Mayya has a desolate ruin that gleams as if it were sheath-linings.)
The meaning is: Mayya has a desolate ruin (ṭalalun mūḥishun); its nominative was right because it followed al-ṭalal, but when it was put first, it could not follow al-ṭalal which comes after it. Its nominative may be permissible if you make it like a noun of which al-ṭalal is an explanation, as you say: "I have a Khurāsānī — a slave girl (khurāsāniyyatun jāriyatun)," though the proper way is the accusative in khurāsāniyya. Some of the Arabs put in the nominative what is placed first with illā according to this explanation. He said: and they recited to us:
بالثِنْىِ أسفلَ من جَمَّاءَ ليس له * إلاَّ بنيهِ وإلا عِرْسَه شِيعَ
