(At the bend below Jammāʾ, he has no followers save his sons and save his wife.)
And it is recited: illā banūhu wa-illā ʿirsuhu. Abū Tharwān recited:
ما كان منذ تركنا أهل أَسْمنُةٍ * إلا الوجيفَ لها رِعْىٌ ولا عَلَفُ
(Since we left the people of Asmuna, she has had no pasture nor fodder save hard travel.)
and someone else recited it in the nominative. Dhū al-Rumma said:
مُقَزَّعٌ أطلسُ الأطمارِ ليس له * إلا الضِرَاءَ وإلا صيدَها نَشَبُ
(Thin-haired, in grey rags, he has no property save his hunting hounds and save what they hunt.)
Its nominative is on the basis that he built his speech on: "he has nothing but the hounds and their prey," and then mentioned (nashab) at the end of the speech; it becomes clear if you put its place at the beginning of the speech.
﴿كَم مِّن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةًً﴾ — in the reading of Ubayy: "كأيّن مِن فِئةٍ قليلة غلبت", and they are two dialects. Likewise ﴿وكأيّن من نبى﴾ — they are all dialects whose meaning is the meaning of kam. If you drop (min), the indefinite noun has the accusative and the genitive. Of that is the saying of the Arabs: "How many a noble man (kam rajulin karīmin) I have seen!" and "How many a vast army (kam jayshan jarrāran) I have defeated!" These are two ways: they are put in the accusative and in the genitive, and the verb in meaning acts on [them]. If the verb does not act on [it] but belongs to the noun [as its agent], the accusative and the genitive are also permissible; and it is permissible to make the verb act and put the indefinite in the nominative by it, saying: "How many a noble man (kam rajulun karīmun) has come to me," putting it in the nominative by its verb; and you make the verb act on it if it falls on it, saying: "How many a vast army (kam jayshan jarrāran) I have defeated," putting it in the accusative by hazamtu. They recited the poet's saying:
كم عمَّة لك يا جَرِيرُ وخالة * فَدْعاء قد حَلَبَتْ علىَّ عِشارِى
(How many a paternal aunt of yours, O Jarīr, and maternal aunt with crooked fingers have milked my ten-month pregnant camels for me!)
in the nominative, the accusative and the genitive. Whoever uses the accusative says: the origin of kam was the interrogative, and the indefinite after it is a specification like the specification of numbers; so we left it in the declarative in its own manner and as it was in the interrogative, and put in the accusative the indefinites after (kam), as you say: "I have such-and-such dirhams (dirhaman)." Whoever uses the genitive says: min has long accompanied the indefinite with kam, so when we deleted it, we made its intention operative, and put it in the genitive, just as the Arabs said, when one of them was asked: "How are you this morning?" — "Well (khayrin), may Allah keep you well," in the genitive, meaning: bi-khayrin. As for whoever uses the nominative, he made the later verb operative [and] intended the verb to come first, as if he said: how many times has a noble man come to me. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
تَبُوصُ وكَمْ مِن دونها من مفازةٍ * وكم أرضُ جَدْب دونها ولُصُوصُ
(She draws away — and how many a desert lies short of her, and how many a barren land and thieves lie short of her!)
He used the nominative on the intention of putting the verb first. The verb is made to come first in intention only because indefinites do not precede their verbs [i.e. their predicates]; do you not see that you say: "There is nothing with me (mā ʿindī shayʾun)," and you do not say: "mā shayʾun ʿindī"?

farraa:161-161.t:
His saying: ﴿إِن الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَمَاتُوا وَهُمْ كُفَّارٌ أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ — "الملائكة والناس" are in the position of the genitive (khafḍ); the curse is annexed to them, in the sense: upon them is the curse of Allah, the curse of the angels and the curse of the people. Al-Ḥasan read it "لعنة اللّهِ والملائِكةُ والناسُ أجمعون", which is permissible in Arabic, even though it differs from the written text. That is because your saying (عليهم لعنة اللّهِ) is like your saying "Allah curses them, and the angels and the people curse them". The Arabs say "ʿajibtu min ẓulmika nafsaka" (I marvelled at your wronging yourself), putting "nafs" in the accusative, because the kāf is nominative in interpretation [i.e. the agent]. And they say "ʿajibtu min ghalabatika nafsuka" (I marvelled at your self's overpowering you), putting "nafs" in the nominative, because the kāf is accusative in interpretation. So build on this whatever comes to you.
Of that is the Arabs' saying "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭi l-buyūti baʿḍuhā ʿalā baʿḍin" and "baʿḍihā ʿalā baʿḍin" (I marvelled at the houses falling one upon another). Whoever uses the nominative refers "baʿḍ" to the interpretation of "the houses", because they are nominative [in sense]; do you not see that the meaning is: I marvelled that they fell, one upon another? And whoever uses the genitive makes it follow the wording of "the houses", as if he said: at the falling of one of them upon another. The nominative is best when the first [noun], which is nominative or accusative in interpretation, has been replaced by a pronoun, as in your saying "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭihā". Here you say "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭihā baʿḍuhā ʿalā baʿḍin", because when the genitive is a pronoun it is ugly to qualify it with an overt noun, so it is referred to the meaning, which would be nominative if overt; and the genitive is permissible. You do the like of this with what is accusative in interpretation, saying "ʿajibtu min idkhālihim baʿḍahum fī ithri baʿḍin" (I marvelled at their bringing in some of them after others): you prefer the accusative in (baʿḍahum), and the genitive is permissible.

farraa:164-164.t: His saying: ﴿وَتَصْرِيفِ ٱلرِّيَاحِ﴾ — it comes once as a south wind, once as a north wind, and as an east wind and a west wind. That is its turning about.

farraa:165-165.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ أَندَاداً يُحِبُّونَهُمْ كَحُبِّ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — He means — and Allah knows best — they love the rivals as the believers love Allah. Then He said: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ أَشَدُّ حُبّاً للَّهِ﴾ than those [are] for the rivals.
His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ يَرَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوۤاْ إِذْ يَرَوْنَ ٱلْعَذَابَ﴾ — He makes "يرى" act upon "أن القوة لله وأن الله", and its answer (jawāb) is left out. And Allah knows best.
(And His saying): ﴿ولَوْ أنَّ قُرْآناً سُيِّرَتْ به الجِبالُ أَوْ قُطِّعَتْ﴾ — leaving out the answer is frequent in the Qurʾān, because the meanings of Paradise and the Fire are repeated and known. If you wish, you give kasra to both "إنّ"s and make "يرى" act upon "إذ" in meaning. Giving fatḥa to both "أنّ"s with the yāʾ [reading يرى] is better than giving them kasra.
Whoever reads "وَلَوْ تَرَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا" with the tāʾ, the normal way of speech would be to say "إن القوة..." with kasra, "وإِن..."; because "ترى" has acted upon (الذين ظلموا), so "إِن — (وإنّ)" are begun afresh. Had you given them fatḥa, by repeating the seeing from "ترى" and from "يرى", it would have been correct, as if He said: "ولو ترى الذين ظلموا إذ يرون العذاب" — they see ﴿أَنَّ ٱلْقُوَّةَ للَّهِ جَمِيعاً﴾.

farraa:170-170.t:
His saying: ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ﴾ — you give this wāw fatḥa, because it is "wa-law" of conjunction onto which the interrogative alif has been brought; it is not (أو) whose wāw is quiescent, because the alif of "أَوْ" may not be dropped, while the interrogative alif can be dropped: you say "wa-law kāna", and "a-wa-law kāna" when you ask a question.
Allah reproached them with this only because they said ﴿بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ مَآ أَلْفَيْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَآءَنَآ﴾. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: O Muḥammad, say ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ﴾. He said "آباؤهم" because of their absence; had it been "آباؤكم" it would be permissible, because the command to speak occurs as an address, as in your saying "Say to Zayd: let him stand" and "Say to him: stand". Similar are ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ الشَّيْطَانُ يَدْعُوهُمْ﴾ and ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾.
Whoever makes the wāw quiescent in His saying ﴿أَوْ آبَاؤُنا الأَوَّلُونَ﴾ in al-Wāqiʿa and the like of it in the Qurʾān makes it "أو" which affirms one of two. And this wāw, in having fatḥa, is like His saying ﴿أَثُمَّ إِذا مَا وَقَعَ﴾: the interrogative alif entered upon "ثُمّ"; and likewise "أفلم يسِيروا".

farraa:171-171.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي يَنْعِقُ﴾ — He annexed the likeness to those who disbelieve, then likened them to the shepherd, and did not say "like the sheep". The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: the likeness of those who disbelieve is (like the likeness of the beasts) which understand nothing of what the shepherd says beyond the sound; if he said to them "graze" or "drink", they would not know what he was saying to them. Such is the likeness of those who disbelieve regarding what comes to them of the Qurʾān and the warning of the Messenger. So the comparison was annexed to the shepherd, while the meaning — and Allah knows best — is about the herd. This is common in the speech of the Arabs: they say "So-and-so fears you as the fear of the lion", the meaning being "as his fear of the lion", because the lion is the one known to be feared. The poet said:
لقد خِفْتُ حتى ما تزِيدُ مخافتِى * على وَعِلٍ فى ذى المَطَارة عاقِلِ
(I feared so much that my fear does not exceed that of a mountain goat taking refuge in Dhū l-Maṭāra.)
The meaning is: until the fear of a mountain goat does not exceed my fear. Another said:
كانت فرِيضةَ ما تقول كما * كان الزِناءُ فرِيضةَ الرَّجْمِ
(What you say was an obligation, just as adultery was the obligation of stoning.)
The meaning is: as stoning was the obligation for adultery. The poet takes liberties with placing the word in its proper order because the meaning is clear to the Arabs. One of them recited to me:
إِن سِراجا لكرِيم مَفْخَرُهْ * تَحْلَى بِهِ العينُ إِذا ما تَجْهَرُهْ
(Sirāj is noble in his glory; the eye is adorned by him when it beholds him.)
The eye is not adorned by him; rather he is adorned by it.
There is another meaning in it: you annex the likeness to (الذين كفروا) while its annexation in meaning is to the admonition, as if you said: the likeness of admonishing those who disbelieve, and of their admonisher, is like that of the one who calls out [to the flock]; just as you say "When you meet so-and-so, greet him with the greeting of the emir", meaning only: as you greet the emir.
The poet said:
فلستُ مُسَلَّما ما دمْتُ حيّاً * على زيدٍ بِتسلِيم الأمير
(As long as I live I will not greet Zayd with the greeting of the emir.)
All is correct.
His saying: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لاَ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ — nominative, and this is the normal way of speech, because it is a fresh statement, as shown by His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, just as you say in speech: "He is deaf, so he does not hear; he is mute, so he does not speak." Had it been accusative by way of censure (shatm), like the words at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, "وتركهم فى ظلماتٍ لا يبصِرون صُمّاً بُكْماً عُمْياً", it would be permissible. [Translator's note: the text has "الشمّ"; it is evidently "الشتم" (censure).]

farraa:173-173.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْمَيْتَةَ وَٱلدَّمَ وَلَحْمَ ٱلْخِنزِيرِ﴾ — accusative, because "حرّم" acts upon them. That is because your saying "إنّا" [Translator's note: so in the text; evidently "إنّما"] has two aspects. One is that you make "إنّما" a single particle, then let the verbs that come after it act upon the nouns: if they are nominative-governing you use the nominative, and if accusative-governing you use the accusative. So you say: "innamā dakhaltu dāraka" (I only entered your house), "innamā aʿjabatnī dāruka" (only your house pleased me), "innamā mālī māluka" (my wealth is only your wealth). Here it is a single particle.
The other aspect is that you make [Translator's note: the text has "بجعل", for "تجعل"] "ما" separate from (إنّ), so that "ما" has the sense of "الذى" (that which). When it is so, you join it to what "الذى" is joined to [i.e. a ṣila], then put the noun that comes after the ṣila in the nominative, as in your saying "inna mā akhadhta māluka" (what you took is your wealth) and "inna mā rakibta dābbatuka" (what you rode is your mount), meaning: inna lladhī rakibta dābbatuka, inna lladhī akhadhta māluka. So treat them according to this.
It occurs in the Revelation in more than one place. Of that is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿إِنَّمَا اللّهُ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ and ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنْت نَذِيرٌ﴾ — these are a single particle, it and "إنّ", because "الذى" is not fitting in the place of "ما".
As for the one in the manner of (الذى), it is His saying ﴿إنَّمَا صَنَعُوا كَيْدُ سَاحِرٍ﴾, meaning: that which they made is the plot of a sorcerer. Had a reader read "إِنما صنعوا كيدَ ساحِرٍ" in the accusative, it would be correct if he made "إنّ" and "ما" a single particle. And His saying ﴿إِنَّمَا اتَّخَذْتُمْ مِنْ دُونِ اللّهِ أَوْثَاناً مَوَدَّةَ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾: some put "المودّة" in the accusative and others in the nominative, according to the two aspects I have explained to you. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "إنما مودَّةُ بَيْنِكُمْ فِى الحياةِ الدنيا"; this is an argument for whoever puts "المودّة" in the nominative, because it is begun afresh and "taking" does not act upon it. So it is like your saying: "What you made is not beneficial — [it is] a friendship among you, then it will be cut off afterwards." If you wish, you make "المودّة" nominative by "بين"; and if you wish, you imply before it a noun that makes it nominative, as in His saying "سُورَةٌ أَنْزَلْنَاهَا", and as in His saying ﴿لم يَلْبَثُوا إِلاَّ سَاعَةً مِنْ نَهَارٍ بَلاَغٌ فَهَلْ يُهْلَكُ﴾.
When you see "إنَّما" with, at its end, a noun denoting people or the like — that to which "مَنْ" applies — do not take "ما" in it in the manner of (الذى), because the Arabs hardly ever use "ما" for people. Of that is "innamā ḍarabtu akhāka" (I only struck your brother); and do not say "akhūka", because "ما" is not used for people.
When the noun after "إنَّما" and its ṣila is not of people, both aspects are permissible for you: you say "innamā sakantu dāraka" (I only lived in your house) and, if you wish, "dāruka" (what I lived in is your house). The Arabs do in some speech use "ما" for people, but it is not frequent. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "وَالنَّهَارِ إِذا تَجَلَّى والذَّكَرِ والأُنْثَى", and in our reading: "ومَا خَلَقَ الذَّكَرَ والأُنْثَى". Whoever makes "ما خلق" refer to the male and the female may put "الذكرِ والأنثى" in the genitive, as if He said: and by the One who created — the male and the female. And whoever puts "الذكر" in the accusative makes "ما" and "خلق" like His saying "and by His creating the male and the female", making "خلق" act upon it. The genitive in it, according to the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, is good, and the accusative is more common.
Had you read "إنّما حَرَّم عليكم الميتةُ" in the nominative, it would be a valid view. Some read "إنما حُرِّم عليكم المِّيتةُ", and here only the nominative of "الميتة" and "الدم" is permissible: because if you make "إنّما" a single particle, you put "الميتة" and "الدم" in the nominative since it is a verb whose agent is not named [i.e. passive]; and if you take "ما" in the manner of (الذى), you put "الميتة" and "الدم" in the nominative because it is the khabar (predicate) of "ما".
His saying: ﴿وَمَآ أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — al-ihlāl: what was called out over the slaughtered animals for other than Allah. [His saying] ﴿فَمَنِ ٱضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلاَ عَادٍ﴾ — [(غير) in this place is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the one compelled, as if you said: whoever is compelled, not transgressing and not exceeding] — it is lawful for him. The accusative here is like His saying ﴿أُحِلَّتْ لَكُمْ بَهِيمَةُ الأَنْعَامِ إِلاَّ مَا يُتْلَى عَلَيْكُمْ غَيْرَ مُحِلِّى الصَّيْدِ﴾, and similar is ﴿إِلاَّ أَنْ يُؤْذَنَ لَكُمْ إِلَى طَعَامٍ غَيْرَ نَاظِرِينَ إِنَاهُ﴾. "غير" here means "لا"; "لا" is fitting in its place, because "لا" fits in the place of "غير". When you see "غير" in whose place "لا" is fitting, it differs from the "غير" in whose place "لا" is not fitting.
Carrion is not lawful for the one compelled if he attacks people with his sword or is on one of the paths of disobedience. It is said that the one who eats it should not eat his fill of it, nor take any of it as provision.
He is only granted a concession in what keeps him alive.

farraa:175-175.t: His saying: ﴿فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ﴾ — there are two views on it. One, its meaning is: what is it that made them endure the Fire? The other view: how bold they are towards the Fire! Al-Kisāʾī said: The judge of Yemen asked me while he was in Mecca, saying: "Two men of the Arabs brought a dispute before me, and one of them swore [falsely] regarding his fellow's right, so [the other] said to him: 'How enduring you are towards Allah (mā aṣbaraka ʿalā llāh)!'" In this it may be meant: how enduring you are of the punishment of Allah; then "the punishment" is dropped and it becomes [complete] speech, as you say "How like your generosity is to Ḥātim", [meaning to Ḥātim's generosity].

farraa:35-35.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَقْرَبَا هَـٰذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا﴾. If you wish, you make ﴿فتكونا﴾ an answer (jawāb), in the accusative; and if you wish, you conjoin it to the beginning of the speech, so that it is jussive (majzūm), as in the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:
فقلتُ له صَوِّبْ ولا تَجْهَدَنَّهُ * فَيُذْرِكَ مِنْ أُخْرَى الْقَطاةِ فَتَزْلِقُ
(I said to him: "Lower him [Translator's note: your horse] and do not overtax him, lest he throw you off the back of his rump and you slip.")
— where he used the jussive. The meaning of the jussive is as if it were a repetition of the prohibition, as when someone says: لا تذهب ولا تعرض لأحد (do not go, and do not accost anyone). The meaning of the answer with the accusative is: do not do this, lest it be done to you in requital. When a word was conjoined to something not of its kind, and at its beginning there was an element (ḥādith) [Translator's note: i.e. the prohibition] that is not appropriate in the second, it was put in the accusative. Similar to it are His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِى﴾, ﴿لاَ تَفْتَرُوا علَىَ اللّهِ كَذِباً فَيُسْحِتَكُمْ بِعَذَابٍ﴾ and ﴿لاَ تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ فَتَذَرُوهَا كَالْمُعَلَّقَةِ﴾. Whatever is a negation has the same [Translator's note: two possibilities] as this. The nominative is not permissible in either of the two ways, unless you intend a fresh start (istiʾnāf), differing from both meanings, as in your saying to a man: لا تركب إلى فلان فيركبُ إليك (do not ride to so-and-so; he will ride to you), meaning: do not ride to him, for he will ride to you. This differs from both meanings because it is a fresh start. The poet said:
أَلَمْ تَسْألِ الَّرْبعَ الْقَدِيمَ فَيَنْطِقُ * وَهَلْ تُخْبِرَنْكَ الْيَوْمَ بَيْدَاءُ سَمْلَقُ
(Did you not ask the old encampment — and it will speak? Yet can a bare, empty desert tell you anything today?)
He meant: did you not ask the encampment, for it will tell you about its people; then he turned back on himself and gave himself the lie, as Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā al-Muzanī said:
قِفْ بِالدِّيارِ التى لَمْ يَعْفُها القِدَمُ * بَلَى وغَيَّرها الأَرْواحُ والدِّيَمُ
(Halt at the abodes that age has not effaced — nay, the winds and the steady rains have changed them.)
— so he gave himself the lie. As for His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَطْرُدِ الّذينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَدَاةِ والْعَشِىّ﴾, its answer is His words: ﴿فَتَكُونَ مِنَ الظَّالِمينَ﴾, while the fāʾ in His words "فَتَطْرُدَهُمْ" is an answer to His words "مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِمْ مِنْ شَىْءٍ". So in His words "فَتَكُونَ مِنَ الظَّالِمينَ" both the jussive and the accusative are possible, as I have explained to you, while in His words "فَتَطْرُدَهُمْ" only the accusative is possible, because the fāʾ there refers back to a maḥall [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term for an adverb or prepositional phrase], namely His words "مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِمْ", and "عليك" is not of the same kind as the verb. Whenever what precedes the fāʾ is a noun containing no verb, or a maḥall such as "عندك", "عليك" and "خلفك", or a past verb such as "قام" and "قعد", only the accusative is possible in the answer with the fāʾ. It was permissible in his words * فَيُذْرِكَ مِنْ أُخْرَى الْقَطَاةِ فَتَزْلُقْ * because what precedes the fāʾ is a yafʿalu [Translator's note: i.e. imperfect] and what follows it is a yafʿalu, and these are of the same kind as one another; because it is a future verb, what applies to the first of it can apply to the last, and what applies to the last can apply to the first, since it is a future verb.

farraa:36-36.t: His words: ﴿وَقُلْنَا ٱهْبِطُواْ بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ وَلَكُمْ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ﴾. He addressed Adam and his wife — and it is also said: Adam and Iblīs — and He said "اهبطوا" (go down, [Translator's note: plural]) meaning him and his offspring, so it is as if He addressed them all. It is like His words: ﴿فَقَالَ لَهَا وللأَرْضِ ائْتِيا طَوْعاً أَوْ كَرْهاً قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا طَائِعِينَ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: we have come, with all the creatures in us, willingly. Similar to it is the saying of Ibrāhīm: "رَبَّنَا وَاجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ", then he said: ﴿وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَاً﴾ — and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh "وَأَرِهِمْ مَنَاسِكَهُمْ" — so he used the plural before his offspring existed. An example of this in ordinary speech, by which the meaning becomes clear, is your saying to a man: قد تزوّجتَ ووُلِدََ لك فكثُرْتم وعَزَزتم (you married and children were born to you, so you [Translator's note: plural] became many and strong).

farraa:37-37.t: His words: ﴿فَتَلَقَّىٰ آدَمُ مِن رَّبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٍ﴾: ﴿آدَمُ﴾ is nominative and «الكلمات» is in the position of the accusative. One of the readers read: "فَتَلَقَّى آدَمَ مِنْ رَبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٌ", making the verb belong to the words; and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is the same, because whatever has met you, you have met it, and whatever has reached you, you have reached it. In our reading it is: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمين", and in the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمُونَ".

farraa:40-40.t:
His words: ﴿ٱذْكُرُواْ نِعْمَتِيَ [ٱلَّتِي أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ]﴾: the meaning is: do not forget My favour; let it be kept in your remembrance. Likewise every mention of remembering the favour means — and Allah knows best — this: keep it and do not forget. In the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: "ادَّكِروا", and in another place: "وتَذَكَّروا ما فيه". An example in ordinary speech is your saying: "اذكُرْ مَكانى مِنْ أبيك" (remember my standing with your father).

As for the fatḥa on the yāʾ of "نِعْمَتِى": every yāʾ of the speaker has two dialects: leaving it unvowelled (al-irsāl), i.e. quiescent, and giving it fatḥa. When it meets alif and lām, the Arabs chose the dialect in which the yāʾ is vowelled and disliked the other, because the lām is quiescent and the yāʾ would drop before it because of its own quiescence; and they found it ugly to say "نعمتِى التى", so that it would seem genitive without annexation. So they took the more secure and clearer of the two ways. Yet making it quiescent before alif and lām is permissible: Allah said: ﴿يا عِبَادِى الّذِيِنَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾, and it has been read with the yāʾ unvowelled and with fatḥa. Likewise, everything in the Qurʾān in which the yāʾ is present [Translator's note: in writing] has both ways; and where the yāʾ is not present, it is not given fatḥa.

As for His words: ﴿فَبَشِّرْ عِبَادِ. الّذِيِنَ يَسْتمِعُونَ الْقَوْلَ﴾, this is without a yāʾ, so its yāʾ is not given fatḥa, since it is dropped; and by this everything of its kind in the Qurʾān is to be measured. His words: ﴿فما آتَانِىََ اللّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا اتَاكُمْ﴾: al-Kisāʾī claimed that the Arabs prefer fatḥa on the yāʾ before every alif with hamza other than the alif and lām [Translator's note: of the article], as in His words: ﴿إِنْ أَجْرِىَ إِلاَّ عَلَى اللّهِ﴾ and ﴿إِنِّىَ أَخَافُ اللّهَ﴾. I have not found that among the Arabs; I have found them leaving the yāʾ unvowelled, saying: عندِى أبوك (your father is with me); they do not say عندىَ أبوك with the yāʾ vowelled — unless they drop the hamza and put its fatḥa on the yāʾ, in this and the like. As for their sayings: لِىَ ألفان (I have two thousand) and بِىَ أخواك كفيلان (your two brothers are guarantors for me), they give fatḥa in these two [Translator's note: words] because of their shortness [Translator's note: lit. "their smallness"] [so they say: لىَ أخواك and لِىَ ألفان, because of their shortness], yet the analogy in these and in what precedes them is one.

farraa:41-41.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَشْتَرُواْ بِآيَاتِي ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً﴾. Everything of this kind in the Qurʾān in which the price is put in the accusative and the bāʾ is attached to the thing sold or bought: that occurs mostly with two things neither of which is a recognised price, like dinars and dirhams. An example is: اشتريتُ ثوبا بكساء (I bought a garment for a cloak): you may make whichever of them you wish the price of the other, because neither is a currency (athmān). Everything that is not a currency — such as slaves, houses and all goods (ʿurūḍ) — follows this rule. But when you come to dirhams and dinars, you put the bāʾ on the price, as He said in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَرَاهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ﴾, because dirhams are always a price, and the bāʾ is attached only to prices. Such are His words: ﴿اشْتَرَوْا بآيَاتِ اللّهِ ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً﴾, ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا بِالآخِرَةِ﴾, ﴿اشتروا الضلالة بالهدى﴾ and ﴿والعذاب بالمغفرة﴾. So attach the bāʾ to whichever of the two you wish, until you come to dinars and dirhams: you attach the bāʾ to them when they are with goods. And if you buy one of them [meaning dinars and dirhams] with the other, you attach the bāʾ to whichever you wish, because each of them in this situation is both thing sold and price. If you want to know the difference between goods and dirhams: you know that whoever buys a slave for a specified thousand dirhams, then finds a defect in him and returns him, has no claim on the seller to take back his own thousand in particular, but only a thousand. But if he bought a slave for a slave-girl and then found a defect in him, he would not get back another slave-girl like her [Translator's note: but that very one]. That is proof that goods are not prices.

His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَكُونُوۤاْ أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ﴾: He made «كافر» singular though a plural precedes it. That is eloquent, good Arabic in a noun derived from a verb, such as the active and passive participle. The meaning intended is: do not be the first who disbelieves (أوّل مَن يكفر); "مَن" is dropped and the verb [Translator's note: i.e. the participle] takes its place, conveying the same feminine and plural that "مَن" conveys, while it is singular in form. In similar speech you may not say: أنتم أفضلُ رجلٍ (you [Translator's note: plural] are the best man), nor أنتما خير رجل (you two are the best man), because «رجل» takes dual, plural and singular, [so] its singular is distinguished from its plural, whereas «القائم» (the one standing) may stand for a thing [Translator's note: i.e. «ما»] and for «مَن», conveying both while singular. Do you not see that you may say: الجيْشُ مقبلٌ والجُنْد منهزمٌ (the army is advancing and the troops are routed), putting the predicate (fiʿl) in the singular because [Translator's note: the subject] is singular; but when you come to [Translator's note: non-derived] nouns you say: الجيش رجالٌ والجند رجالٌ (the army are men, the troops are men)? In this there is a clear explanation. The poet said:
وإذا هُمُ طَعِمُوا فَأَلأَمُ طاعِم * وإذا هُمُ جاعُوا فشَرُّ جِياعِ
(When they eat, they are the meanest of eaters; and when they are hungry, the worst of the hungry.)
So both its plural and its singular are permissible and good.

farraa:42-42.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَلْبِسُواْ ٱلْحَقَّ بِٱلْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُواْ ٱلْحَقَّ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. If you wish, you take "وتكتموا" to be in the position of the jussive, meaning: do not mix truth with falsehood and do not conceal the truth; you drop "لا" because it has come at the beginning of the speech. In the reading of Ubayy: "وَلاَ تَكُونُوا أَوّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ وَتَشْتَرُوا بِآيَاتِى ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً"; this is proof that the jussive in His words ﴿وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ﴾ is sound and correct. Similar to it: ﴿وَلاَ تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتُدْلُوا بِهَا إِلى الْحُكّامِ﴾, and likewise His words: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِيِنَ آمَنُوا لاَ تَخُونُوا اللّهَ وَالرَّسُولَ وَتَخُونُوا أَمَانَاتِكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. And if you wish, you make these words conjoined by the wāw accusative according to what the grammarians call al-ṣarf (diversion). If you say: What is al-ṣarf? I say: it is that you bring a wāw conjoining [Translator's note: a verb] to speech at whose beginning there is an element (ḥādith) that cannot properly be repeated on what is conjoined to it. When that is so, it is al-ṣarf, as in the words of the poet:
لاتَنْهَ عنْ خُلُقٍ وتأتِىَ مِثْلُهُ * عارٌعليْكَ إذا فَعلتَ عظِيمُ
(Do not forbid a trait while doing the like of it yourself; a great shame on you if you do.)
Do you not see that "لا" cannot be repeated in "تأتى مثله"? That is why it is called ṣarf: it is conjoined, yet the element preceding it cannot properly be repeated in it. Similar to it among nouns, which the Arabs put in the accusative though they are conjoined to a nominative, are their sayings: لَوْ تُركتَ والأسدَ لأكلَك (had you been left with the lion, it would have eaten you) and لَوْ خُلِّيت ورأيَك لَضَلَلْتَ (had you been left to your own opinion, you would have gone astray). Since it is not good in the second to say: "had you been left and had your opinion been left, you would have gone astray", they shrank from conjoining a word in which what occurred in the preceding one does not fit. He said: But the Arabs allow the nominative: لو تُرك عبدُالله والأسدُ لأكله (had ʿAbd Allāh and the lion been left, it would have eaten him). So is it permissible for verbs put in the accusative by the wāw by way of ṣarf to be referred back to what precedes them, while they carry the meaning of ṣarf? I say: Yes. The Arabs say: لستُ لأبِى إِنْ لم أقتُلْك أو تذهبْ نفسى (I am not my father's son if I do not kill you or lose my life), and they say: والله لأضربنّك أو تسبقَنِّى فى الأرض (by Allah, I shall strike you, unless you outrun me across the land). This is referred back to the beginning of the speech, yet its meaning is ṣarf, because in the second the jussive with «لم» cannot be repeated, nor can the oath be repeated as "by Allah, you will outrun me". You will find this when you test the speech. Al-ṣarf with particles other than "لا" is frequent, but we have deferred mentioning it until its places come.

farraa:48-48.t:
His words: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً لاَّ تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْئاً﴾. Reference back to "day" and "night" may be made sometimes with the hāʾ alone and sometimes with the ṣifa [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term for a preposition, here «في» with its pronoun], and that is permissible: as when you say "لا تجزى نفس عن نفس شيئا" and imply the ṣifa, then make it overt and say: "لا تجزى فيه نفس عن نفس شيئا" (on which no soul will avail another soul at all). Al-Kisāʾī did not allow implying the ṣifa in relative clauses (ṣilāt), and said: If I allowed implying the ṣifa here, I would allow: "أنت الذى تكلمتُ" (you are the one I spoke), when I mean "الذى تكلمتُ فيه" (the one about whom I spoke). Others, of the people of Basra, said: We do not allow the hāʾ, and it does not occur; in such a place it is only the ṣifa that is implied. Some Arabs recited to me:
يارُبَّ يَوْم لو تَنَزّاهُ حول * أَلْفَيْتَنى ذا عنزٍ وذا طول
(Many a day — had a crafty one leapt at it [Translator's note: i.e. at me on it], you would have found me resistant and strong.)
And another recited to me:
قد صَبَّحتْ صبَّحها السّلامُ * بِكَبِدٍ خالَطها سَنامُ * فى ساعة يُحَبُّها الطّعامُ *
(She brought in the morning — may peace greet her morning — a liver mixed with hump-fat, at an hour in which food is loved.)
— and he did not say «يُحَبّ فيها». What al-Kisāʾī imposed on himself does not apply to him, because in this place the ṣifa and the hāʾ agree in meaning: do you not see that you say آتيك يومَ الخميس and فى يوم الخميس (I will come to you [Translator's note: on] Thursday), and you see the meaning is one? But when you say كلمتُك (I spoke to you), it is different from كلّمتُ فيك (I spoke about you); and since the meaning differs, it is not permissible to imply the hāʾ in place of "فى", nor "فى" in place of the hāʾ.

farraa:258-260.t:
His saying: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِي حَآجَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ — the Arabs' insertion of (ilā) in this place is by way of expressing wonder (taʿajjub), as you say to a man: "Do you not see [look at] this!" The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: Have you seen the like of this, or have you seen anything like this! The proof of that is that He said: ﴿أَوْ كَٱلَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرْيَةٍ﴾, as though He said: Have you seen [anyone] like the one who disputed with Abraham about his Lord ﴿أَوْ كَٱلَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرْيَةٍ وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا﴾. This, in its manner, is like what I told you about mā laka and mā manaʿaka. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿قل لِمن الأرض وَمن فيها إن كنتم تعلمون. سيقولون لِلّه﴾, then He said, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿قل من ربُّ السموات السّبْع وربّ العرش العظيم. سيقولون لله﴾ — He made the lām the answer although it is not in the beginning of the speech. That is because when you say: "Who is the owner of this house?" and someone says to you: "It belongs to Zayd (li-Zaydin)," he has answered you with what you want; so his saying "Zayd" and "li-Zayd" are equal in meaning. He said: one of Banū ʿĀmir recited to me:
فأَعلمُ أننى سأكونُ رَمْساً * إذا سار النواجعُ لا يَسير
فقال السائرون لمن حفرتم * فقال المخبرون لهم: وزير
(I know that I shall become a buried grave which, when the seekers of pasture move on, does not move; and the travellers will say: For whom have you dug? And those who inform them will say: Wazīr.)
Similar to it in speech: a man says to you: "How are you this morning (kayfa aṣbaḥta)?" and you say: "Well (ṣāliḥun)," in the nominative; had you answered him according to his very word, you would have said: ṣāliḥan. Your informing about your state spared you from keeping to his word. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿ما كان محمد أَبا أَحدٍ مِن رِجالِكم ولكِن رسول الله﴾ — if you use the accusative, you mean: but he was the Messenger of Allah; and if you use the nominative, you give a statement, and the statement spares you from what precedes it. His saying: ﴿ولا تحسبن الذيِن قتِلوا فِى سبيل الله أمواتا بل أَحياء﴾ — nominative, and it is more proper than the accusative, because had it been accusative it would be on: but reckon them alive; and removing doubt from this place is better. Had it been accusative it would be correct, as you say: "Do not think him a liar; rather think him truthful." Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿أيحسب الإنسان أن لن نجمع عِظامه بلى قادِرين على أن نسوّى بنانه﴾ — if you wish, you derive the accusative of qādirīna from this interpretation, as if in similar speech someone says: "Do you think I will not visit you? Rather, soon, if Allah wills," as if he said: "Yes indeed — so reckon me your visitor." Even though the verb has fallen on (an lan najmaʿa), in interpretation it falls on the nouns. One of Banū Faqʿas recited to me:
أجِدَّك لن ترى بثُعَيلِبات * ولا بَيْدان نَاجيةً ذَمولا
ولا متداركٍ والشمسُ طِفْلٌ * ببعض نواشغ الوادى حُمولا
(Truly, you will not see at Thuʿaylibāt nor at Baydān a swift, ambling she-camel, nor one overtaking — while the sun is just setting — at some of the valley's water-channels, the litters of the departing.)
He said "wa-lā mutadārikin," and that shows that he meant: you are not one who sees at Thuʿaylibāt such-and-such, nor one overtaking.
Some grammarians say: we put (qādirīna) in the accusative on the basis that it was turned away from naqdiru; that is nothing. But there may be another way in it besides what I explained to you: it may come out of (najmaʿa) [as a ḥāl], as if in speech someone says: "Do you think I will not hit you? Yes indeed — being able to kill you," as if he said: "Yes indeed, I will hit you, being able to do more than hitting you."
His saying: ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾ — the speech has run with the assimilation (idghām) of the thāʾ, since it met the tāʾ while it was quiescent.
In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (اتَّخَتُّمُ العجل) and (وإنى عُتُّ بربى وربكم), so the dhāl was also assimilated before the tāʾ. That is because they are related in the closeness of their point of articulation; the thāʾ and the dhāl have a heavy point of articulation, so assimilation was applied to them because of their heaviness; do you not see that their point of articulation is from the tip of the tongue? Likewise the ẓāʾ shares their heaviness. So whatever of these three letters comes to you, assimilate it. Not assimilating is not an error; it is only [a matter of] finding it heavy. The ṭāʾ and the dāl are also assimilated before the tāʾ when they are made quiescent, as in His saying: ﴿أحطت بما لم تحِط به﴾ — the ṭāʾ comes out in pronunciation as tāʾ, and it is closer to the tāʾ than the first letters; you find that when you test their two points of articulation.
His saying: ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ — the explanation came: it has not changed [by the passing of years over it, taken from al-sana]. The hāʾ may be part of its root [from your saying: "I sold it to him musānahatan (by the year)"; it is kept both in continuous reading and in pause. Whoever reads it continuously without the hāʾ derives it from al-musānāt, because the hāʾ and the wāw alternate as the final radical of sana], or it may be redundant, an extension, like His saying ﴿فبِهداهم اقتدِهْ﴾. Whoever makes the hāʾ redundant makes the faʿʿaltu form of it tasannaytu; do you not see that you make the plural of sana sanawāt, so tafaʿʿaltu is sound [on that basis]? And whoever says in [the diminutive of] sana: sunayna — even if that is rare — then tasannaytu may be tafaʿʿaltu with the nūn replaced by yāʾ because the nūns became many, as they said taẓannaytu, whose origin is al-ẓann. They have also said it is taken from His saying ﴿من حمإٍ مسنون﴾, meaning: changed. If it is so, it is also among those whose nūn is replaced by a yāʾ. We hold that its meaning is taken from al-sana, i.e. the years have not changed it. And Allah knows best.
Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna narrated to me, tracing it back to Zayd ibn Thābit, who said: there was written on a stone: "نَنشِزها" and "لم يتسن" and "وانظر"; and Zayd ibn Thābit [Translator's note: the text reads «وانظر إلى زيد بن ثابت», apparently garbled; rendered by sense] put four dots on the shīn and the zāy, and wrote (يتسنه) with the hāʾ. If you wish, you read it in continuous recitation in two ways: you keep the hāʾ and make it quiescent, or if you wish, you delete it. One of them recited to me:
فليست بسَنْهاء ولا رُجَّبِيَّة * ولكنْ عَرَايَا فى السنينَ الجوائح
(She is neither an old palm (sanhāʾ) nor a propped-up one, but [her fruit is] gifts in the devastating years.)
Al-rujjabiyya is the one that is about to fall, so it is supported around with stones. Al-sanhāʾ is the old palm tree. This is support for whoever pronounces the hāʾ in continuous reading.
His saying: ﴿وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾ — the wāw was put in it only on the intention of an implied verb after it, as if He said: and so that We make you a sign, We did that. This is frequent in the Qurʾān. His saying ﴿آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾: when he was raised up, his beard and head were black while his grandchildren were grey, so he was a sign by that.
His saying ﴿ننشزها﴾ — Zayd ibn Thābit read it so; al-inshāz is moving them to their place.
Ibn ʿAbbās read it "nunshiruhā"; its inshār is bringing it to life. He argued from His saying: ﴿ثم إذا شاء أنشره﴾. Al-Ḥasan read — according to what has reached us — (nanshuruhā), taking it toward spreading out (nashr) as opposed to folding. The proper way is that you say: Allah anshara the dead, and they nasharū, when they came to life, as al-Aʿshā said:
* يا عجبا للميت الناشِرِ *
(How amazing — the dead man coming back to life!)
And I heard one of Banū al-Ḥārith say: "He had mange, then nashara," i.e. he recovered and came back to life. His saying: "فلما تبين له قال أعلم أنّ الله على كل شىء قدير" — Ibn ʿAbbās read it in the jussive [i.e. the imperative iʿlam], and in the readings of both Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh it is: "قيل له اعْلَمْ" ("it was said to him: Know"). Ibn ʿAbbās argued, saying: Is he better than Abraham and more knowledgeable? It was said to him: ﴿وَٱعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾. The generality read: "aʿlamu anna Allāha" ("I know that Allah"), and it is a good way, because the meaning is like a man's saying, at a display of power that becomes clear to him from the command of Allah: (I bear witness that there is no god but Allah). The other way is also clear.
His saying ﴿فَصُرْهُنَّ إِلَيْكَ﴾ — the generality read the ṣād with ḍamma, and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh used to read the ṣād with kasra. They are two dialects. As for the ḍamma, it is common; as for the kasra, it is among Hudhayl and Sulaym. Al-Kisāʾī recited to me from one of Banū Sulaym:
وفَرْعٍ يصير الجِيدَ وَحْفٍ كأنه * على اللِيتِ قِنْوانُ الكروم الدوالح
(And thick hair that inclines the neck, as if, on the side of the neck, it were the heavy-laden clusters of vines.)
Its meaning is explained as: cut them up; and it is said: turn them [toward you]. We have not found "cut them up" known from these two forms; but I hold — and Allah knows best — that if it is from that, it is from ṣaraytu taṣrī, with its yāʾ moved forward, as they said ʿithtu and ʿathaytu. And the poet said:
صَرَتْ نظرة لو صادفت جَوْزَ دارِع * غَدَا والعَوَاصِى من دمِ الجوف تنعَرُ
(She cut short a glance which, had it met the middle of a mailed warrior, he would have gone off with his veins gushing blood from his inside.)
The Arabs say: "He spent the night yaṣrī in his basin," when he draws water, then stops, then draws water; perhaps it is from that.
And the poet said:
يقولون إن الشأم يقتلُ أهلَه * فمَنْ لِىَ إن لم آتِه بخُلُود
تَعَرَّب آبائى فهَلاَّ صَرَاهم * من الموت أن لم يذهبوا وجُدُودِى
(They say Syria kills its people — but who will grant me immortality if I do not go to it? My fathers and my grandfathers lived as Bedouin — did their not going [there] hold them back from death?)

farraa:177-177.t:
His saying: ﴿لَّيْسَ ٱلْبِرَّ أَن تُوَلُّواْ وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ — if you wish, you put "البِرّ" in the nominative and make "أن تولوا" in the position of the accusative; and if you wish, you put it in the accusative and make "أن تولّوا" in the position of the nominative, as He said: ﴿فَكَانَ عاقِبَتَهُمَا أَنَّهُمَا فِى النّارِ﴾, in much of the Qurʾān. In one of the two readings it is "ليس البِرُّ بِأن"; for that reason we chose the nominative in "البِرّ". The meaning of His saying ﴿ليس البِرُّ بِأن تولوا وجوهكم قِبل المشرِقِ والمغرِبِ﴾ is: righteousness does not lie wholly in your turning towards prayer and the difference between the two qiblas — ﴿وَلَكِنّ البِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللّهِ﴾; then He described what He described to the end of the verse. These are among the attributes of the prophets, not of others.
As for His saying ﴿وَلكِنَّ البِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللّهِ﴾, it is of the speech of the Arabs to say: "Righteousness is only the truthful one who maintains his ties of kinship and conceals his charity", making the noun [i.e. person] the predicate of the action and the action the predicate of the noun, because it is a matter whose meaning is known.
As for the action made the predicate of a noun, it is His saying ﴿ولا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ بِمَا آتَاهُمُ اللّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ هُوَ خَيْراً لَهُمْ﴾: (هو) is a pronoun standing for the stinginess. This is for whoever makes "الذِين" in the position of the accusative and reads it "تحسبنَّ" with tāʾ. Whoever reads it with yāʾ makes "الذِين" in the position of the nominative and makes (هو) a support (ʿimād, i.e. separating pronoun) for the implied stinginess, making do with the mention of stinginess that is overt in "يبخلون". Similar to it in speech:
هم الملوك وأبناء الملوكِ لهم * والآخِذون بِهِ والساسة الأُوَلُ
(They are the kings and sons of kings; theirs it is; they are those who hold it and the foremost governors.)
His saying "به" means: the kingship. Another said:
إِذا نُهِى السفِيهُ جَرَى إليهِ * وخالف والسفِيه إِلى خِلافِ
(When the fool is forbidden, he runs towards it and disobeys — the fool inclines to disobedience.)
He means: towards foolishness.
As for the actions made predicates of persons, it is the poet's saying:
لعمرك ما الفِتيان أن تَنْبُت اللحى * ولكِنما الفِتانُ كُلُّ فتىً نَدِى
(By your life, young men are not [a matter of] beards sprouting; rather, young men are every generous youth.)
So he made "أنْ" [with its verb] the predicate of "الفتيان".
His saying: ﴿مَنْ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ﴾ — (من) is in the position of the nominative, and what follows it is its ṣila, until it reaches His saying ﴿وَٱلْمُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِهِمْ﴾; you refer "الموفون" back to "مَنْ", and "والموفون" is of the description of "مَن", as if: whoever believed, and whoever did and fulfilled. "الصابرِين" is put in the accusative because it is of the description of "مَنْ"; it was put in the accusative only because it is of the description of a single noun, so it is as if he took it towards praise. The Arabs break off from the attributes of a single [noun], when they run long, with praise or blame: they use the nominative when the noun is nominative, and they put some of the praise in the accusative, as if they intend to set apart what is in the accusative with renewed praise not following on from the beginning of the speech. Of that is the poet's saying:
لا يَبْعَدَنْ قومى الذين هُمُ * سُمُّ العُدَاةِ وآفة الجُزُرِ
النازِلِين بِكلّ معترَكٍ * والطَيِّبِينَ مَعاقِدَ الأُزُرِ
(May my people not perish, who are poison to enemies and the bane of slaughter-camels; who alight at every battlefield, and are pure where their waist-wrappers are tied.)
Sometimes they put (النازلون) and (الطيبون) in the nominative, and sometimes in the accusative by way of praise; the nominative is by making the end of the speech follow its beginning. One of the poets said:
إلى الملِكِ القَرْمِ وابنِ الهُمَام * وليثَ الكتِيبةِ فى المُزْدَحَمْ
وذا الرأى حين تُغَمُّ الأُمور * بِذاتِ الصليلِ وذاتِ الُّلجُمْ
(To the king, the chief, son of the valiant — the lion of the squadron in the press, the man of judgement when matters are clouded by [battles] of clanging [arms] and bridled [horses].)
He put (ليث الكتيبة) and (ذا الرأى) in the accusative by way of praise, while the noun before them is genitive, because they are of the description of one [person]; had the lion been other than the king, it could only be a follower [in case], as you say "I passed by the man and the woman" and the like. He said: one of them recited to me:
فليت التِى فيها النجوم تواضعت * على كل غثّ مِنهمُ وسَمينِ
غيوثَ الحَيَا فى كل مَحْلٍ ولَزْبَةٍ * أسود الشَّرَى يحمِين كلَّ عَرِينِ
(Would that [the sky] in which are the stars had come down upon every lean and fat one of them — rains of life-giving in every drought and hardship, lions of al-Sharā guarding every den.)
So he used the accusative. And we consider that in His saying ﴿لَكِنِ الرَّاسِخُونَ فى الْعِلْمِ مِنْهُمْ وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاَةَ وَالْمُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ the accusative of "المقِيمِين" is because it is a naʿt (adjective) of "الراسِخِين": its description grew long, and it was put in the accusative as I explained to you.
In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "والمقِيمون — والمؤتون", and in the reading of Ubayy: "والمقِيمين"; and our reading and the reading of Ubayy did not agree except upon what is correct. And Allah knows best.
Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Abū Muʿāwiya al-Ḍarīr narrated to me from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha, that she was asked about His saying ﴿إنّ هَذَانِ لَسَاحِرَانِ﴾, about His saying ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا والَّذِينَ هَادُوا وَالصَّابِئُونَ﴾ and about His saying ﴿وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاَةَ وَالْمُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾, and she said: "O son of my brother, this was a mistake of the scribe."
Al-Kisāʾī said about it: "والمقيمين" is in the position of the genitive, referred back to His saying ﴿بِما أنزِل إليك وما أنزِل مِن قبلِك﴾: and they believe in those who establish the prayer — they and those who give the zakāt.
He said: it is like His saying ﴿يُؤْمِنُ بِاللهِ ويُؤْمِنُ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The grammarians used to say that "المقيمين" is referred back to ﴿بما أنزِل إِليك وما أنزِل مِن قبلك... إلى المقِيمِين﴾ [i.e. and to those who establish]; some of them [said]: "لكِنِ الراسِخون فِى العِلِم مِنهم" and of "المقيمين"; and some of them: "مِن قبلك" and before "المقيمين".
He — meaning al-Kisāʾī — refused the approach of praise which I explained to you only because he said: the one praised is not put in the accusative except when the sentence is complete, and the sentence is not complete in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.
Do you not see that when you say "لكن الراسخون فى العلم منهم" up to His saying "والمقيمين — والمؤتون", you are as if waiting for its predicate? Its predicate is in His saying ﴿أُولئِك سَنُؤْتِيهِمْ أَجْراً عَظِيماً﴾. Most speech is as al-Kisāʾī described; but the Arabs, when the description runs long, treat the speech in the incomplete and the complete alike. Do you not see that they said in poetry:
حتى إِذا قَمِلت بطونُكُمُ * ورأيتُم أبناءكم شبُّوا
وقلبتم ظهر المِجَنِّ لنا * إنّ اللئِيم العاجزُ الخِبُّ
(Until, when your bellies grew fat and you saw your sons had grown up, and you turned the back of the shield against us — truly, the base one is the feeble, the deceitful.)
He made the answer of (حتى إذا) with the wāw, while there ought to have been no wāw in it, and it was made do with by following on, with no predicate after that. This is the most extreme of what I have described to you.
Similar is His saying ﴿حَتّى إِذَا جَاءُوهَا وَفُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُهَا وَقَالَ لَهُمْ خَزَنَتُها﴾, and similar is His saying ﴿فَلَمَّا أَسْلَمَا وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ وَنَادَيْنَاهُ أَنْ يَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ﴾ — He put it with the wāw. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "فَلَمَّا جَهَّزَهُمْ بِجَهَازِهِمْ وَجَعَلَ السِّقَايَةَ", and in our reading it is without the wāw. All is good Arabic.
Some of them said: "وآتى المال على حبهِ ذوِى القربى — والصابِرِين", putting "الصابرين" in the accusative by making the verb act upon them. The right view is that it is accusative with the intention of praise, because it is of the description of one thing. The Arabs say with indefinites what they say with definites: they say "marartu bi-rajulin jamīlin wa-shābban baʿdu" (I passed by a handsome man, and young besides), and "marartu bi-rajulin ʿāqilin wa-sharmaḥan ṭuwālan" (I passed by an intelligent man, and tall, very tall); and they recite his saying:
ويَأوِى إلى نِسوةٍ بائساتٍ * وشُعْثاً مراضِيعَ مِثل السَّعَالِى
(And he takes refuge with wretched women — dishevelled, nursing, like ghouls.)
(and "وَشُعْثٍ"): they make it genitive by having it follow the beginning of the speech, and accusative with the intention of blame in this place.

farraa:178-178.t:
His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِصَاصُ فِي ٱلْقَتْلَى ٱلْحُرُّ بِالْحُرِّ وَٱلْعَبْدُ بِٱلْعَبْدِ وَٱلأُنثَىٰ بِٱلأُنْثَىٰ﴾ — it was revealed about two tribes of the Arabs, one of which had superiority over the other in numbers and nobility; they used to marry their women without dowries. The lower of the two tribes killed some of the noble one, and the noble one swore that they would kill a male for a female and a free man for a slave, and double the [retaliation for] wounds. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed this to His Prophet; then it was abrogated by His saying ﴿وَكَتَبْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِيهَا أَنَّ النَّفْسَ بِالنَّفْسِ﴾ to the end of the verse. So the first is abrogated and is not judged by.
As for His saying ﴿فَٱتِّبَاعٌ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَأَدَآءٌ إِلَيْهِ بِإِحْسَانٍ﴾, it is nominative; and it has the status of a command in outward form, as you say "man laqiya l-ʿaduwwa fa-ṣabran wa-ḥtisāban" (whoever meets the enemy — then patience and seeking reward!). This is accusative, and its nominative is permissible. And His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿فَٱتِّبَاعٌ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is nominative, and its accusative is permissible. The nominative was the normal way of speech in it only because it is general for whoever does [it], and is meant also for whoever has not done [it]; so it is as if He said: the rule in it is thus — hence the nominative. The verbal noun is put in the accusative when it is a command at a thing that happens and is not permanent, as in your saying to a man: "When you take up your work, then diligence, diligence! and pace, pace!"
You used the accusative because you did not intend generality by it, such that it would become like something binding upon whoever came to it and did it. Similar is His saying ﴿وَمَنْ قَتَلَهُ مِنْكُمْ مُتَعَمِّداً فَجَزَاءٌ مِثْلُ مَا قَتَلَ مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾, and similar is ﴿فَإمْسَاكٌ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أَوْ تَسْرِيحٌ بِإحْسَانٍ﴾; and the like of it in the Qurʾān is much, all nominative, because they are general.
So it is as if He said: whoever does this, upon him is this.
As for His saying ﴿فَضَرْبَ الرِّقَابِ﴾, He was urging them to kill when they meet the enemy, and the urging was not like something made binding by an act before it; for that reason it is accusative. It is like your saying: "When you meet the enemy, then [say] lā ilāha illā llāh, Allāhu akbar, and [show] truthfulness at that encounter (tilka l-waqʿa)" — (al-Farrāʾ said: "dhālika" and "tilka" are the dialect of Quraysh, and Tamīm say "dhāka" and "tīka l-waqʿa") — as if it is urging them, and it is not obligatory upon them to say "Allāhu akbar". There is nothing of this whose accusative is not permissible, by making the command act upon it: "let him fast three days", "let him keep [her] in a keeping with kindness, or release [her] in a release with excellence".

farraa:179-179.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَكُمْ فِي ٱلْقِصَاصِ حَيَاةٌ﴾ — He says: when the offender knows that retaliation will be taken from him — that if he kills he will be killed — he refrains from killing, and so [the other] lives.
That is His saying: "حياة" (life).

farraa:180-180.t:
His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ — its meaning throughout the Qurʾān is: it has been made obligatory upon you.
His saying: ﴿ٱلْوَصِيَّةُ لِلْوَالِدَيْنِ وَٱلأَقْرَبِينَ﴾ — a man used to bequeath whatever he liked of his wealth to whomever he wished, heir or other; then it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance. So there is no bequest for an heir, and the bequest is within the third and does not exceed it. Before this, one would bequeath all his wealth or whatever he liked of it.
"الوصِيَّة" is nominative by "كُتِب"; and if you wish, you take "كُتِب" in the sense of "قِيل" (it was said) and put "الوصية" in the nominative by the lām in "الوالدين" [i.e. as mubtadaʾ with its khabar], like His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿يوصِيكم الله فِى أولادِكم لِلذكر مِثل حظّ الأنثيين﴾.

farraa:182-182.t: His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ خَافَ مِن مُّوصٍ جَنَفاً﴾ — the Arabs say "waṣṣaytuka" and "awṣaytuka"; and in one of the two readings it is "وأوصى بِها إبراهِيم" with the alif. Al-janaf is injustice. ﴿فَأَصْلَحَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ — He mentioned only the testator; He said "بينهم" (between them) meaning the heirs and the beneficiaries of bequests. For that reason He said "بينهم" without mentioning them, because the meaning indicates that reconciliation can only be among the heirs and those to whom bequests were made.

farraa:265-266.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَوَدُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ لَهُ جَنَّةٌ مِّن نَّخِيلٍ وَأَعْنَابٍ﴾, then after that He said ﴿وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ﴾, then He said ﴿فَأَصَابَهَآ إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَٱحْتَرَقَتْ ﴾. Someone may say: Is it permissible in speech to say: "Would you like to obtain wealth and it was lost (fa-ḍāʿa)," meaning: and it is lost (fa-yaḍīʿu)? I said: Yes, that is permissible with wadidtu, because the Arabs meet it once with (an) and once with (law); they say: "I would like it if (law) you went away from us," [and] "I would like that (an) you go away from us." Since it is suitable with law and with an, and the meaning of both is the future, they allowed themselves to return faʿala in the interpretation of law onto yafʿalu with an. Therefore He said: fa-aṣābahā, and it is, in its manner, equivalent to law, since [law] resembles in in the sense of condition, so it was put in its places, and in was answered with the apodosis of law, and law with the apodosis of in. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿ولا تنكِحوا المشرِكاتِ حتى يُؤْمِنَّ ولأَمَةٌ مؤمنة خير مِن مشرِكة ولو أعجبتكم﴾, and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: even if (in) they please you. Then He said ﴿ولئن أَرْسَلْنَا رِيحا فرأوه مصفرا لظلوا [من بعده يكفرون]﴾, so la-in was answered with the answer of law, and the meaning of both is future. For that reason He said in the reading of Ubayy: "ودّ الذين كفروا لو تغفلون عن أسلِحتكم وأمتِعتِكم فيمِيلوا" — he referred it back to the interpretation: they would like you to (an) do. If you put (fa-yamīlūna) in the nominative, you refer it to the interpretation of law, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿ودّوا لو تدهِن فيدهنون﴾, and He also said ﴿وتودّون أن غير ذات الشوكةِ تكون لكْم﴾. Sometimes the Arabs combine both together; Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿وما عمِلت من سوء تودّ لو أن بينها وبينه أمدا بعيدا﴾. It is like the Arabs' combining mā and in, both being negations. The poet said:
قد يكسِبُ المالَ الهِدَانُ الجافى * بغير لا عَصْفٍ ولا اصطراف
(The coarse dullard may gain wealth without any toil or striving.)
And another said:
ما إن رأينا مثلهن لمعشر* سُود الرءوس فوالج وفُيُول
(We have never seen the like of them belonging to any folk — black-headed: Bactrian camels and elephants.)
That is because the difference of the two wordings makes one of them redundant (laghw). Similar to it is the poet's saying:
من النفر اللاء الذين إذا هُمُ * تهاب اللئام حَلْقة الباب قعقعوا
(Of the band who, when the base are in awe of the door-ring, rattle it.)
Do you not see that he said al-lāʾ alladhīna, and the meaning of both is alladhīna? Combining them was permitted because their wordings differ; had they agreed it would not be permissible: "mā mā qāma Zayd" is not permissible, nor "I passed by alladhīna alladhīna who go round." As for the poet's saying:
كماما أمرؤٌ فى معشرٍ غيرِ رَهطِه * ضعيفُ الكلام شخصُه متضائل
(Just as a man among a folk other than his own clan is weak of speech, his person diminished.)
they permitted combining mā with [mā] only because the first was joined to the kāf — as if it and the kāf were one noun — while the second was not joined, so combining them was found good. And it is in the saying of Allah ﴿كلاَّ لا وَزَر﴾: lā was joined [in kallā], and the other came separately, so their coupling was good. So if someone says: (mā mā qultu bi-ḥasanin, "what I said is not good"), that is permissible without fault, because he makes the first mā a negation and the second in the manner of alladhī. [Likewise if he said: "man man ʿindaka? (Who is the one with you?)" it is permissible, because he made the first man interrogative and the second in the manner of alladhī.] So when the meaning of the two words differs, combining them is permissible.
As for the poet's saying:
* كم نِعْمةٍ كانت لهاكم كم وكم *
(How many a favour was hers to you — how many, how many!)
this is only repetition of a word; had you stopped at the first, it would suffice you instead of the second. It is like your saying to a man: "Yes, yes," repeating it, or your saying: "Hurry, hurry," to intensify the meaning. This has nothing to do with the two preceding chapters. And the poet said:
هلاَّ سألتَ جُمُوعَ كنـ * دَةَ يوم ولَّواْ أين أينا
(Why did you not ask the hosts of Kinda, on the day they turned their backs: where, where?)
As for his saying: (lam arahu mundhu yawma yawma, "I have not seen him since such-and-such a day"), by the second is intended other than the first day; in meaning it is only: I have not seen him since a day you know. As for his saying:
نحمِى حقيقتَنا وبعـ * ضُ القوم يسقط بينَ بينا
(We defend what we must protect, while some of the folk fall in between.)
he meant: he falls neither among these nor among those. Their combination in this place is like their saying: "He is my neighbour bayta bayta (house by house)," and "I met him kaffata kaffata (face to face)," because the two kaffas are one from you and one from him. Likewise "He is my neighbour bayta bayta," from it: my house and his house are adjoining.
He said: How did He say His saying: ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ﴾, when this matter has passed? It was said: (kāna) is implied, so the speech is sound. Similar to it is that you say: "I have freed two slaves; and if I did not free two, then one at their value," the meaning being: unless I be [one who freed]; because it is past, kāna must be implied, since the speech is conditional. Similar to it is the poet's saying:
إذا ما انتسبنا لم تلِدْنى لئيمةٌ * ولم تجِدِى مِن أن تُقِرّى بها بُدّا
(When we trace our lineage, [you will find that] no base woman bore me, and you will find no escape from acknowledging it.)

farraa:267-267.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَسْتُمْ بِآخِذِيهِ إِلاَّ أَن تُغْمِضُواْ فِيهِ﴾ — (an) after illā was given fatḥa although it is in the manner of a condition. It was given fatḥa only because illā fell on it with a sense of the genitive that fits. So when you see (an) in a condition affected by a sense of genitive, accusative or nominative, it takes fatḥa. This is of that kind. The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: you would not take it except on closing your eyes, or with closing your eyes, or from closing your eyes — an unspecified preposition (ṣifa). What shows you that it is a condition is that you find the meaning: if you closed your eyes somewhat, you would take it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿إلا أن يخافا ألاَّ يقِيما حدودَ الله﴾, and similar to it ﴿إلاَّ أن يعفون﴾ — all this is condition; and His saying ﴿ولا تقولنَّ لِشىءٍ إنى فاعل ذلك غدا إلا أن يشاء الله﴾ — do you not see that the meaning is: do not say "I will do it" except with "if Allah wills" along with it? So when (illā) cut it off from the meaning of beginning, together with the intention of the genitive governor in it, it took fatḥa. Had (illā) not been in it, it would have been left with its kasra. Of that is your saying: "Do good, if (in) it is accepted from you." If you put in (illā), you say: "Do good, unless (illā allā) it is not accepted from you." Similar to it is His saying ﴿وأن تعفوا أقربُ للتقوى﴾, ﴿وأن تصوموا خير لكم﴾ — it is a condition, the meaning being: if you fast, it is better for you. When (an) became nominative by (khayr), it had something with which it stands in mutual nominative relation, so it took fatḥa and left the bounds of the condition. The accusative governor is likewise.
Similar to it — of the condition which, when a genitive, nominative or accusative governor falls on it, loses its jussive — is your saying: "Hit him, whoever he is (man kāna)," and "I will not come to you as long as I live (mā ʿishtu)." Man and mā are in the position of a condition, and the verb in both is nominative in meaning, because kāna and the verb before it have fallen on (man) and (mā), so it changed from the jussive without leaving the interpretation of the condition. The poet said:
فلستُ مقاتِلا أبداً قُرَيشا * مُصيبا رَغْمُ ذلك مَنْ أصابا
(I will never fight Quraysh, striking — despite that — whomever it strikes.)
in the interpretation of the nominative, because muṣīb falls on man.
Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic ﴿وللّهِ على الناسِ حِجّ البيتِ منِ استطاع﴾: if you make (man) referred back to the genitive of (al-nās), it is of this kind, and (اسْتَطَاعَ) is in the position of the nominative; and if you intend a fresh start with man, it is a condition, and the verb after it is jussive, and you are content with what came before it as its apodosis. Likewise you say in speech: "Whichever of them stands (ayyuhum yaqum), hit [him]"; if you put the hitting first and make it act on ayy, you say: "Hit whichever of them stands (iḍrib ayyahum yaqūmu)." One of the Arabs said: "fa-ayyuhum mā akhadhahā rakiba ʿalā ayyihim yurīdu" ("whichever of them takes it, rides on whichever of them he wants"). And of it is the poet's saying:
فإنى لآتيكم تشَكُّرَ ما مضى * من الأمر واستيجابَ ما كان فى غد
(I come to you in gratitude for what has passed, and to earn whatever may be tomorrow.)
because, had it not been a condition, it would not be permissible to say: "kāna tomorrow," since (kāna) was created only for the past, except in the condition, where it is suitable for the future. It is as though he said: to earn whatever thing may be tomorrow.
Similar to in in the condition, in turning from kasra to fatḥa when a nominative governor affects it, is the saying of the Arabs: (qultu innaka qāʾim, "I said: you are standing"): inna takes kasra after "saying" in all its inflections. If you put in place of "saying" something with its meaning that can produce a genitive, nominative or accusative, you give anna fatḥa, saying: "I called out that you are standing (annaka)," and "I summoned," "I shouted," and "I cried out." That is because you say: "I called Zayd," "I summoned Zayd," "I called out to Zayd (bi-Zaydin)," ("I cried out to Zayd"), so you find these words stand alone with Zayd alone; whereas with "saying" it is not proper to say "I said Zayd (Zaydan)," nor "I said to Zayd (bi-Zaydin)." So quotation (ḥikāya) went through with "saying" and did not go through with calling, because it is satisfied with nouns. Unless a poet is compelled to give inna kasra after calling and the like; then it is permissible for him, as in his saying:
إنى سأبدى لك فيما أُبدِى * لى شَجَنان شَجَنٌ بنجد * وشَجَن لى ببلاد الهند *
(I shall disclose to you, among what I disclose: I have two longings — a longing in Najd, and a longing of mine in the land of India.)
Had inna appeared in this place, the proper way would have been to give it fatḥa. By analogy it takes kasra, because the nominative of the two shajans is evidence of the intention of "saying"; and giving anna fatḥa, had it appeared, would require you to say: "lī shajanayni shajanan bi-Najd."
So when you see "saying" fall on something in meaning, anna has fatḥa. Of that is that you say: "I said to you what I said: that you are unjust (annaka ẓālim)," because mā is in the position of the accusative. Likewise: "I said 'Zayd is righteous' — that he is righteous (annahu)," because your saying (I said Zayd is standing) is in the position of the accusative. Had you wanted inna to be referred back to the word before it, you would give it kasra and say: "I said what I said: your father is standing (inna abāka qāʾim)" — (and it is the [same] word as what precedes it); and if you give it fatḥa, it is something other than it. The saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted ﴿فلينظر الإنسان إلى طعامه أنَّا﴾ and innā — it has been read both ways. Whoever gives fatḥa intends to make anna in the position of the genitive and make it an explanation of the food and its cause, as if He said: to Our pouring the water and Our causing to grow what We caused to grow. Whoever gives kasra intends cutting off the looking from innā, as if He said: Let man look at his food; then He informed by way of a fresh start.

farraa:50-50.t: His words: ﴿فَأَنجَيْنَاكُمْ وَأَغْرَقْنَا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ وَأَنْتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ﴾. It is said: They were too occupied to look, screened by the sea that surrounded them from seeing Pharaoh and his drowning. But in speech it is like your saying: قد ضُرِبتَ وأهلُك يَنْظُرون فما أتَوْك ولا أغاثوك (you were beaten while your family were looking on, yet they did not come to you or help you); he means: they were near, within sight and hearing. Similar to it in the Qurʾān: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ الظِّلَّ﴾: there is no seeing here; it is only knowledge. «رأيت» has two senses: seeing of knowledge and seeing of the eye, as when you say: رأيتُ فِرعَوْنَ أعْتَى الخلق وأخْبَثَه (I saw Pharaoh to be the most insolent and wicked of creatures), though you did not see him; it only reached you. In this there is a clear explanation.

farraa:51-51.t: His words: ﴿وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسَىٰ أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾; then He said in another place: ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَا مُوسَى ثَلاَثِينَ ليلةً وأتْمَمْناها بِعَشْرٍ فَتَمَّ مِيقاتُ رَبِّهِ أرْبَعينَ ليلةً﴾. Someone may say: Why did He mention thirty and complete it with ten, when forty can be made up of twenty and twenty, or twenty-five and fifteen? It is answered: That was — and Allah knows best — because thirty was the number of a month, so the thirty were mentioned separately because of the month, namely Dhū al-Qaʿda, and "We completed it with ten" of Dhū al-Ḥijja. So the commentators said. It is for this story that the ten and the thirty were singled out for separate mention.

farraa:53-53.t:
His words: ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ وَٱلْفُرْقَانَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُون﴾. There are two ways in it. One: He meant ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ﴾, i.e. the Torah, and [Translator's note: gave] Muḥammad ﷺ ﴿ٱلْفُرْقَانَ﴾, ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُون﴾. His words ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ﴾ are as though He addressed them, saying: We have given you the knowledge of Moses and Muḥammad, peace be upon them both, "that you may be guided"; because the Torah was revealed all at once and was not revealed in separate parts as the Qurʾān was separated. That is one way. The other way: you make the Torah guidance and al-Furqān the like of it, so that it means: We gave Moses guidance as We gave Muḥammad ﷺ guidance. Everything the prophets brought is guidance and light. The Arabs do combine two words that are one in meaning when their wordings differ, as ʿAdī ibn Zayd said:
وقَدَّمَتِ الأَدِيمَ لِراهِشَيْهِ * وأَلْفَى قَوْلَها كذِباً ومَيْنَا
(She set the leather mat beneath his two wrist-veins [Translator's note: for him to be bled], and he found her word to be a lie and a falsehood.)
And their saying: بُعْداً وسُحْقاً (away! and far off!), where البُعد and السُّحق are one. That is another way. Some commentators said: the Book is the Torah, and al-Furqān is the parting of the sea for the Children of Israel. And some of them said: al-Furqān is the lawful and the unlawful that are in the Torah.

farraa:57-57.t: His words: ﴿ٱلْمَنَّ وَٱلسَّلْوَىٰ﴾. It has reached us that al-mann is this substance that falls on the thumām and ʿushar shrubs; it is sweet like honey. One of the commentators used to call it the taranjabīn that we know. And it has reached us that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Truffles are of the mann, and their water is a cure for the eye." As for al-salwā, it was a bird that came down upon them when they grew weary of the mann, resembling these quails (al-sumānā); al-salwā has no singular.

farraa:58-58.t:
His words: ﴿وَقُولُواْ حِطَّةٌ﴾. He says — and Allah knows best —: say what you have been commanded, i.e. "it is ḥiṭṭa (relief [Translator's note: from sins])"; but they turned instead to a phrase in Nabataean, and that is His words: ﴿فَبَدّلَ الَّذيِنَ ظَلَمُوا قَوْلاً غَيْرَ الَّذِى قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾.

It has reached me that Ibn ʿAbbās said: They were commanded to say: "We seek Allah's forgiveness." If that is so, then "حِطّة" ought to be accusative in the reading, because you say: قلتُ لا إله إلا الله (I said "there is no god but Allah"), and someone says: قلتَ كلمةً صالحة (you said a good word). Quotation (ḥikāya) applies only when something that governs the nominative, genitive or accusative could be implied before it; but when you gather all of that and make it a single "word", it is accusative by «القول», as when you say: مررت بزيد (I passed by Zayd), and then make this a "word" and say: قلت كلاما حسنا (I said a fine utterance); then you say: قلتُ زيدٌ قائمٌ (I said "Zayd is standing"), and he says: قلتَ كلاما (you said an utterance). And you say: قد ضربتُ عمرا (I have struck ʿAmr), and he likewise says: قلتَ كلمةً صالحة.

As for the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلاَثَةٌ رَابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ up to the end of the numbers He mentioned, it is nominative because a pronoun standing for their names precedes it: they will say: they are three — to the end of the verse. His words ﴿وَلاَ تَقُولُولُوا ثَلاَثَةٌ انْتَهُوا خَيْراً لَكُمْ﴾ [Translator's note: «تَقُولُولُوا» so in the text, for «تَقُولُوا»] are nominative, i.e. say: Allah is One, and do not say: the gods are three. His words: ﴿قَالُوا مَعْذِرَةً إِلى رَبِّكُم﴾ have two ways: if you mean "what we said is an excuse to your Lord", you use the nominative, and that is the preferred way; and if you mean "we said what we said as an excuse to Allah", that is a way of the accusative. As for His words: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ طاعَةٌ فإذا بَرَزُوا﴾, the Arabs say it only in the nominative. That is because people are commanded with something they dislike, and one of them says: سمعٌ وطاعةٌ (hearing and obedience), i.e. we entered upon this religion at its outset on the basis that we would hear and obey; so they say: we owe you what we began with; then they go out and act contrary, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فإذا بَرَزُوا مِن عِندِك[بيَّتَ طائفةٌ منهم غير الذى تقول]﴾ — [i.e.] when they go out from your presence, they change. Had you meant in similar speech "we will obey", so that obedience is an answer to the command itself, the accusative would be permissible, because every maṣdar (verbal noun) that stands in the place of faʿala and yafʿalu may be accusative, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿مَعَاذَ اللهِ أَنْ نَأخُذَ﴾ [its meaning, and Allah knows best, being: we seek refuge in Allah from taking]. Similar to it in al-Nūr: ﴿قُلْ لاَ تُقْسِمُوا طاعّةٌ مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾: the nominative is on the sense "let there be from you what the people of hearing and obedience say". As for His words in al-Naḥl: ﴿وَإذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ ْمَاذَا أَنْزَلَ رَبُّكُم قالوا أَساطِيرُ الأَوّلِينَ﴾, this is the saying of the deniers, because they said: He has not sent down anything; this is only the legends of the ancients. As for those who believed, they affirmed it and said: أنزل ربُّنا خيراً (our Lord has sent down good). Had «خير» been nominative, on the sense "what He has sent down is good", it would have been correct; it would then be like His words: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ ماذَا يُنْفِقُونَ قُلِ الْعَفْوَ﴾ and ﴿قُلِ الْعَفْوُ﴾: the accusative is by the verb — "they spend the surplus" — and the nominative is on "what they spend is the surplus of wealth". His words: ﴿قَالُوا سلاماً قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾: as for «السلام» (the first), it is (an utterance that is said), so it is accusative because the verb falls on it, as though you said: قلتُ كلاماً (I said an utterance).

As for His words: ﴿قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾, it came to mean: we are "سَلاَمٌ" (peace), and you are "قَوْمٌ مُنْكَرُونَ" (a people unknown).

Some commentators say: ﴿قَالُوا سَلاَماً قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾ means they greeted him with peace and he returned it to them. Someone may then say: Why was «السلام» not nominative in both or accusative in both? I say: «السلام» has two meanings: when you mean by it an utterance, you put it in the accusative; and when you imply "عليكم" with it, you put it in the nominative. If you wish, you omit the implication from one of the two words and imply it in the other; if you wish, you put both in the nominative; and if you wish, you put both in the accusative. When the Arabs meet and say سلامٌ, [Translator's note: the others say]: سلامٌ, meaning they said "peace be upon you" and the others returned it. The accusative is permissible in one of the two readings: "قَالوا سَلاَماً قَالَ سَلاَماً". Someone of the Banū ʿUqayl recited to me:
فَقُلْنا السَّلامُ فاتَّقَتْ مِنْ أَمِيرِهَا * فَما كَانَ إِلاَّ وَمْؤُهَا بِالْحَواجِبِ
(We said: "Peace!" — and she was wary of her guardian, so there was nothing but a sign she made with her eyebrows.)
He put «السلام» in the nominative because he meant: we greeted her, and she was wary of returning the greeting to us. It is also permissible to put «السلام» in the accusative, as in your saying: قلنا الكلام (we said the utterance) — قلنا السلامَ. Similar to it: قرأت "الحمدَ" and قرأتُ "الحمدُ" (I read al-Ḥamd): when you say قرأت "الحمدَ" you make the verb fall on it; and when you use the nominative you make it a quotation, as in قرأتُ "الحمدُ لله".

farraa:60-60.t:
His words: ﴿ٱضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلْحَجَرَ فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْناً﴾: its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: so he struck, and there gushed forth. By His saying "فَانفَجَرَتْ" it is known that he struck, so the answer sufficed, since it conveys the meaning. Likewise His words: ﴿أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ فَانْفَلَقَ﴾. Similar to it (in ordinary speech) is your saying: أنا الذى أمرتك بالتجارة فاكتسبت الأموال (I am the one who commanded you to trade, and you acquired wealth); the meaning is: so you traded and acquired.

As for His words: ﴿قَدْ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُنَاسٍ مَّشْرَبَهُمْ﴾, someone may say: What need did the people have to know their drinking places, when we see rivers made to flow for people as a favour from Allah and His bounty to His servants, and He did not say of others: "every people knew their drinking place"? That was only — and Allah knows best — because it was a stone from which twelve springs gushed forth, according to the number of the tribes (asbāṭ), a spring for each tribe. When the people set out, or had drunk what sufficed them, the stone returned to what it had been and the springs went away; and when they needed them, the springs gushed forth from those same places, and each tribe came to their own spring from which they used to drink.

farraa:61-61.t:
As for His words: ﴿وَفُومِهَا وَعَدَسِهَا وَبَصَلِهَا﴾, al-fūm, according to what has been mentioned, is an old dialect word, (and it is) wheat; and bread too — both have been mentioned. One of them said: We heard (Arabs of) the people of this dialect say: فَوِّموا لنا (make bread for us), with doubling only, meaning: bake bread. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "وَثُومِهَا" (its garlic), with thāʾ, and that seems the nearer of the two meanings to being correct, because it goes with what resembles it: lentils, onions and the like. The Arabs substitute fāʾ for thāʾ, saying جَدَثٌ and جَدَفٌ (grave), "they fell into an ʿāthūr of evil" and "an ʿāfūr of evil", and الأَثاثىّ and الأَثافىّ (hearth-stones). And I have heard many of the Banū Asad call (المَغافير "المغاثير").

His words: ﴿أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِي هُوَ أَدْنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِي هُوَ خَيْرٌ﴾: i.e. what is nearer, from al-dunuww (nearness); and it is also said: from al-danāʾa (baseness). The Arabs say: إنه لَدنىٌّ [and they do not use the hamza] يُدَنِّى فى الأمور, i.e. he pursues the base and petty side of affairs. Zuhayr al-Furqubī used to pronounce the hamza: "أَتَسْتَبْدِلونَ الّذِى هُوَ أدْنَأ بِالّذِى هو خيرٌ"; but we have not found the Arabs using the hamza in أدنى when it is from baseness, though in that connection they say: إنه لَدَانِئٌ خَبِيثٌ (he is base and vile) [when he is shameless], with the hamza. Someone of the Banū Kilāb recited to me:
باسِلَةُ الوَقْعِ سَرَابِيلُها * بِيضٌ إِلى دانِئِها الظَّاهِرِ
(Fierce in onset, its coats of mail are white, down to its lowly ones in plain view.)
He means the coats of mail, from its elite — meaning the squadron — down to its lowliest; he said "دانئها" meaning the lowliest.
