We used to hear the elders say: ما كنتَ دانِئاً ولقد دَناتَ (you were not base, yet you have become base), while the Arabs [Translator's note: generally] drop the hamza; and I do not think they transmitted it without having heard it.

His words: ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ مِصْراً﴾ is written with an alif. Names of countries are diptotes, whether light or heavy, whereas names of women, if one of them is light, are declined when they have three letters with the middle one quiescent, such as دَعْد, هِنْد and جُمْل. They are declined when women are named with them only because they recur and are much used as names, so they become light through their frequency, whereas names of countries hardly ever recur. If you wish, you take the alif in "مِصْرَا" as an alif on which one pauses, so that in connected speech you do not give it tanwīn, just as they wrote "سَلاَسِلاً" and "قَوَارِيراً" with alif, and most readers decline to inflect them (tark al-ijrāʾ). And if you wish, you take "مِصْرَ" to be other than the well-known Miṣr (Egypt), meaning: go down to some town (miṣr) among the towns, for what you have asked for is found only in villages and towns. The first way is dearer to me, because in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "اهْبِطوا مِصْرَ" without alif, and in the reading of Ubayy: "اهْبِطُوا فَإنّ لَكُمْ ما سَأَلْتُم واسْكُنُوا مِصْرَ"; and confirming that, it is without alif in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللّهُ آمِنِينَ﴾.

Al-Aʿmash, when asked about it, said: It is the Miṣr over which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī is [Translator's note: governor].

farraa:63-63.t: His words: ﴿خُذُواْ مَآ آتَيْنَاكُم بِقُوَّةٍ﴾: He says: with earnestness, and by carrying out what has been made obligatory on you in it.

farraa:66-66.t: His words: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا نَكَالاً لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا وَمَوْعِظَةً لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: He means the transformation (al-maskha) into which they were transformed; it was made an exemplary punishment for the sins that had passed and for what would be done after it, so that [Translator's note: others] would fear doing what those who were transformed did, and be transformed [Translator's note: likewise].

farraa:183-183.t: His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ — it may be asked: what was prescribed for those before us, when we see the Christians fasting more than our fasting and in a month other than ours? Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Muḥammad ibn Abān al-Qurashī narrated to me from Abū Umayya al-Ṭanāfisī, from al-Shaʿbī, that he said: "Even if I fasted the whole year, I would break my fast on the day of doubt, of which it is said 'it is of Shaʿbān' and it is said 'it is of Ramaḍān'." That is because the month of Ramaḍān was made obligatory on the Christians as it was made obligatory on us, and they moved it to a [fixed] season. That is because they would sometimes fast it in the intense heat, so they counted it thirty days. Then a generation of them came after them and took the safe course for themselves, fasting a day before the thirty days and a day after; then each later one kept following the practice of the earlier, until it reached fifty. That is His saying ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾.

farraa:184-184.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَّاماً مَّعْدُودَاتٍ﴾ — it is accusative because with every verb whose agent is not named [i.e. passive], when there are two nouns in it, one other than the other, you put one in the nominative and the other in the accusative, as you say "uʿṭiya ʿAbd Allāhi l-māla" (ʿAbd Allāh was given the wealth); and it does not matter whether the accusative one is definite or indefinite. If the second is a naʿt (adjective) of the first and both are overt, you put both in the nominative, saying "ḍuriba ʿAbd Allāhi l-ẓarīfu" (ʿAbd Allāh the elegant was struck) — you put it in the nominative because it is ʿAbd Allāh. If it is indefinite you put it in the accusative, saying "ḍuriba ʿAbd Allāhi rākiban" (riding), "maẓlūman" (wronged), "māshiyan" (walking) and "rākiban".
His saying: ﴿فَعِدَّةٌ مِّنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ — nominative, as I explained to you regarding His saying "فاتباع بالمعروفِ"; had it been accusative, it would have been correct.
His saying: ﴿وَعَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ فِدْيَةٌ﴾ — it is said: upon those who are able to fast but do not fast is to feed a poor person in place of every day on which they break the fast. And it is said: upon those who are able to is the fidya, meaning the ransom (fidāʾ). Then this was abrogated, and He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَأَن تَصُومُواْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾ than feeding.

farraa:185-185.t:
His saying: ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ﴾ — nominative, begun afresh, i.e. and for you is "شهر رمضان" ﴿ٱلَّذِيۤ أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْآنُ﴾. Al-Ḥasan read it in the accusative by way of repetition: "وان تصوموا" the month of Ramaḍān "خير لكم"; and the nominative is better.
It may also be accusative from His saying "كتِب عليكم الصيام" شهرَ رمضان, making the fasting act upon it: that you fast the month of Ramaḍān.
His saying ﴿فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ الشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ﴾ is evidence for the abrogation of feeding. He says: whoever is sound, not sick, or resident, not travelling, let him fast; ﴿وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضاً أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ﴾ makes it up. ﴿يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ﴾ in breaking the fast when travelling, ﴿وَلاَ يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ﴾ — fasting in it.
His saying: ﴿وَلِتُكْمِلُواْ ٱلْعِدَّةَ﴾ — in making up what you broke. This lām in His saying "وَلِتُكْمِلُوا الْعِدَّةَ" is the lām of kay (purpose); had [the wāw] been dropped, it would have been correct. The Arabs put it in their speech with a verb implied after it, and [with the wāw] it is not a condition for the verb before it. Do you not see that you say "I came to you so that you might be good to me", and you do not say "I came to you and so that you might be good to me"? If you say it, you mean: and so that you might be good to me, I came to you. It is frequent in the Qurʾān. Of it is His saying ﴿ولِتصغى إليهِ أفئدة الذِين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة﴾, and of it is His saying ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نُرِى إِبْرَاهِيمَ مَلَكُوتَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ ولِيَكُونَ مِنَ الْموُقِنِينَ﴾: had there been no wāw in it, it would be a condition, in the sense of your saying "We showed him the dominion of the heavens so that he might be". When there is the wāw in it, it has a verb implied after it: ﴿ولِيكون مِن الموقنين﴾ We showed him. And of it (other than with) the lām is His saying ﴿إِنّا زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِزِينَةٍ الْكَوَاكِبِ﴾, then He said "وحِفْظاً": had there been no wāw, "الحفظ" would be accusative by "زيّنا". When there is the wāw in it and there is nothing before it to which it can be conjoined, it is evidence that it is accusative by a verb implied after "الحفظ", as in your saying in speech "qad atāka akhūka wa-mukriman laka" (your brother has come to you, and honouring you): you put "mukrim" in the accusative only by implying "atāka" after it.

farraa:186-186.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ — the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "How can our Lord be near, hearing our supplication, when you tell us that between us and Him are seven heavens, the thickness of each heaven a journey of five hundred years, and between each two the like of that?" So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ — I hear what they call. ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِى﴾ — it is said: it is the talbiya (the pilgrim's response "Labbayk").

farraa:187-187.t:
His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ ٱلصِّيَامِ ٱلرَّفَثُ إِلَىٰ نِسَآئِكُمْ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "فلا رُفُوث ولا فسوق"; it is sexual intercourse, according to what they mentioned. You put it in the nominative by "أحل لكم", because you did not name its agent.
His saying: ﴿فَٱلآنَ بَاشِرُوهُنَّ﴾ — He says: upon the concession which was revealed, and which they did not have before that. His saying ﴿وَٱبْتَغُواْ مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ وَكُلُواْ وَٱشْرَبُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ﴾ — it is said: the child; and it is said [read]: "اتبِعوا" with the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about the two and said: they are the same.
His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ ٱلْخَيْطُ ٱلأَبْيَضُ مِنَ ٱلْخَيْطِ ٱلأَسْوَدِ﴾ — a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Is it the white thread and the black thread?" The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "You are broad of nape [i.e. dull]; it is the night from the day."
His saying: ﴿وَتُدْلُوا بِهَا إِلىَ الْحُكَّامِ﴾ — in the reading of Ubayy: "ولا تأكلوا أموالكم بينكم بِالباطِلِ ولا تدلوا بِها إِلَى الحُكَّامِ". This is like His saying ﴿وَلاَ تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ﴾, meaning: and do not conceal. If you wish, when "لا" is dropped from it, you may make it accusative by ṣarf (diversion), as you say "lā tasriq wa-tataṣaddaqa" (do not steal and [at the same time] give charity), meaning: do not combine this and that. The poet said:
لا تنه عن خُلُقٍ وتأتِىَ مِثله * عارٌ عليك إذا فعلتَ عظِيم
(Do not forbid a trait while doing its like; it is a great shame upon you if you do.)
The jussive is permissible in this verse, i.e. do not do either one of these two.

farraa:189-189.t:
His saying: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلأَهِلَّةِ﴾ — the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the waning and waxing of the moon: what is it? So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: that is for the appointed times of your Ḥajj and your ʿUmra, the falling due of your debts and the ending of your women's waiting periods.
His saying: ﴿وَلَيْسَ ٱلْبِرُّ بِأَن تَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِن ظُهُورِهَا وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ وَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِنْ أَبْوَابِهَا﴾ — that is because among the people of the Jāhiliyya — except Quraysh and those Arabs to whom Quraysh gave birth — a man, when he entered iḥrām outside the months of Ḥajj, in a house of clay or of hair or a tent, would make an opening in his house at its back and go out and come in through it, not going out by the door; and if he was of the people of tents and pavilions, he would go out from its back and come in by it. Once, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in iḥrām, and a man in iḥrām was watching him, he went in through the gate of a walled garden, and that man followed him. He said to him: "Keep away from me." He said: "Why?" He said: "You entered by the gate while in iḥrām." He said: "I am content with your practice and your guidance." The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "I am an Aḥmas." He said: "If you are an Aḥmas, then I am an Aḥmas." So Allah granted the man success, and Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed ﴿وَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِنْ أَبْوَابِهَا وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾. [Translator's note: the text has "ألا قريشا", evidently for "إلا قريشا" (except Quraysh). Aḥmas: one of the Ḥums, Quraysh and their kin, who held strict religious observances.]

farraa:191-191.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُقَاتِلُوهُمْ عِنْدَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ حَتَّىٰ يُقَاتِلُوكُمْ فِيهِ فَإِن قَاتَلُوكُمْ فَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ﴾ — this is a way the general body [of Readers] read it. The companions of ʿAbd Allāh read: "ولا تَقْتلوهم عِند المسجِد الحرام حتى يَقْتلوكم فيه، فإن قَتَلوكم فاقتلوهم" (do not kill them … until they kill you …), and the meaning here is: if they begin with killing you, then kill them. The Arabs say "Banū so-and-so have been killed" when one of them has been killed.
On this basis is the reading of the companions of ʿAbd Allāh; and all is good.
His saying: ﴿فإنِ انْتَهَوْا﴾ — and do not begin against you — ﴿فلا عُدْوَانَ﴾ against those who desisted; aggression is only against whoever did wrong: against whoever began against you and did not desist.
If someone says: "What about His saying ﴿فَلاَ عُدْوَانَ إِلاَّ عَلَى الظَّالمِينَ﴾ — is it aggression, when Allah has made it lawful for them?" we say: it is not aggression in meaning; it is only a word on the pattern of what came before it. Do you not see that He said: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾? The aggression of the polytheists in wording is injustice in meaning, while the aggression which Allah made lawful and commanded the Muslims with is only retaliation; and retaliation is not injustice, even though its wording is the same. Similar is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَجَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُهُا﴾; it is not from Allah with the same meaning it has from the evildoer, because it is a recompense.

farraa:273-273.t: His saying: ﴿لاَ يَسْأَلُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ إِلْحَافاً﴾ — nor without importunity. Similar to it in speech is your saying: "Seldom have I seen the like of this man," when perhaps you have seen neither few nor many of his likes.

farraa:275-275.t: His saying: ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ ٱلرِّبَا﴾, i.e. in this world, ﴿لاَ يَقُومُونَ﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿إِلاَّ كَمَا يَقُومُ ٱلَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ ٱلشَّيْطَانُ مِنَ ٱلْمَسِّ ﴾. Al-mass is madness; one says: a mamsūs man.

farraa:278-278.t:
His saying: ﴿وَذَرُواْ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَا﴾ — someone may say: What is this usury that has a remainder, when a remainder can only be of something that has passed? That is because Thaqīf used to lend at usury to some people of Quraysh; then they made a settlement that the usury owed to them by Quraysh would not be reduced, while the usury owed by Thaqīf would be remitted from them. When the term fell due for Quraysh and the due was demanded of them, there was sent down to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿يٰأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَذَرُواْ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَا إِن كُنْتُمْ مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾. This is the explanation of the remainder. They were commanded to take the principal sums, but they did not find them readily available, and they refused to remit the usury and defer the principal sums; so Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent down: ﴿وَإنْ كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ فَنَظِرَةٌ إِلىَ مَيْسَرَةٍ وَأَنْ تَصَّدّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾.
﴿وإن كان ذو عُسْرة﴾ of Quraysh, ﴿فنظرة﴾ O Thaqīf, (إلى ميسرة) — and they were needy. Then He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وأن تصدّقوا﴾ with the principal sums ﴿خير لكم﴾.

farraa:281-281.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾ — Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us from al-Farrāʾ, who said: Abū Bakr ʿAyyāsh [Translator's note: so in the text; i.e. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh] narrated to me from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The last verse that Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought down was this: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾; then he said: Put it at the head of the two hundred and eightieth [verse] of al-Baqara.

farraa:282-282.t:
His saying: ﴿إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى﴾ — this command is not an obligation; it is only good conduct and a mercy from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. If one writes, it is good, and if one does not write, there is no harm. It is like His saying ﴿وإذا حللتم فاصطادوا﴾, i.e. hunting has been made permissible to you. Likewise His saying ﴿فإذا قُضِيت الصلاة فانتشروا فى الأرض﴾ — dispersing and seeking are not an obligation after the Friday prayer; it is only a permission.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ كَاتِبٌ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ كَمَا عَلَّمَهُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ — the scribe was commanded not to refuse because of the scarcity of scribes in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
His saying ﴿فَلْيَكْتُبْ وَلْيُمْلِلِ ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾ — He commanded the one who owes the debt to dictate because he is the one against whom witness is borne.
Then He said ﴿فَإن كَانَ ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ سَفِيهاً﴾, meaning ignorant, ﴿أَوْ ضَعِيفاً﴾ — a minor or a woman — ﴿أَوْ لاَ يَسْتَطِيعُ أَن يُمِلَّ هُوَ﴾ — being incapable of dictating — ﴿فَلْيُمْلِلْ وَلِيُّهُ﴾, meaning the owner of the debt. If you wish, you make the hāʾ refer to the one who has charge of the debt, and if you wish, you make it refer to the one from whom it is claimed.
All of that is permissible.
Then He, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ﴾, i.e. then let there be a man and two women; so it is put in the nominative by referring it back to the being [kāna, as its agent]. And if you wish, you say: then it is a man and two women. And [it would be permissible] had both been in the accusative, i.e. if they are not two men, then call to witness a man and two women. Most of what has come in the Qurʾān of this kind is in the nominative, so this ran along with it.
His saying ﴿مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ أَن تَضِلَّ إْحْدَاهُمَا﴾ — with fatḥa on an, and it is also read with kasra. Whoever gives it kasra intends a beginning with it and makes it cut off from what precedes it. Whoever gives it fatḥa, it too is by way of condition, except that he intends there to be a fronting and postponing (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr) in it, so the condition and its apodosis became like a single word. Its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: call two women to witness in place of the man, so that the one who remembers may remind the one who forgets, if she forgets. When the condition was put first, it connected to what preceded it, and its apodosis was referred back to it.
Similar to it in speech is your saying: (It pleases me that the beggar asks and is given): what pleases you is the giving if he asks; neither the asking nor the poverty pleases you. Similar to it: "I secured myself with five camels lest a Muslim fall, so that I carry him" — you secured yourself with them only to carry the one who falls, not so that a Muslim should fall. This is evidence of the fronting and postponing.
Similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿ولولا أن تصِيبهم مصيبة بما قدّمت أيديهم فيقولوا ربنا لولا أرسلت إلينا رسولا﴾ — do you not see that the meaning is: were it not that they would say, if a calamity befell them because of what their hands had sent forth: why did You not send us a messenger? This is a clear approach.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُواْ﴾ — to the judge.
﴿إِلاَّ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَارَةً حَاضِرَةً﴾ — it is read in the nominative and the accusative. If you wish, you make ﴿تُدِيرُونَهَا﴾ in the position of the accusative, so that kāna has a nominative and an accusative. And if you wish, you make "تُدِيرُونَهَا" in the position of the nominative. That is because it is permissible with indefinites for their verbs [i.e. predicates/attributes] to follow their nouns; for you say: "If there is a righteous one (aḥadun ṣāliḥun), then it is so-and-so," then you drop (aḥad) and say: "If there is a righteous [one] (ṣāliḥun), then it is so-and-so"; it is not specified, so its attribute was fit to be in place of its noun, since both were unknown. That was not fit with the definite, because the definite is specified and known, and its predicate does not agree with its wording or its meaning. If you say: "Then is it permissible to say: kāna akhūka al-qātilu, putting both in the nominative, because the predicate is definite and the noun is definite, so that they are put in the nominative because of agreement when both are definite, just as they were put in the nominative because of agreement with the indefinite?" I say: that is not permissible, because the attribute of a definite is an indication of it when it is identified, while the attribute of an indefinite is connected to it like the ṣila of alladhī. Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī recited to me:
أفاطمَ إنى هالك فتبيَّنى * ولا تجزعى كُلُّ النساء يئيم
ولا أُنَبأنْ بأنَّ وجهك شانَه * خُمُوشٌ وإن كان الحميم الحميم
(O Fāṭima, I am perishing, so be clear about it, and do not grieve — every woman is widowed; and let me not be told that scratches have marred your face, even if the close kinsman is the close kinsman.)
He put both in the nominative. He put the second ḥamīm in the nominative only because it is an intensification of the first; had al-ḥamīm not been in the speech [a second time], he would have put the first in the nominative [all the same]. Similar to it in speech: "We were nothing when you came to be (ḥīna kunta)," meaning when you became and came; so (kāna) is satisfied with the noun.
Among the indefinites put in the nominative is His saying ﴿وَإِنْ كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ﴾; in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy: "وإن كان ذا عسرة". Both are permissible; when you use the accusative, you imply a noun in kāna, like the poet's saying:
لله قومى أىُّ قوم لحُرَّة * إذا كان يوما ذا كواكب أشنعا!
(To Allah belong my people — what a people for a free woman, when it is a hideous day with stars [visible at noon]!)
And another said:
أعينَىَّ هلاَّ تبكِيان عِفَاقا * إذا كان طعنا بينهم وعِناقا
(O my eyes, will you not weep for ʿIfāq, when it was spearing among them and grappling?)
They needed to imply a noun in (kāna) with the accusative only because the structure of (kāna) is that it have a nominative and an accusative; they found that (kāna) admits a nominative companion, so they implied it as unspecified.
His saying ﴿فإن كُنَّ نساء فوق اثنتين﴾ — here the nouns have been made overt. Had He said: fa-in kāna nisāʾ, the nominative and the accusative would be permissible. Similar to it ﴿إلا أن تكون تجارة عن تراض منكم﴾, and similar to it ﴿إلا أن يكون ميتة أو دما مسفوحا﴾; whoever says (takūna maytatun) [Translator's note: so in the text], both the nominative and the accusative are permissible in it. I said (takūna) because of the femininity of al-mayta. And His saying ﴿إنها إن تك مثقال حبة من خردل﴾ — if you say: al-mithqāl is masculine, so how did He say (taku)? I say: because al-mithqāl is in construct with al-ḥabba, and the meaning is in it, as though He said: if it be a grain. And the poet said:
على قبضة مرجوّة ظهرُ كفّه * فلا المرء مُسْتَحْىٍ ولا هو طاعم
(The back of his palm [is closed] on a hoped-for handful; the man is neither ashamed nor fed.)
because he took it toward the palm [Translator's note: the verse as quoted has no feminine verb; the relevant feminine agreement is evidently in the original context]. Similar to it is the other's saying:
وتَشْرَق بالقول الذى قد أذعته * كما شرِقت صَدْرُ القناة من الدم
(You will choke on the speech you have spread abroad, as the upper part of the spear chokes with blood.)
and his saying:
أبا عُرْوَ لا تبعَدْ فكلُّ ابن حُرَّة * ستدعوه داعى مَوْتة فيجيب
(O Abū ʿUrwa, may you not perish! Every son of a free woman — the caller of a death will call him and he will answer.)
He made the verb of al-dāʿī feminine although it is masculine, because he took it toward al-mawta. And another said:
قد صرَّح السيرُ عن كُتْمانَ وابتُذِلت * وَقْعُ المحاجِن بالمَهْرِيَّة الذُّقُن
(The journey has laid bare [the way] past Kutmān, and the blows of the crooks on the drooping-lipped Mahrī camels have become commonplace.)
He made the verb of al-waqʿ feminine although it is masculine, because he took it toward al-maḥājin.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يُضَآرَّ كَاتِبٌ وَلاَ شَهِيدٌ﴾ — i.e. let a scribe not be summoned while he is busy, nor a witness.

farraa:283-283.t:
His saying: ﴿فَرِهَانٌ مَّقْبُوضَةٌ﴾ — Mujāhid read "فرُهُن" as the plural of rihān, just as He said "كلوا من ثُمُره" as the plural of thimār.
His saying: ﴿وَمَن يَكْتُمْهَا فَإِنَّهُ آثِمٌ قَلْبُهُ﴾ — [some permitted (قلبَه) in the accusative]; if it is correct, it is on the pattern of your saying: "You made your judgement foolish (safihta raʾyaka)" and "you made your heart sinful (athimta qalbaka)."

farraa:285-286.t:
His saying: ﴿غُفْرَانَكَ رَبَّنَا﴾ — a maṣdar (verbal noun) that has occurred in the position of a command, so it is put in the accusative. Similar to it: "The prayer, the prayer (al-ṣalāta al-ṣalāta)!" All nouns, maṣdars and others, are put in the accusative when you intend a command. As for nouns, it is your saying: "Allah, Allah (Allāha Allāha), O people!" Had it been put in the nominative on your saying: "It is Allah," so that it is a statement carrying the interpretation of a command, it would be permissible. One of them recited to me:
إن قوما منهم عُمَير وأشبا * ه عمير ومنهم السفّاح
لجديرون بالوفاء إذا قا * ل أخو النجدة السلاح ُالسلاحُ
(A people among whom are ʿUmayr and the likes of ʿUmayr, and among whom is al-Saffāḥ, are worthy of keeping faith when the man of valour says: "Weapons, weapons!")
Similar to it is that you say: "O you people, the night (al-laylu) — so hasten," meaning: this is the night, so hasten. Whoever puts al-layl in the accusative makes an implied verb before it act on it. Had it been said: ghufrānuka rabbanā (nominative), it would be permissible.
His saying ﴿لاَ يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْساً إِلاَّ وُسْعَهَا﴾.
Al-wusʿ is a noun of the same kind of meaning as al-wujd and al-juhd. Whoever says, for the like of al-wujd, al-wajd, and for the like of al-juhd, al-jahd, would say in similar speech: "lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wasʿahā."
Had it been said: wasʿahā, it would be permissible, but we have not heard it.
His saying ﴿رَبَّنَا وَلاَ تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَآ إِصْراً﴾ — al-iṣr is the covenant; likewise He said in Āl ʿImrān ﴿وأخذتم على ذلكم إصرى﴾. Al-iṣr here is the sin — the sin of the compact when they neglect it — as was made severe upon the Children of Israel.
The Readers have read "فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ مِنَ الله" — He says: then know it yourselves.
And some read: fa-ādhinū, i.e. then make known.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: "فإن لم تجدوا كاتبا فرهان مقبوضة" [Translator's note: he read كِتابًا? the text has كاتبا], and he said: a scribe may be found while the sheet and the inkwell are not found.

farraa:196-196.t:
His saying: ﴿وَأَتِمُّواْ ٱلْحَجَّ وَٱلْعُمْرَةَ للَّهِ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "وأَتِمُّوا الْحَجَّ والْعُمْرَةَ إلى البيت لِلّهِ". Had a reader read "والعمرةُ لله", putting "العمرة" in the nominative [it would be possible], because the one performing ʿUmra, when he comes to the House and circles it and [goes] between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa, is released from his ʿUmra; while in the Ḥajj he comes to ʿArafāt and all the rites. That is His saying ﴿وَأَتِمُّواْ ٱلْحَجَّ وَٱلْعُمْرَةَ للَّهِ﴾; He says: complete the ʿUmra up to the House, and the Ḥajj to the furthest of its rites.
﴿فَإنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ﴾ — the Arabs say of one whom fear or illness prevents from reaching the completion of his Ḥajj or ʿUmra, and of everything in which he is not forcibly constrained as with detention and prison, (it is said of the sick man): "qad uḥṣira" (he has been prevented); and in detention and constraint: "qad ḥuṣira" (he has been confined). This is the difference between them. Had you intended, regarding the constraint of the ruler, that it is a preventing cause, without going towards the act of an agent, you could say: "the man uḥṣira".
And had you said of illness and the like, "the illness — or the fear — has confined him (ḥaṣarahu)", you could say "ḥuṣirtum". And His saying "وسَيِّدا وحصورا" — [it is said] he is the one held back from women, because it is a cause [within him] and he is not detained. So build upon this.
His saying: ﴿فَمَا ٱسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ ٱلْهَدْيِ﴾ — "ما" is in the position of the nominative, because most of what has come of its like in the Qurʾān is nominative.
Had you used the accusative, [it would be] on [the sense of] your saying: offer "ما استيسر" (what is easy).
The explanation of al-hady (offering) in this place is a camel, a cow or a sheep.
﴿فَمَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ﴾ the offering, fasts three days, the last of them being the day of ʿArafa, and the [other] two days within the ten; as for the seven, he fasts them when he returns, on his way, or if he wishes, when he reaches his family. "السبعة" may take the genitive, following "الثلاثة". If you put it in the accusative, it is permissible by a renewed verb, as you say in speech: "lā budda min liqāʾi akhīka wa-Zaydin" and "wa-Zaydan" (one must meet your brother and Zayd).
His saying: ﴿ذٰلِكَ لِمَن لَّمْ يَكُنْ أَهْلُهُ حَاضِرِي ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾ — He says: that is for whoever is among the strangers, not of the people of Mecca; as for the people of Mecca, that is not upon them. "ذلِك" is in the position of the nominative. "على" is fitting in the place of the lām, i.e. that is upon the strangers.
His saying: ﴿الْحَجُّ أَشْهُرٌ مَعْلُومَاتٌ﴾ — its meaning: the time of the Ḥajj is these months. Even though "فى" (in) is fitting in it, it is said only in the nominative; such is the speech of the Arabs: they say "the cold is two months, the heat is two months", and they do not use the accusative, because it is the measure of the Ḥajj. Similar is His saying: ﴿ولِسُلَيْمَانَ الرِّيحَ غُدُوُّهَا شَهْرٌ وَرَوَاحُهَا شَهْرٌ﴾. Had the months, or the month, been known [i.e. definite] in this sense, the accusative would be fitting in it. The normal way of speech is the nominative, because a noun, when it has the sense of a qualifier or of a place, is strengthened [in the accusative] when annexed to something. Do you not see that the Arabs say "huwa rajulun dūnaka" and "huwa rajulun dūnun" (he is a man inferior [to you])? They use the nominative when they use it alone, and the accusative when they annex it. And of their speech: "the Muslims are a side (jānibun), and the unbelievers are a side"; when they say "the Muslims are jāniba ṣāḥibihim" (at the side of their fellow), they use the accusative. That is because "the fellow" indicates a place, as you say "naḥwa ṣāḥibihim" (towards their fellow) and "qurba ṣāḥibihim" (near their fellow); when "the fellow" is dropped, you do not find it a place that you can tie to nearness to something or distance from it.
The known months are Shawwāl, Dhū l-Qaʿda and ten [days] of Dhū l-Ḥijja. The sacred months are al-Muḥarram, Rajab, Dhū l-Qaʿda and Dhū l-Ḥijja. It was only permissible to call them "months" when they are two months and ten [days] of a third, because the Arabs, when the time is for a thing in which the Ḥajj and the like take place, make it in naming for three and two; as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَاذْكُرُوا اللّهَ فِى أَيَّامٍ مَعْدُودَاتٍ فَمَنْ تَعَجَّلَ فِى يَوْمَيْنِ﴾, while he only hastens in a day and a half; and likewise it is on the third day of the days of Tashrīq, and none of them is complete. Likewise the Arabs say: "It is two days today since I have not seen him", while it is only a day and part of another. This is not permissible outside of [such] times, because the Arabs may do an act in less than an hour and then apply it to the day, the year, the nights and the days; it is said "I visited him this year", "I came to you today", "So-and-so was killed in the nights when al-Ḥajjāj was governor", because neither the beginning nor the end of the time is meant, so it is not taken in the sense of the whole number; only (that time) is meant.
As for His saying ﴿فَلاَ رَفَثَ وَلاَ فُسُوقَ وَلاَ جِدَالَ﴾ — it is said that al-rafath is sexual intercourse, al-fusūq is reviling, and al-jidāl is disputing — ﴿فِى الْحَجِّ﴾: the Readers put all of that in the accusative by the [lā of] exculpation (tabriʾa, i.e. the lā of generic negation), except Mujāhid, who put "الرفث" and "الفسوق" in the nominative and "الجدال" in the accusative. All of that is permissible. Whoever uses the accusative makes the end of the speech follow its beginning; and whoever puts some in the nominative and some in the accusative [does so] because the tabriʾa has two aspects: the nominative with nunation, and the accusative without the nunation. Had "الفسوق" and "الجدال" been put in the accusative with nunation, that would be permissible outside the Qurʾān; because the Arabs, when they begin with the tabriʾa and put it in the accusative, do not put it in the accusative with nunation; then when they conjoin to it with "لا", there are two aspects in it: if you wish, you make "لا" suspended (muʿallaqa), [such that] its omission is permissible, and so with this intention you use the accusative with nunation, because "لا" has the sense of a ṣila (filler); and if you intend a fresh start by it, it is like its fellow and not suspended, so you use the accusative without nunation. The poet said about that:
رأت إبلى برمل جَدُودَ أ[نْ] لا * مَقِيلَ لها ولا شِرْباً نَقُوعا
(My camels saw in the sands of Jadūd that there was no midday resting place for them, and no thirst-quenching drink.)
He put nunation on "شرب", intending "لا" to be [as if] omitted; as another said:
فلا أبَ وابنا مِثلَُ مروان وابنِهِ * إذا هو بالمجدِ ارتدى وتأزّرا
(There is no father and son like Marwān and his son, when he dons glory as cloak and wrap.)
In its approach it is like the one addressed in the vocative: you say "yā ʿAmru wa-l-Ṣalta aqbilā" (O ʿAmr and al-Ṣalt, come forward), making "al-Ṣalt" follow ʿAmr while it has the alif and lām, because you intended it to follow him without the intention of "يا" with the alif and lām. If you did intend it, you would say "yā Zaydu wa-yā ayyuhā l-Ṣaltu aqbilā". If you drop "يأيها" while intending it, you use the accusative, as in the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿يَا جِبَالُ أَوِّبِى مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ﴾; "الطير" is accusative in two ways: with the intention of a vocative renewed for it, since calling it with what the mountains were called with was not sound; or, if you wish, you make a verb act upon it: "and We subjected to him the birds", the intention then being upon "We subjected". So in that it is a follower, as in the poet's saying:
ورأيت زوجَكِ فى الوغى * متقلِّدا سيفا ورمحا
(I saw your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear.)
And if you wish, you may put some of the tabriʾa in the nominative and some in the accusative; this is not of the reading of the Readers, but it comes in poems. Umayya said:
فلا لَغْوٌ ولا تأْثِيمَ فِيها * وما فاهوا به لَهُمُ مقيم
(There is no idle talk and no sinful speech in it, and what they utter abides for them.)
And another said:
ذاكم - وجَدِّكم - الصَّغَار بِعينهِ * لا أمَّ لِى إِن كان ذاك ولا أب
(That — by your fortune — is abasement itself; may I have no mother and no father if that should be.)
And before it:
وإِذا تكونُ شدِيدةٌ أُدعَى لها * وإِذا يحاس الحَيْس يدْعى جُنْدب
(When there is a hardship, I am called to it; and when the ḥays [date-and-butter dish] is mixed, Jundab is called.)

farraa:200-200.t:
His saying: ﴿فَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَآءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْراً﴾ — the Arabs, when they performed the Ḥajj in their Jāhiliyya, would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, and each of them would mention his father by his finest deeds: "O Allah, he used to maintain kinship ties and host the guest." So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿فَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَآءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْراً﴾ — for I am the One who did that for you and for them.
His saying: ﴿فَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ رَبَّنَآ آتِنَا فِي ٱلدُّنْيَا﴾ — the people of the Jāhiliyya used to ask for wealth, camels and sheep, so Allah revealed: "of them is one who asks for this world, and he has no خَلاَق in the Hereafter", meaning a share.

farraa:203-203.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ فِيۤ أَيَّامٍ مَّعْدُودَاتٍ﴾ — they are the ten [days]; [and] the known [days] (al-maʿlūmāt) are all the days of Tashrīq: the day of sacrifice and the three days of Tashrīq.
Some of the exegetes make the counted days (al-maʿdūdāt) the days of Tashrīq as well; as for the known days, they make them the day of sacrifice and two of the days of Tashrīq, because the slaughter takes place only on these three days. And some of them make the slaughter [extend] to the last of the days of Tashrīq, so that both "counted" and "known" apply to them, and the ten do not enter into them.
His saying: ﴿لِمَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ﴾ — He says: [whoever guards against] killing game in the Sanctuary. [Translator's note: the text says only "قتل الصيد فى الحرم", "killing game in the Sanctuary"; the bracketed words supply the evident sense.]

farraa:204-204.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيُشْهِدُ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا فِي قَلْبِهِ﴾ — this was a man whose talk pleased the Prophet ﷺ; he would tell him that he was with him and swear to that, saying "(Allah knows)". That is His saying "ويشهِد الله", i.e. he calls Allah to witness. It is also read "ويَشْهَدُ اللّهُ", in the nominative, "على ما فِى قلبِهِ" (and Allah bears witness to what is in his heart). His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ أَلَدُّ ٱلْخِصَامِ﴾ — one says of a man "he is aladd (most contentious)", of a people "ludd", of a woman "laddāʾ", and of women "ludd". The poet said:
اللدُّ أقرانُ الرجالِ اللُدِّ * ثم أُرَدِّى بِهِمُ مَنْ يَرْدِى
(The contentious are the match of contentious men; then with them I bring down whoever would fall.)
And it is said: "You were not aladd, but you have become contentious (ladidta), and you are contentious (taladdu)." When you overcome the man in disputation, (you say: ladadtuhu), so I overcome him (aludduhu) laddan.
The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَيُهْلِكَ الْحَرْثَ وَالنَّسْلَ﴾ — it is accusative. Some of them put "ويهلكُ" in the nominative, not referring it back to "لِيفسِد" but making it referred back to His saying ﴿ومِن الناسِ من يعجِبك قوله...ويهلِك﴾. The first view is better.

farraa:205-205.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ لاَ يُحِبُّ ٱلفَسَادَ﴾ — some of the Arabs say "fasada l-shayʾu fusūdan", like their saying "dhahaba dhuhūban" and "dhahāban", and "kasada kusūdan" and "kasādan".

farraa:208-208.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَتَّبِعُواْ خُطُوَاتِ ٱلشَّيْطَانِ﴾ — i.e. do not follow his traces, for they are disobedience.

farraa:210-210.t: His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلاَّ أَن يَأْتِيَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ مِّنَ ٱلْغَمَامِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ﴾ — nominative, referred back to (الله), blessed and exalted. Some of the people of Medina put it in the genitive, meaning "in canopies of cloud and among the angels". The nominative is better, because in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "هل ينظرون إِلا أن يأتيهم الله والملائكة فى ظللٍ من الغمامِ".

farraa:211-211.t:
His saying: ﴿سَلْ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ — it is not pronounced with hamza anywhere in the Qurʾān, because had it been with hamza it would be "اسْأَل" with an alif. (Its hamza was dropped) only in the imperative specifically, because it occurs very frequently in speech; for that reason its hamza was dropped, as they said "kul" and "khudh" (eat, take): they did not use the hamza in the imperative, but used it in the prohibition and elsewhere. The Arabs may use the hamza in it; but in the Qurʾān it has come without the hamza. Ḥamza al-Zayyāt used to pronounce the hamza in the imperative when the fāʾ or the wāw was in it, as in His saying ﴿واسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الّتِى كُنَّا فِيهَا﴾ and His saying ﴿فاسْأَلِ الّذِينَ يَقْرَءُونَ الْكِتَابَ﴾. I do not like that, because had it been with hamza, the alif would have been written in it, as they wrote it with the alif in His saying ﴿فاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقاً﴾ and ﴿واضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلاً﴾.
His saying: ﴿كَمْ آتَيْنَاهُم﴾ — its meaning: We brought them it [of a sign]. The Arabs say "ataytuka bi-āyatin" (I brought you a sign); when they drop the bāʾ, they say "ātaytuka āyatan", as came in al-Kahf: "آتِنا غداءنا", meaning: bring us our lunch.

farraa:67-67.t:
His words: ﴿أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُواً قَالَ﴾. This [Translator's note: i.e. «قال» without the fāʾ] is frequent in the Qurʾān, and that is because it is an answer whose first part can stand without its last by pausing on it. One says: What did he say to you? And the speaker says: He said such-and-such. So it is as though the fact that a pause is good there allows the fāʾ to be dropped. You see it good at the heads of verses, since they are breaks (fuṣūl); for example: ﴿قال فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّها الْمُرْسَلونَ. قَالُوا إنّا أرْسِلْنا﴾. Yet the fāʾ is also good, as in His words: ﴿فَقَالَ الْملأَ الّذِين كَفَروا﴾. If it were within a single utterance, the Arabs would not drop the fāʾ from it; for example: قُمْتُ ففَعَلْت (I stood up and did): they do not say قمت فعلت, nor قلت قال, but rather قُلْتُ فقال (I said, and he said) and قُمْتُ فقام (I stood up, and he stood up), because these are a sequence (nasaq), not a question on which one pauses. Do you not see: "قال" Pharaoh "لِمَنْ حَوْلَه أَلاَ تَسْتَمِعُونَ. قال رَب‍ُّكم ورَبُّ آبائكم الأوّلين", in more places than I can count? Similar to it, apart from the verb, is frequent in the Book of Allah, with the wāw and without the wāw. As for what is with the wāw, it is His words: ﴿قُلْ أؤُنَبِّئُكُم بِخَيْرٍ مِنْ ذَلِكُمْ لِلّذينَ اتَّقَوْا عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾, then after that He said: ﴿الصّابِرينَ والصّادقينَ والْقَانِتينَ والْمُنفِقينَ والْمُسْتَغْفِرِينَ بالأَسْحاِر﴾. And He said in another place: ﴿التّائِبُونَ الْعَابِدُونَ الْحَامِدُونَ﴾ [Translator's note: i.e. without the wāw]. And He said elsewhere: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِيِنَ فَتَنُوا الْمُؤْمِنينَ والْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾, then in the following verse He said: ﴿إِنّ الّذينَ آمَنُوا﴾, and did not say «وإنّ». So learn from what has gone the explanation of what remains, for it comes only according to what I have told you of breaks, or of self-sufficient speech to which an answer comes. Some Arabs recited to me:
لمّا رأيتُ نَبَطاً أنْصَارَا * شَمَّرتُ عن رُكْبَتِىَ الإزَارَا * كُنْتُ لها مِنَ النَّصارى جَارَا *
(When I saw Nabataeans as helpers, I tucked up my waist-wrapper from my knees — I was, for her, a neighbour from among the Christians.) [Translator's note: the last hemistich follows without a conjunction, which is the point of the citation.]

farraa:68-68.t: His words: ﴿لاَّ فَارِضٌ وَلاَ بِكْرٌ عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذٰلِكَ﴾. «العوان» (middle-aged) is not a naʿt (adjective) of «البكر» (young), because she is neither old nor young: the speech ends at His words ﴿وَلاَ بِكْرٌ﴾, then He begins afresh and says: ﴿عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذٰلِكَ﴾. Of العوان one says: قد عوَّنَت (she has become middle-aged). Of الفارض (old): قد فَرَضَت, and some say: قد فَرُضَت. (As for البكر, we have not) heard a verb for it. البِكر has kasra on its first letter when it is a virgin among women, and البَكْر has fatḥa on its first letter, from the young ones (bikāra) of camels. Then He said "بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ", and "بَيْن" (between) is appropriate only with two nouns or more; it was appropriate with "ذلك" alone only because it carries the sense of two. Two actions [Translator's note: or clauses] may be gathered up by "ذلك" and "ذاك": do you not see that you say: أظنُّ زيدا أخاك (I think Zayd is your brother) and كان زيدٌ أخاك (Zayd was your brother) — «كان» must have two things, and «أظن» must have two things — and then you may say: قد كان ذاك (that was so) and أظنُّ ذلك (I think that)? The meaning in the two nouns that «ذلك» gathers up is: between old age and youth. Had one said in ordinary speech: بَيْنَ هاتَيْن or بين تَيْنِك (between these two / those two), meaning the old one and the young one, it would have been correct. And if they were mentioned again (it would appear only in the dual), because they are two nouns, not two actions; with actions [Translator's note: i.e. verbal nouns] you make what follows them singular: you say: إِقْبالُك وإِدْبارُك يَشُقُّ علىّ (your coming and your going is hard on me), but you do not say: أخوك وأبوك يزورُنِى (your brother and your father visits me). Among the things to which "بَيْن" may apply while being singular in form, standing for two or more, are His words: ﴿لاَنُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ﴾; but one may not say: لا نفرق بين رجل منهم (we make no distinction between a man of them), because «أحد» is not put in the dual as «رجل» is put in the dual and plural. If you wish you take «أحد» as meaning two, and if you wish as meaning more; of that kind is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَمَا مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ عَنْهُ حاجِزِينَ﴾. And you say: بَيْنَ أيِّهِم الْمَالُ؟ (among which of them is the wealth?) and بَيْنَ مَنْ قُسِم المالُ؟ (among whom was the wealth divided?): you treat "مَن" and "أَىّ" like «أحد», because they may stand for one and for many.

farraa:69-69.t:
His words: ﴿ٱدْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوْنُهَا﴾. «اللون» is nominative because you did not intend to make "ما" a ṣila (redundant particle) and say: بيّن لنا ما لونَها (make clear to us its colour) — though had a reader read it so, it would have been correct. Rather He meant — and Allah knows best —: pray to your Lord for us to make clear to us what thing its colour is. It was not appropriate for the verb to fall on «أيّ», because the basis of "أىّ" is the gathering together of a dispersed question: the speaker says: بين لنا أسوداءُ هى أم صَفْراء؟ (make clear to us: is it black or yellow?). Since it is not appropriate for «التبيّن» (making clear) to fall on the question in its dispersed form, it does not fall on «أيّ», because «أيّ» is the gathering up of that dispersed question. The same applies to everything like it in the Qurʾān: let "ما" and "أىّ" be governed by the verb after them, and do not let the verb before them govern them when it is derived from knowledge, as in your saying: ما أعلم أَيُّهم قال ذاك (I do not know which of them said that), لا أعلمنّ أَيُّهم قال ذاك, and ما أدرِى أَيَّهم ضربت (I do not know which of them you struck). In knowing, informing, telling and the like, it is as I have described to you. Of this kind is the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَاهِيَهْ﴾ and ﴿وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ ما يَوْمُ الدَّينِ﴾: the second "ما" is nominative, made nominative by «يوم», as in your saying: ما أدراك أىُّ شئ يومُ الدّين (what will make you know what thing the Day of Judgement is?). Likewise the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ أَىُّ الْحِزْبَيْنِ أَحْصَى﴾: you made it nominative by «أحصى». And when the verb [Translator's note: after it] falls on «أيّ», you say: ما أدرى أَيَّهم ضربت. You refrained from letting the preceding verb of knowledge and the like fall on «أيّ» only because you find that the verb does not fall on «أيّ» in meaning. Do you not see that when you say: اذْهَبْ فاعلم أيُّهما قام (go and find out which of the two stood), you ask someone other than the two about their state, so you find the verb falling on the one who informs you — just as you say: سل أيُّهُمْ قام (ask which of them stood), meaning: ask people which of them stood? If you let the verb fall on "أىّ" and said: اسأل أيَّهُمْ قام, you would be as if implying «أيّ» a second time; because you say: سل زيدا أيُّهُمْ قام (ask Zayd which of them stood): when you let the verb fall on Zayd, "أىّ" comes after it. So likewise, when you let the verb fall on "أىّ", it leaves the meaning of the question; and that, if you intend it, is permissible: you say: لأضْرِبَنَّ أيَّهُم يقول ذاك (I will surely strike whichever of them says that), because striking does not fall on [a noun after which a question then comes; and that is because striking does not fall on] two [Translator's note: objects]. In asking you say: سل عبدالله عن كذا (ask ʿAbd Allāh about such-and-such), as though you said: سله عن كذا (ask him about such-and-such); but one may not say ضربت عبدالله كذا وكذا (I struck ʿAbd Allāh such-and-such), unless you mean a description of the striking; as for nouns, no.

The word of Allah: ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعةٍ أيُّهُم أشَدُّ على الرّحْمَنِ عِتيّاً﴾: whoever puts «أيّ» in the accusative lets «النزع» (plucking out) fall on it, and it is not a question; as though He said: then We shall surely pull out the insolent one who is the most severe. There are two ways of the nominative in it. One is that you make the verb content with «من» as what it falls on, as you say: قد قتلنا من كل قوم (we have killed some of every people) and أصبنا من كل طعام (we have had some of every food); then you begin «أيّ» afresh and make it nominative by what follows it, as He, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿يَبْتَغُونَ إلى رَبِّهِمُ الْوَسِيلَةَ أيُّهُمْ أَقْرَبُ﴾, i.e. they look to see which of them is nearest. Similar to it: ﴿يُلْقُونَ أقْلاَمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ﴾. As for the other way: in His words ﴿ثم لَنَنْزِعَنّ مِنْ كلِّ شِيعَةٍ﴾ [Translator's note: the meaning is] We shall pull out from those who formed factions (tashāyaʿū) over this, looking, in their factionalism, to see which of them is fiercest and most wicked, and which of them is most severe in insolence against the Most Merciful; «الشيعة» and «يتشايعون» are the same in meaning. There is a third way of the nominative: that you take ﴿ثُمّ لَننْزِعَنَّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ﴾ as [Translator's note: pulling out] by calling, i.e. We shall surely call out: ﴿أيُّهُمْ أشدُّ على الرّحْمَنِ عِتيّاً﴾ — but this is not the way they intend. Similar to it, by which you can recognise it, are His words: ﴿أفَلَمْ يَيْأَسِ الَّذِيِنَ آمنَوُا أَنْ لَوْ يَشَاءُ اللَّهُ لهَدَى النَّاس جَميعاً﴾: some commentators said ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَيْأَسِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ means: did they not know? And the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: have they not despaired, knowing that had Allah willed He would have guided all people? Likewise "لَنَنْزِعَنّ": he says it means We shall pull them out by calling.

farraa:71-71.t: His words: ﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ لاَّ شِيَةَ فِيهَا﴾, without hamza. He says: there is no colour in her other than yellow. Some of them said: she is yellow, even her hooves and her horns are yellow.

farraa:72-72.t: His words: ﴿وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْساً فَٱدَّارَأْتُمْ فِيهَا﴾, and His words: ﴿وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسَى أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ and ﴿وَإِذْ فَرَقْنَا بِكُمُ الْبَحْرَ﴾. Someone may say: Where is the answer of "إذ", and to what is it conjoined? There are many like it in the Qurʾān with the wāw and with no overt answer. The meaning — and Allah knows best — rests on implying "واذكروا إذ أنتم" (and remember when you were) or "إذ كنتم"; His saying "اذكروا" at the beginning of the speech sufficed, and then "إذ" came with the wāw, referring back to that. Similar to it, apart from "إذ", is the word of Allah: ﴿وإِلى ثَمُودَ أَخَاهُم صَالحاً﴾: there is nothing before it that you can see governing «صالح» in the accusative; but from the mention of the prophet ﷺ [Translator's note: so in the text, with the blessing formula, referring to Ṣāliḥ] and of those to whom he was sent, it is known that «أرسلنا» (We sent) is implied in it. Similar are His words: ﴿ونُوحاً إِذْ نَادَى مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾, ﴿وذَا النُّونِ إِذْ ذَهَبَ مُغَاضِباً﴾ and ﴿وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ إِذْ قَالَ لِقَوْمِهِ﴾. This runs like what He said in "Ṣād": ﴿وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ وإِسْحَقَِ﴾, then He mentioned the prophets who came after them without "واذكر", because their meaning is agreed and known, so that was permissible. It is shown that "واذكروا" is implied with "إذ" by the fact that He said: ﴿وَاذْكُرُوا إِذْْْْْْْْْْْ أَنْتُمْ قَلِيلٌ مُسْتَضْعَفُونَ فِى الأَرْضِ﴾ and ﴿واذْكُرُوا إِذْ كُنْتُمْ قَلِيلاً فَكَثّرََكُمْ﴾; even if "واذكروا" were not present here, you would infer that it is intended, since it has been mentioned before that. The like of this is not permissible in ordinary speech with the wāw dropped, unless its answer is with it, before or after, as in your saying: ذكرتُك إذ احتجتُ إليك (I remembered you when I needed you) or إذ احتجتُ ذكرتُك (when I needed [Translator's note: you], I remembered you).

farraa:73-73.t: His words: ﴿فَقُلْنَا ٱضْرِبُوهُ بِبَعْضِهَا﴾. It is said that he was struck with the right thigh, and some say: he was struck with the tail. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ﴾; its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: ﴿ٱضْرِبُوهُ بِبَعْضِهَا﴾ and he will come to life; ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ﴾, i.e. take heed and do not deny the Resurrection. "And he will come to life" (فيحيا) is implied, as He said: ﴿أَنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصَاكَ البَحْرَ فانْفَلَقَ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: so he struck the sea and it split.

farraa:74-74.t: His words: ﴿وَإِنَّ مِنَ ٱلْحِجَارَةِ لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهُ ٱلأَنْهَارُ﴾. The masculine of ﴿منه﴾ can be explained in two ways. If you wish, you take it — meaning "منه" — to refer to the fact that the "some" is a stone, which is masculine. And if you wish, you make the "some" plural in meaning and make it masculine following the masculine of «بعض», as you say to women: ضربنى بعضُكنّ (some of you [Translator's note: feminine] struck (ḍarabanī, masculine) me). And if you wish, you could make it feminine here following the feminine of the meaning, as the readers read: "وَمَنْ يَقْنُتْ مِنْكُنَّ لِلَّهِ" and "وَمَنْ تَقْنُتْ", with yāʾ and with tāʾ, according to the meaning; and in the reading of Ubayy it is: "وَإِنَّ مِنَ الْحِجَارَةِ لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهَا الأَنْهَارُ".

farraa:76-76.t: His words: ﴿أَتُحَدِّثُونَهُم بِمَا فَتَحَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: this is from the saying of the Jews to one another, i.e. do not tell the Muslims that you find the description of Muḥammad ﷺ in the Torah while you do not believe in him, so that they would have the argument against you. ﴿أَفَلاَ تَعْقِلُونَ﴾. Allah said: ﴿أَوَلاَ يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ مَا يُسِرُّونَ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ﴾: this is the answer to them, from the word of Allah.

farraa:212-212.t:
His saying: ﴿زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ ٱلْحَيَاةُ ٱلدُّنْيَا﴾ — He did not say "زُيّنت", and that is permissible. The verb was made masculine while the noun is feminine only because [the noun] is derived from a verb, in the manner of a maṣdar (verbal noun). Whoever makes it feminine treats the speech according to the wording, and whoever makes it masculine goes towards the masculinity of the maṣdar. Similar to it are ﴿فَمَنْ جَاءَهُ مَوْعِظَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ فانْتَهَى﴾, ﴿قَدْ جَاءَكُمْ بَصَائِرُ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَأَخَذَ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا الصَّيْحَةُ﴾, according to what I have explained to you.
As for nouns that are primary coinages (al-asmāʾ al-mawḍūʿa), the Arabs hardly ever make the verb of a feminine masculine, except in poetry out of necessity.
A noun may not be formed from a verb and have a sense of femininity while being masculine; then it is permissible to make the verb feminine or masculine, once according to the wording and once according to the meaning. Of that is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿وكذَّبَ بِهِ قَوْمُكَ وَهُوَ الْحَق﴾; He did not say "كَذَّبَتْ", and had it been said, it would be correct, as He said ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ and ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ لُوطٍ﴾, going towards the femininity of "the nation" (al-umma). The like of it in speech, in poetry, is much; of it is the poet's saying:
فإن كِلاباً هذهِ عَشْرُ أَبطنٍ * وأَنت برِئ مِن قبائِلِها العَشْرِ
(Kilāb is these ten clans, and you are quit of its ten tribes.)
He ought to have said "ʿasharatu abṭunin", because "baṭn" (clan) is masculine; but in this place it has the sense of "qabīla" (tribe), so he made it feminine because of the femininity of "qabīla" in meaning. Likewise another's saying:
وقائِع فى مُضَرٍ تِسعة * وفى وائلٍ كانتِ العاشِره
(Battles among Muḍar, nine; and among Wāʾil was the tenth.)
He said "tisʿatun", whereas he ought to have said "tisʿun", because "waqʿa" (battle) is feminine; but he went towards "the days" (al-ayyām), because the Arabs say "the days" in the sense of battles: it is said "he is learned in the days of the Arabs", meaning their battles. As for the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وجُمِعَ الشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ﴾, what is meant by it — and Allah knows best — is: the two lights were brought together. And there is nothing in their saying that the verb of "the sun" was made masculine only because stopping [at it] is not good in "the sun" until the moon is with it; had it been as was said, they would have said "the sun was brought together, and the moon". The like of this is not permissible. And if you wish, you make it masculine because "the sun" is a feminine noun with no hāʾ in it indicating femininity, and the Arabs sometimes make the verb of a feminine masculine when the signs of femininity are absent from it. Al-Farrāʾ said: one of them recited to me:
فهِى أَحوى مِن الربعِىّ خاذِلة * والعَين بالإثمد الحارِىّ مكحول
(She is a dark-lipped [gazelle] of the spring-born, lagging behind [her herd], the eye kohl-lined (makḥūl) with Ḥīran antimony.)
He did not say "makḥūla", although "the eye" is feminine, for the reason I have told you. He said: one of them recited to me:
فلا مُزْنَةٌ وَدَقَتْ وَدْقَها * ولا أَرضَ أَبْقَل إبقالها
(No rain cloud poured down its downpour, and no land put forth (abqala) its herbage as she did.)
He said: Yūnus — meaning the Basran grammarian — recited to me from the Arabs the saying of al-Aʿshā:
إِلى رجلٍ مِنهم أَسِيفٍ كأنما * يضمّ إلى كَشْحَيهِ كفَّا مخضبا
(To a grieving man among them, as if he were pressing to his flanks a hennaed (mukhaḍḍaban) palm.)
As for His saying: ﴿السَّمَاءُ مُنْفَطِرٌ بِهِ﴾, if you wish you may make "the sky" feminine like "the eye": since there is no hāʾ in it of the kind that indicates femininity, its verb [predicate] was made masculine, as was done with "the eye" and "the land" in the two verses.
Some of the Arabs make "the sky" masculine, because it is a collective, as if its singular were samāwa or samāʾa. He said: one of them recited to me:
فلو رَفَع السماءُ إليهِ قوما * لحِقنا بالسماءِ مع السحابِ
(Had the sky raised (rafaʿa) a people up to it, we would have joined the sky along with the clouds.)
If someone says: "What about the verb when it comes after feminine maṣdars — may it be made masculine after the nouns as it may before them?" I say: that is ugly, yet permissible. It is ugly only because when the verb comes after the noun, it contains a pronoun standing for the noun, and they considered it ugly to imply a masculine [pronoun] preceded by a feminine. Those who allowed it said: it is taken according to the meaning, and it is the same whether put before or after. The poet said:
فإن تعهدِى لامرِئ لِمَّةَ * فإن الحوادِث أَزْرَى بِها
(If you once knew a man to have a full head of hair — the vicissitudes (al-ḥawādith) have disgraced (azrā) it.)
He did not say "azrayna bihā" nor "azrat bihā". "Al-ḥawādith" is a plural, but he took it in the sense of "al-ḥadathān" (the vicissitude of time). Likewise another said:
هنِيئا لِسعدٍ ما اقتضى بعد وقعتِى * بِناقةِ سعدٍ والعشِيَّةُ باردُ
(Enjoy, Saʿd, what you exacted after my fall from Saʿd's she-camel, while the evening (al-ʿashiyya) was cold (bāridun).)
As if "al-ʿashiyya" had the sense of "al-ʿashiyy"; do you not see the saying of Allah ﴿أَنْ سَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيّاً﴾? Another said:
إن السماحة والشجاعة ضُمِّنا * قبرا بِمَرْوَ على الطرِيقِ الواضح
(Generosity and courage have been placed (ḍummina) in a grave at Marw, upon the clear road.)
He did not say "ḍumminatā", although "al-samāḥa" and "al-shajāʿa" are feminine because of the hāʾ in them. He said: "Then is it permissible to take 'al-ḥadathān' in the sense of 'al-ḥawādith' and make its verb feminine before it, saying 'ahlakatnā l-ḥadathānu'?" I said: Yes; al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
ألا هَلَك الشِهاب المستنير * ومِدْرَهُنا الكَمىُّ إذا نغِير
وحَمَّال المئِين إذا ألمّت * بنا الحَدَثانُ والأَنفِ النَصُور
(Lo, the shining meteor has perished — our spokesman, the armoured warrior when we raid, the bearer of hundreds [in blood-money] when the vicissitudes (al-ḥadathān) befell (alammat) us, the proud one who brings victory.)
This suffices of what is needed of this kind.
As for His saying: ﴿وإِنّ لكم فِى الأنعامِ لعِبرة نسقِيكم مِما فِى بطونِهِ﴾ — He did not say "بطونِها" although "الأَنْعَامِ" is feminine, because He took it in the sense of "النَّعَم" (livestock), and "النَّعَم" is masculine. It was permissible to take it in the sense of its singular only because the singular comes in meaning in the sense of the plural, as the poet said:
إذا رأيت أنْجُما مِن الأَسَدْ * جَبْهتَهُ أو الخَرَاتَ والكَتَدْ
بال سُهَيلٌ فى الفَضِيخِ ففسدْ * وطاب أَلبانُ الِلقاحِ فبردْ
(When you see stars of Leo — its forehead, or al-Kharāt and al-Katad — Canopus has made water in the date-wine so it spoiled, and the milks (albān) of the milch-camels became good and it (barad) grew cool.)
Do you not see that "laban" (milk) is a collective that suffices for "albān"? Al-Kisāʾī used to take the masculine of "الأَنْعَامِ" along the lines of the poet's saying:
ولا تَذْهَبْن عيناكِ فى كل شَرْمَح * طُوَالٍ فإن الأقصرين أمازِرُهْ
(Let your eyes not be carried away by every tall, lanky man, for the shorter ones are the more vigorous of him.)
He did not say "amāziruhum", but used the masculine while meaning "the more vigorous of what we mentioned". [Al-Farrāʾ replies:] Were that so, it would be permissible to say "huwa aḥsanukum wa-ajmaluhu" (he is the best of you and the most handsome of him); rather, he took it that this kind [of construction] appears with an unspecified indefinite in which something like the sense of the indefinite is implied. For that reason the Arabs said "huwa aḥsanu l-rajulayni wa-ajmaluhu" (he is the better of the two men and the more handsome of him), because a singular pronoun suits the meaning of the speech: you could say "he is the best man among the two". Likewise your saying "hiya aḥsanu l-nisāʾi wa-ajmaluhu": whoever said "wa-ajmaluhu" [meant] the most beautiful thing among women, and whoever said "wa-ajmaluhunna" treated it according to the wording. He [al-Kisāʾī] adduced the poet's saying:
* مثل الفِراخ نَتَقَتْ حواصله *
(Like the chicks whose crops (ḥawāṣiluhu) have swollen.)
He did not say "ḥawāṣiluhā". He made it masculine only because "al-firākh" (chicks) is a plural not built on its singular, so it was permissible to take the plural in the sense of the singular. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-Mufaḍḍal recited to me:
ألا إن جيرانى العشيةَ رائح * دعتهم دواعٍ من هوى ومنازِحُ
(Lo, my neighbours this evening are departing (rāʾiḥ); callers of love and far-off places have called them.)
He said "rāʾiḥ" and did not say "rāʾiḥūn", because "al-jīrān" (neighbours) has been treated as a singular collective, since its plural is not built on its singular.
Had you said "al-ṣāliḥūn" [in such a construction], that would not be permissible, because its plural is built on the form of its singular. Likewise with "al-ṣāliḥāt" we say that is not permissible, because with the form of the singular [kept] in the plural, the notion of singularity has left it. Do you not see that the Arabs say "ʿindī ʿishrūna ṣāliḥūna" (I have twenty righteous ones), using the nominative, and say "ʿindī ʿishrūna jiyādan" (I have twenty fine horses), putting "jiyād" in the accusative, because it is not built on its singular, so it is taken in the sense of the singular; and that is not done with "al-ṣāliḥīn". ʿAntara said:
فيها اثنتانِ وأربعون حَلُوبةً * سُوداً كخافِيةِ العرابِ الأسحمِ
(Among them are forty-two milch-camels, black (sūdan) as the inner wing-feathers of the jet-black raven.)
He said "sūdan" and did not say "sūdun", while it is a naʿt (adjective) of "the forty-two", for the reason I have told you. Some of the Readers read "زَيَّن لِلذِين كفروا الحياةَ الدنيا", and it is said that it is Mujāhid alone.

farraa:78-78.t: His words: ﴿لاَ يَعْلَمُونَ ٱلْكِتَابَ إِلاَّ أَمَانِيَّ وَإِنْ هُمْ﴾. «الأماني» has two aspects in meaning and two in Arabic. As for Arabic, some Arabs lighten the yāʾ and say: "إِلاَّ أَمَانِىَ وَإِنْ هُمْ", and some double it, which is the better of the two. Likewise whatever is like أمنيّة, أضحيّة and أغنيّة has two ways in its plural: lightening and doubling. You double it only because you intend the pattern afāʿīl, so it is doubled through the combination of the yāʾ of the plural pattern with the original yāʾ; and if you lighten it, you drop the yāʾ of the plural and lighten the original yāʾ. It is as one says القَراقير and القَراقر (ships): (whoever says الأمانِىَ, lightened,) is the one who says القراقِر, and whoever doubles الأماني is the one who says القراقير. In meaning, al-umniyya is recitation, as in the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إِلاَّ إِذَا تَمَنَّى أَلْقَى الشَّيْطَانُ فى أُمْنِيَّتِهِ﴾, i.e. in his recitation. Al-amānī is also a man's fabricating fabricated reports: one of the Arabs said to Ibn Daʾb while he was narrating to people: "Is this something you have transmitted, or something you have tamannaytahu?" meaning: fabricated. They were reports they heard from their elders, not from the Book of Allah. This is the clearer of the two aspects.

farraa:80-80.t: His words: ﴿إِلاَّ أَيَّاماً مَّعْدُودَةً﴾. It may be asked: How is it permissible in speech to say: لآتينك أياما معدودة (I will come to you for a counted number of days), without stating their number? That is because they had in mind the days in which they worshipped the calf, and said: We shall not be punished in the Fire except for those forty nights in which we worshipped the calf. Since its meaning was a fixed, known period for them, they described it as «معدودة» and «معدودات» (counted). So Allah said: Say, O Muḥammad: Do you have a covenant from Allah for this that you have said, ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مَا لاَ تَعْلَمُونََ﴾.

farraa:81-81.t: His words: ﴿بَلَىٰ مَن كَسَبَ سَيِّئَةً﴾. ﴿بَلَى﴾ was established for every affirmation [Translator's note: replying to speech] that has a negation (jaḥd) at its beginning, and "نَعَم" was established for a question that contains no negation. So "بلى" is like "نَعَمْ" (yes), except that it is used only for what has a negation at its beginning. Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿فَهَلْ وَجَدْتُمْ مَا وَعَدَ رَبُّكُمْ حقاً قَالُوا نَعَمْ﴾: "بلى" is not appropriate in this place. As for negation, it is His words: ﴿أَلَمْ يَِِِأتِِكُمْ نَذِيرٌ. قَالُوا بَلَى قَدْ جَاءَنَا نَذِيرٌ﴾: the particle "نَعَمْ" is not appropriate here. That is because a question requires an answer with "نَعَمْ" or "لا" as long as it contains no negation; but when negation enters the question, it is not right to say "نَعَمْ" to it, for you would be as if affirming the negation along with the verb after it. Do you not see that if someone said to you: أما لك مالٌ؟ (do you not have wealth?), and you said "نعم", you would be affirming the statement with only the question removed, as though you said: «نعم مالى مالٌ» ("Yes, I have no wealth")? So they wanted to turn back from the negation and affirm what follows it, and they chose "بَلَى", because its origin was a pure turning back from negation, as when they said: ما قال عبدالله بل زيدٌ (ʿAbd Allāh did not say [Translator's note: it], rather Zayd). "بَلْ" was a word of conjunction and retraction on which one cannot pause, so they added an alif to it on which one can pause, and it became a retraction from the negation only and an affirmation of the verb after the negation. So they said "بلى", and it indicated the meaning of affirmation and of "yes", while the form "بل" indicated retraction from negation only.

farraa:83-83.t:
His words: ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ لاَ تَعْبُدُونَ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهَ﴾. ﴿تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ is nominative because "أَنْ" could properly enter it; when the particle governing the accusative was dropped, it became nominative, as Allah said: ﴿أَفَغَيْرَ اللّهِ تَأْمُرُونِّى أَعْبُدُ﴾ (he recited the verse), and as He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾, which in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh is "وَلاَتَمْنُنْ أَنْ تَسْتَكْثِر". This is one way of the nominative: since you did not bring the governing particle, you used the nominative. In the reading of Ubayy: "وإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثاَقَ بَنِى إِسْرائيلَ لاَ تَعْبُدُوا", whose meaning is the jussive of prohibition, and it is not the answer to an oath. Do you not see that He said: ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيِثَاقَكُم ورَفَعْنا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ خُذُوا ما آتَيْناكُمْ بِقُوّةٍ﴾ — so they were commanded, and a command cannot be the answer to an oath: one cannot say in speech: واللّهِ قُمْ (by Allah, stand!), nor: والله لا تَقُمْ (by Allah, do not stand!)? It is indicated that it is a prohibition and jussive by the fact that He said: ﴿وَقُولُوا لِلنّاَسِ حُسْناً﴾, as you say: "do, and do not do", or "do not do, and do". And if you wish, you make ﴿لاَتَعْبُدُونَ﴾ the answer to the oath, since the taking of a covenant is an oath; so you say: لا يعبدون (they will not worship) and لا تعبدون (you will not worship), and the meaning is the same. It is permissible to say لا يعبدون and لا تعبدون though they are absent only as He said: ﴿قُلْ لِلّذينَ كَفَرُوا سَيُغْلَبُونَ﴾ and "سَتُغْلَبُونَ", with yāʾ and tāʾ: "سَيُغْلَبُونَ" with yāʾ following the wording of absence, and with tāʾ following the meaning, because when he comes to them or meets them they become the ones addressed. Likewise your saying: استحلفتُ عبدَالله ليقومنّ (I made ʿAbd Allāh swear that he would stand), because he is absent, and استحلفتُه لتقومنّ (I made him swear: "you will stand"), (because) I had addressed him. In this it is also permissible to say: استحلفتُ عبدالله لأقومَنّ (I made ʿAbd Allāh swear: "I will stand"), i.e. I said to him: Swear, "I will stand", as in your saying: قُلْ لأقومَنّ (say: "I will stand"). So when you say استحلفتُ and make your verb fall on someone made to swear, his verb may be with yāʾ, tāʾ or alif; but when he is the one swearing and there is no one made to swear with him, it is with yāʾ and with alif, not with tāʾ. For example: حَلَف عبدُالله ليقومنّ فلم يَقُمْ (ʿAbd Allāh swore he would stand, but he did not stand), and حَلَف عبدالله لأقومَنّ (ʿAbd Allāh swore: "I will stand"), because it is like your saying: قال لأقومَنّ (he said: "I will stand"). It is not permissible with tāʾ, because he cannot be addressing himself, since the tāʾ is only for a man you are addressing; and since there is no one made to swear, the address falls away.

His words: ﴿قَالُوا تَقَاسَمُوا بِاللّهِ لَنُبَيِّنَنَّهُ وأَهْلَهُ﴾ [Translator's note: «لَنُبَيِّنَنَّهُ» as printed; the verse (al-Naml 27:49) reads «لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ»]: there are three readings in it: "لَتُبَيِّتُنَّهُ", "لَيُبَيِّتُنَّهُ" and "لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ", with tāʾ, yāʾ and nūn — when you take "تَقَاسَمُوا" as a past verb (faʿalū). But when you put it in the position of the jussive [Translator's note: i.e. as an imperative], you say: تقاسموا لتبيتنُه and لنبيتنَه, and it is not permissible with yāʾ. Do you not see that you say to a man: احلِفْ لتقومَنّ (swear that you will stand) or احلف لأقومنّ (swear: "I will stand"), as you say: قل لأقومنّ; but you may not say to a man: احلِف ليقومنّ, for it would become as though it were about someone else? This is what there is to say about oaths.

farraa:85-85.t:
His words: ﴿وَهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكُمْ إِخْرَاجُهُمْ﴾. If you wish, you make ﴿هُوَ﴾ a pronoun (kināya) referring to the expelling [Translator's note: in] ﴿وَتُخْرِجُونَ فَرِيقاً مِّنْكُمْ مِّن دِيَارِهِمْ﴾, i.e. "and it is forbidden to you", meaning: their expulsion is forbidden to you; then He repeated «الإخراج» once more as a repetition (takrīr) of "هو", since (words intervened between «الإخراج» and "هو"); so «الإخراج» is nominative by repetition of "هو". And if you wish, you make "هو" an ʿimād [Translator's note: the Kufan term for what the Basrans call ḍamīr al-faṣl/al-shaʾn] and make «الإخراج» nominative by «محرّم» [Translator's note: printed «بمجرم», evidently for «بمحرّم»], as Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿وَمَا هُوَ بِمُزَحْزِحِهِ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ أنْ يُعَمَّرَ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: long life will not remove him from the punishment. If you say: The Arabs put the ʿimād only with verbs of supposing (ẓann), because they govern the accusative; with "كان" and "ليس", because they govern the nominative; and with "إنّ" and its sisters, because they govern the accusative; and it is not fitting for the wāw, which governs neither the accusative, nor the nominative, nor the genitive, to have an ʿimād — I say: The ʿimād was not established for the sake of the accusative, the nominative or the genitive; it was established in every place where the noun is placed first, before the verb. So when you see the wāw in a place where it seeks a noun rather than a verb, the ʿimād is appropriate there; as in your saying: أتيت زيدا وأبوه قائم (I came to Zayd while his father was standing): it is ugly to say: أتيت زيدا وقائم أبوه, or أتيت زيدا ويقوم أبوه, because the wāw seeks «الأب»; so when you began with the verb, while the wāw seeks only a noun, they introduced "هو" for it, because it is a noun. Al-Farrāʾ said: I heard one of the Arabs say: كان مرّة وهو ينفع النّاسَ أحسابُهم (there was a time when people's noble lineage was of benefit to them). And one of the Arabs recited to me:
فأَبلِغْ أبا يَحيى إذا ما لَقِيتَهُ * على العِيسِ فى آباطِها عَرَقٌ يَبْسُ
بِأنّ السُّلاَمِىَّ الذى بِضَريَّةٍ * أَمِيرَ الحِمَى قَدْ باعَ حَقّى بَنِى عَبْسِ
بِثَوْبٍ ودِينارٍ وشاةٍ ودِرهمٍ * فهَلْ هو مَرْفوعٌ بما هْا هنا رَأْسُ
(Convey to Abū Yaḥyā, when you meet him on the white camels with dried sweat in their armpits, that al-Sulāmī who is at Ḍariyya, the governor of the protected pasture, has sold my right to the Banū ʿAbs for a garment, a dinar, a sheep and a dirham — so is any head here raised by that?)
He put the ʿimād with "هَلْ", though it governs neither the nominative nor the accusative, because «هل» seeks nouns more than it seeks a verb. He said: Likewise "ما" and "أمّا": you say: ماهو بذاهب أحدٌ (no one is going), and أمّا هو فذاهبٌ زيد (as for [Translator's note: it], Zayd is going), because أمّا ذاهب فزيد is ugly.

farraa:88-88.t: His words: ﴿فَقَلِيلاً مَّا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾. Someone may ask: Did they have little faith or much? There are two ways in it in Arabic. One: that they did not believe at all, neither little nor much. Similar to it, among the things the Arabs say using "little" to negate the action altogether, is their saying: قَلَّ ما رأيتُ مثلَ هذا قَطّ (rarely have I ever seen the like of this). Al-Kisāʾī reported from the Arabs: مررتُ بِبلادٍ قَلَّ ما تُنبت إلاّ البصلَ والكرّاث (I passed through a land that rarely grows anything but onions and leeks), i.e. it grows nothing but these two. Likewise the Arabs' saying: ما أكاد أَبرحُ منزلى (I hardly leave my home), when he does not leave it — though it may be that he leaves it a little. The other way: that they believed in something a little and disbelieved in everything besides it — in the Prophet ﷺ — and so they are unbelievers. That is because it is said to them: Who created you? Who provides for you? And they say: Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He; yet they disbelieve in everything besides it: in the Prophet ﷺ and in the signs of Allah. That is His words: ﴿قَلِيلاً مَا يُؤْمنُونَ﴾. Likewise the commentators explained the word of Allah: ﴿وَمَا يُؤْمِنُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ باللّهِ إلاَّ وَهُمْ مُشْرِكُونَ﴾ according to this interpretation.

farraa:89-89.t:
His words: ﴿وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمْ كِتَابٌ مِّنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٌ﴾. [If you wish,] you put «المصدّق» in the nominative, intending it as a naʿt (adjective) of «الكتاب», since it is indefinite. Had you put it in the accusative, making «المصدّق» a fiʿl [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term here for the ḥāl (circumstantial)] of «الكتاب», it would have been correct. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh in Āl ʿImrān: "ثُمَّ جاءكم رَسُولٌ مُصَدِّقاً", making it a fiʿl. When the indefinite has been joined to something other than its adjective and then the adjective comes, the accusative as fiʿl is more firmly established than when the indefinite is not so joined. That is because what is joined to the indefinite becomes like something that specifies (muwaqqita) it: do you not see that when you say: مررتُ برجل فى دارك (I passed by a man in your house) or بعبدٍ لك فى دارك (by a slave of yours in your house), it is as though you said: بعبدك (by your slave) or بسايس دابّتك (by your animal's groom)? Measure by this. One of the poets said:
لو كان حَىٌّ ناجياً لَنجَا * مِنْ يومِهِ المُزَلَّمُ الأَعْصَمْ
(If any living thing were to escape, the white-legged mountain goat with its dewlaps would escape its day [Translator's note: of death].)
He used the accusative [Translator's note: «ناجياً»] without joining the indefinite to anything, and that is permissible. As for His words: ﴿وَهَذا كِتابٌ مُصَدِّقٌ لِسَاناً عَرَبِيّاً﴾, the accusative of «اللسان» can be explained in two ways. One is that you imply something on which «المصدّق» falls, as though you said: and this confirms the Torah and the Gospel ﴿لِساناً عربيّاً﴾ (as an Arabic tongue) — (because the Torah and the Gospel were not Arabic) — so «اللسان العربي» became a tafsīr (specification). The other way is according to what I explained to you: since you joined «الكتاب» to «المصدّق», you detached "لساناً" from the pronoun in "مُصَدّق" referring back to [Translator's note: the Book]. Had «اللسان» been nominative, it would have been correct, as an adjective, even though it is distant.

His words: ﴿فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمْ مَّا عَرَفُواْ كَفَرُواْ بِهِ﴾, preceded by "وَلَمَّا". The first has no answer [Translator's note: of its own]; the answer of the first became, as it were, in the fāʾ of the second, and ﴿كَفَرُواْ بِهِ﴾ sufficed as the answer to both together. Similar to it in ordinary speech: ما هو إلاّ أنْ أتانى عبدالله فلما قَعدَ أوسعتُ له وأكرمتُه (no sooner had ʿAbd Allāh come to me, and when he sat down, than I made room for him and honoured him). Similar too are His words: ﴿فإمّا يَأتيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّى هُدىً فَمَنْ تَبِعَ هُدَاىْ﴾ in al-Baqara and ﴿فَمَنِ اتَّبَعَ هُدَاىَ﴾ in Ṭā Hā: one answer sufficed for both together — ﴿فَلاَ خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ in al-Baqara and ﴿فَلاَ يَضِلُّ وَلاَ يَشْقَى﴾ in Ṭā Hā. The fāʾ in His words ﴿فَمَنْ تَبِعَ﴾ became as though it were the answer of "إمّا": do you not see that the wāw is not appropriate in place of the fāʾ? That is proof that the fāʾ is an answer and not a sequential conjunction (nasaq).

farraa:90-90.t:
His words: ﴿بِئْسَمَا ٱشْتَرَوْاْ بِهِ أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾: its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: [Translator's note: for which] they sold themselves. The Arabs have two usages for شَرَوْا and اشْتَرَوْا. The more common is that شَرَوْا means "they sold" and اشتروا means "they bought"; but sometimes they make both mean "they sold". Likewise البيع: one says بعت الثوب (I sold the garment), meaning I let it go out of my hand, and بعته meaning I bought it; this is the dialect of Tamīm and Rabīʿa. I heard Abū Tharwān say to a man: بِعْ لى تمرا بدرهم (sell [Translator's note: i.e. buy] me dates for a dirham), meaning: buy for me. And someone of Rabīʿa recited to me:
ويأْتِيكَ بالأَخْبارِ مَنْ لَم تَبِعْ لَهُ * بَتَاتاً ولم تَضْرِبْ له وقْتَ مَوْعِدِ
(And the news will be brought to you by one for whom you did not buy provisions, nor set him the time of an appointment.)
In the sense "you did not buy provisions for him". Al-Farrāʾ said: al-batāt is travel provisions. His words: ﴿بِئْسَمَا ٱشْتَرَوْاْ بِهِ أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ — "أَنْ يَكْفُروا" is in the position of the genitive or of the nominative. As for the genitive, you refer it back to the hāʾ in "به" by repetition (takrīr), [Translator's note: making it] two statements, as though you said: they sold themselves for unbelief. As for the nominative, it is also a repetition, of the position of the "ما" that follows "بِئس". It cannot be nominative after the pattern of your saying بئس الرجل عبدالله (wretched is the man ʿAbd Allāh), though al-Kisāʾī used to say that. Al-Farrāʾ said: «بئس» is not directly followed by a specified (muwaqqat) nominative nor by a specified accusative. It has two ways. When you join it to an indefinite that could become definite by acquiring alif and lām, you put that indefinite in the accusative, as in your saying: بِئس رجلاً عمرو (a wretched man is ʿAmr) and نِعم رجلاً عمرو (an excellent man is ʿAmr). When you put a definite directly after it, let it be unspecified, in the manner of the indefinite: do you not see that you use the nominative and say: نِعم الرجلُ عمرو and بِئس الرجلُ عمرو? If you annex the indefinite to an indefinite, you use the nominative or the accusative, as in your saying: نِعم غلامُ سفر زيدٌ and غلامَ سفر زيدٌ (an excellent travel-servant is Zayd). And if you annex something to a definite, you use the nominative and say: نِعم سائسُ الخيل زيدٌ (an excellent groom of the horses is Zayd), and the accusative is not permissible unless a poet is forced to it, because when they annexed to an indefinite they used the nominative, so when they annex to a definite they are all the more unlikely to use the accusative. And when you put directly after نِعم and بِئس an indefinite that can never be definite, such as "مثْل" and "أَى", the speech is corrupt: it is wrong to say نِعْمَ مِثْلُك زيدٌ or نعم أَىُّ رجل زيد, because these two cannot serve as specification (mufassir). Do you not see that you do not say: [لله] دَرُّك مِن أىّ رجل, as you say: لِلّه دَرُّك مِن رجل (how excellent you are as a man!)? Nor is it right to put "الذى", "مَنْ" or "ما" directly after نِعْم and بِئْسَ, unless you intend them to be self-sufficient, without a nominative noun coming after that. An example is your saying: بِئسما صنعت (wretched is what you did): this is self-sufficient; and ساء ما صنعت (evil is what you did). But one may not say: ساء ما صنيعك. Al-Kisāʾī allowed it in his book on this approach. Al-Farrāʾ said: We do not know what his reasoning is. He [Translator's note: al-Kisāʾī] said: The Arabs wanted to make "ما" like «الرجل», a complete word, and then they implied "ما" for «صنعت», as though he said: بئسما ما صنعت. This is his view, and I allow it. When you make "نِعْمَ" (a ṣila with «ما») like your saying "كُلّما" and "إنّما", it becomes like "حَبّذَا", and you put nouns in the nominative by it; of that kind is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إِنْ تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقَاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِىَ﴾: you made "هِىَ" nominative by "نِعِمَّا". There is no feminine and no dual in "نِعم" when you make "ما" a ṣila to it, so "ما" with "نِعم" becomes like "ذا" in "حَبّذَا": do you not see that "حبذا" takes neither feminine nor plural? But had you made "ما" a filler (ḥashw), as you say: عما قليلٍ آتيك (in a little while I will come to you), the feminine and the plural would be permissible in it, and you would say: بئسما رجلين أنتما (wretched men are you two) and بئست ما جاريةً جاريتُك (a wretched slave-girl is your slave-girl). I have heard the Arabs say, with "نِعم" made self-sufficient by «ما»: بئسما تزويجٌ ولا مهر (wretched is a marriage with no dowry), putting «التزويج» in the nominative by "بئسما".

His words: ﴿بَغْياً أَن يُنَزِّلُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾: the position of "أنْ" is that of a conditional (jazāʾ). Al-Kisāʾī used to say of "أنْ" that it is in the position of the genitive; but it is only a conditional. When nothing preceding the conditional falls on it (and) it is intended for the future, you give "إنْ" a kasra and use the jussive with it, saying: أكرمك إنْ تَأتنِى (I will honour you if you come to me). If it is past, you say: أكرمك أن تَأتِيَنى (I honour you because you come to me), and clearer than that is to say: أكرمك أنْ أتَيْتَنى (I honour you because you came to me). So the poet said:
أتَجْزَعُ أنْ بَانَ الخَلِيطُ المُوَدّعُ * وحَبْلُ الصَّفَا مِنْ عَزَّةَ المُتَقَطِّعُ
(Are you distressed that the departing companions have parted, and that the bond of pure love with ʿAzza is cut?)
He means: are you distressed by the fact that, or because, that happened? Had he meant the future and a pure conditional, he would have given "إنْ" a kasra and used the jussive with it, as in the word of Allah, Majestic is His praise: ﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نفْسَكَ على آثارِهِمْ إنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾, which the readers read with kasra; and had it been read with fatḥa on "أن", in the sense [since they did not believe], and "because they did not believe", and "from the fact that they did not believe", [it would have been correct]. The interpretation of "أن" is that it is in the position of the accusative, because it was only a particle like "إذْ"; so it is in the position of the accusative when you drop the genitive-governing preposition and what precedes it is complete. But when you give it a verb, or make a verb fall on it, or bring a preposition for it, it is in the position of whatever nominative, accusative or genitive affects it.

His words: ﴿فَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٍ﴾: (بَاءُوا) is not used alone until it is joined with the bāʾ. One says: باءَ بإثم يَبُوءُ بَوْءاً (he incurred a sin).

His words ﴿بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٍ﴾ [Translator's note: mean] that Allah was angry with the Jews for their saying: ﴿يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾; then He was angry with them for denying Muḥammad ﷺ when he entered Medina. That is His words: ﴿فَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٍ﴾.
